_README: Approach variants — PICKET RANGE and WASHINGTON PASS, Washington, 2026-08-19. 88 routes, 94 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name, and the merge script
re-checks all 88 against the live rows before writing. That matters more in this batch than usual: 25 of the 88 ids
carry no peak name at all (wa_south_face_5 is INSPIRATION PEAK, wa_east_ridge_4 is also Inspiration, wa_south_ridge_2 is
LUNA, wa_south_ridge_3 is BLACK PEAK, wa_north_ridge_2 is WHATCOM, wa_north_ridge_3 is CUTTHROAT, wa_east_ridge_3 is
SILVER STAR, wa_south_face_4 and wa_northwest_face_2 are KANGAROO TEMPLE, wa_south_face_2 is PERNOD, wa_south_face_center
is CONCORD TOWER, wa_the_west_face is NORTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE, and so on). One id is actively wrong about its peak:
wa_mount_fury_east_mongo_ridge is filed under wa_mount_fury_WEST, which is correct — Mongo Ridge is West Fury's Southwest
Buttress. A name-shaped id is not evidence of which peak you are on.
SCOPE: the 33 peaks named in the request, plus Frenzel Spitz and both McMillan Spires as separate area rows.
109 routes in those areas had an EMPTY approach_variants; 88 are written here and 21 were deliberately skipped — see _SKIPPED.
Nothing outside those areas was touched, and no route that already carries approach_variants was touched.
The Cascade Pass / Eldorado cluster was left alone.
WHAT MAKES THIS PAIR OF CLUSTERS DIFFERENT FROM EARLIER BATCHES, and it shaped how the baseFindings are written:
WASHINGTON PASS is the densest per-route base-finding problem in the catalog so far. Two trailheads about 2.5 road
miles apart on opposite sides of the pass — the BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD to the west and the HAIRPIN POND PULLOUT to the
east — serve the same summits from opposite sides, and the FIRST thing several entries here test is which car you are
standing at. On Liberty Bell's East Face, seven routes start within a couple of hundred feet of each other along one
talus base, and the rows themselves admit it ('verify you're at the correct start, since several route lines begin
within a short distance of each other'). That admission is not a base finding, so the ordering was researched and is
now written into every one of those seven entries as the same left-to-right sequence, each stated from that route's
own point of view: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft LEFT of Liberty Crack (the only line left of it), LIBERTY CRACK,
FREEDOM OR DEATH on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, THIN RED LINE, LIBERTY AND INJUSTICE FOR ALL 10 m
right of that, LIVE FREE OR DIE, and THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE at the far right or north edge under the red Baer Ceiling
roof. Similar per-route offsets are written for the four South Early Winters Spire west-side lines (the chockstone
chimney, then 20 ft downhill on bolts, 40 ft down-and-right on a plain crack, or a traverse into a steep corner), the
four Big Kangaroo south-face lines, the three Burgundy/Chianti east-side lines, and the two Lexington east-face lines.
THE PICKETS are the opposite problem. Almost nothing there is confusable with anything else, and the routes are so
remote that the question 'have I arrived' is answered by shape of ground rather than by a flake. So those baseFindings
are handrails, altimeter tests and countable sequences: hold 6,300-6,600 ft across the basin to the 7,050 ft notch on
East Fury's Direct East Ridge; cross a rocky rib and rope up the moment you are on its far side on the Southeast
Glaciers; leave the Terror Glacier at the bergschrund and climb 300 ft of gully on Inspiration's West Ridge, versus a
small rock buttress touching the ice at the lower-LEFT corner for its South Face; two lakes in sequence on Blum and on
Black Peak; one chockstone in one broad shallow gully on Big Kangaroo's West Face; a red boulder, then a cave you can
walk 25 yards into, on Tower Mountain.
SOURCING: 73 of the 88 entries are marked `re-homed` — every fact in them already existed in that route's own columns
(approach, approach_logistics, climbing_route, descent_text, waypoints) and was moved, not researched, so `_sources` is
empty by design. 12 are marked `corroborated` and carry the URLs that were actually fetched or returned by search; 3 are
marked `single-source`, meaning a route with one published ascent where the entry says so in the baseFinding itself.
No URL was pattern-guessed, and no source name, URL or publication appears inside any name/notes/baseFinding/hazards
field.
CONTAMINATION REJECTED DURING THIS BATCH, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- SILVER STAR MOUNTAIN. There are two in Washington: the 8,876 ft Okanogan County peak above Washington Pass (area
wa_silver_star_mountain_okanogan, which is the one here) and the 4,353 ft Silver Star Mountain in Clark County near
Vancouver, WA, a popular Yacolt Burn hike with an entirely separate literature. The area id already disambiguates;
the entry says so in prose as well.
- LAKE ANN. Black Peak and Corteo Peak are both approached from the Lake Ann / Maple Pass trailhead at RAINY PASS.
There is a second Lake Ann below Mount Shuksan on the Mount Baker Highway, about 80 km away, and that pair has
already contaminated this catalog once. Both entries name the Rainy Pass one explicitly.
- WHISTLER MOUNTAIN. The area is wa_whistler_mountain_okanogan at 48.5156/-120.7079, above Rainy Pass. The catalog
also holds wa_whistler_canyon_trailhead_oroville at 48.90/-119.42 with 66 routes — a different place roughly 100
miles away — and Whistler, British Columbia dominates any open search for the name. Only Rainy Pass material was used.
- LUNA PEAK and SWISS PEAK. The catalog holds wa_que_luna_boulders (Gold Bar) and wa_lunar_buttress (Tumwater Canyon),
and wa_swiss_project_boulder_the (Icicle Creek). None are related to the Picket peaks and none contributed anything.
- MOUNT TERROR, DAVIS PEAK and MOUNT DESPAIR all have namesakes elsewhere; only Southern Pickets material filed under
the wa_picket_range subtree was used, and Davis Peak and Mount Despair are outside the named scope and untouched.
- The POLTERGEIST PINNACLE row filed under Mount Challenger carries an approach paragraph copied verbatim from a Mount
Fury route. That is contamination already present in the data rather than something introduced here; it is skipped
and recorded in both _SKIPPED and _DEFECTS.
KNOWN AND NOT RE-LITIGATED, as instructed:
- wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route is named for the southeast while the published standard route is on the NORTHWEST
aspect (its aspect column already says NW). The entry notes this and does not re-argue it; the rename is pending.
- wa_liberty_bell_nw_face and wa_pernod_spire_standard had rappel lengths nulled as rope-capacity errors. Neither
entry restates a rappel length as a distance; both describe the descent by anchor type and rope needed instead.
- wa_east_face (Middle Gunsight) is outside this scope and was not read or touched.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The Whatcom Glacier traverse is the season-limiting piece: in low-snow years it has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542, Trail #674 climbs a well-graded 2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. That pass is the last easy water and the point where the two approaches to Challenger split.

This one drops the far side, losing roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley at Boundary Camp, crosses the Chilliwack, and follows the Chilliwack River Trail past Copper Creek Camp to the Whatcom Pass backcountry camp. Log crossings of the Chilliwack are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack.

From Whatcom Pass you still have to get round Whatcom Peak. The direct North Ridge is loose, extremely exposed and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side. Treat that as glacier travel.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PERFECT PASS IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU KNOW IT BECAUSE THE GROUND STOPS AND THE GLACIER STARTS. From the pass, getting down onto the Challenger Glacier at about 7,000-7,200 ft can involve roughly 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The exact entry point moves year to year with crevasse conditions, so do not look for a particular spot; look for the lowest place you can step from rock onto continuous ice.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME THING AS ARRIVAL AT THE GLACIER: the technical climbing on this route is 50 ft long and it is the last 50 ft. Above the bergschrund the glacier steepens into a snow arete, then a clean 3rd-class scramble runs out at the base of a short, well-protected 5.5-5.7 pitch. THAT PITCH IS THE ROUTE. If you are roping up anywhere lower than the foot of a single unbroken 50 ft wall with a rappel anchor visible at its top, you have roped up too early.

THE MOAT IS THE MARKER YOU WILL MEET FIRST, AND IN FOG IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Just below the summit rocks a moat has been reported up to about 5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to hunt a snow bridge. Reaching an uncrossable gap where the snow has pulled away from the summit rock means you are at the base, not lost.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing east along the crest away from the summit block puts you on the connecting ridge toward Poltergeist Pinnacle and Crooked Thumb, which is a different day entirely.
hazards: Unreliable log crossings of the Chilliwack River; parties have lost the crossing and been forced to bushwhack
The Whatcom Glacier traverse has been found down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years
About 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing, sometimes with a short rappel across a moat, just to get off Perfect Pass onto the glacier
A bergschrund on the Challenger Glacier and a moat below the summit rocks that can be impassable late season
No bailout worth the name once you are past Whatcom Pass

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the Impasse notch can make the direct crossing either easier or impossible depending on the year
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative from the same trailhead. From the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge and climb steeply onto the ridge, site of an old fire lookout. A faint climbers' path follows the crest past tarns and slabby sections, over Easy Peak, to a notch known as the Impasse, then continues cross-country toward Perfect Pass.

Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles, so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass or Perfect Pass, or both.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE IMPASSE IS THE CHECKPOINT, NOT THE BASE, AND CONFUSING THE TWO IS THE COMMON ERROR IN CLOUD. It is a notch in the ridge guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 step to regain the crest beyond.

BEYOND IT, THE TEST IS THE SAME AS ON THE OTHER APPROACH: Perfect Pass, then step onto ice, then keep going until the walking stops at a 50 ft rock wall. Nothing on this route is technical until that wall.

A NAMED WHITEOUT TRAP ON THIS LINE: on the snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, parties in fog have headed for Whatcom Peak's summit wall instead of the pass. If the ground in front of you is steepening into a wall rather than levelling into a saddle, you are aimed at the wrong feature. Perfect Pass is a saddle with running water; Whatcom's wall has neither.
hazards: The Impasse: deep snow moats on both sides and wet down-sloping slabs, with an 800 ft drop-and-re-climb workaround on exposed class 4
Fords of the Chilliwack River
Whiteout navigation between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, where parties have mistaken Whatcom Peak's summit wall for the pass
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier and the moat below the summit rocks

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with open moats late in the season
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE FOOT OF A SNOW COULOIR ON THE NORTHWEST SIDE, AND THE COULOIR IS THE ONLY THING ON THE PEAK YOU CAN IDENTIFY IN CLOUD. From the moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, the line goes up a 40-45 degree northwest-facing snow couloir to the saddle just north of the peak. In fog, do not navigate by the summit; navigate by the fact that you are in a confined snow gully with rock walls on both sides, steepening steadily to about 45 degrees. If the ground opens out and flattens, you are on the glacier, not in the couloir.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP, WHICH IS THE HARDER FIND: the camp is a LATERAL MORAINE, i.e. a ridge of rubble sitting on the ice, reached by descending through West Challenger Notch off the Challenger Glacier bench at about 8,100 ft. The notch is the crux of the navigation, not the couloir. You are through it when the ground stops dropping and you are standing on loose rock with ice on both sides.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: above the couloir the route works along loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles, and the crux is a single roughly 10 ft near-vertical crack, 5.8+ or 5.2 with a point of aid, taken at the top of a headwall. A rock horn draped with old slings sits below those pinnacles. If you have climbed the couloir and are on clean, moderate rock with good stances, you are not on this route; everything here is described as horribly loose.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the Challenger Glacier past the 8,100 ft bench instead of dropping through the notch takes you toward Challenger's own summit rocks, which is a different peak.
hazards: A mandatory, somewhat exposed hand-pulled cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River; the river is not reliably fordable
Blowdown on the Chilliwack River Trail, measured at roughly two hours per 1.5 miles in bad years
Crevasses and open moats on the Whatcom, Challenger and Crooked Thumb Glaciers
Loose class 4-5 rock throughout the upper route, described in trip reports as horribly loose
Weathered fixed tat on the north-ridge horn that should not be trusted without backing up
A 40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake water taxi, Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col and Luna Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134 at 2,150 ft, walk about a mile down to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock and cross to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, 11.5 miles of dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail up-valley takes roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp at about the 4.7-hour mark.

About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp a large log crossing of Big Beaver Creek, roughly 15 inches in diameter, marks the turnoff. Leave the trail there and head up Access Creek: a real bushwhack of about a mile gaining 1,900 ft, starting in valley-bottom devil's club, crossing to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then huckleberry and a final half-mile of talus into Access Basin.

From the basin a long, steep, loose scree chute gains about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft, 2-3 hours, and it can be brutally hot with no shade. From the col, 3-4 miles of notoriously steep heather and talus lead to Luna Pass, where most parties camp near lingering snow patches for water.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROCKY RIB IS THE GATE, AND THE GLACIER STARTS ON THE FAR SIDE OF IT. From Luna Pass the day goes along the Northeast Ridge crest, then down a steep, narrow heather chute of about 500 ft into a talus basin around 6,500 ft, then contours southwest across talus, heather and polished slabs until a ROCKY RIB BLOCKS EASY PASSAGE. That rib is the landmark. It has two ledge options: take the LOWER one, exposed scrambling on wet mossy rock and steep heather, in preference to the looser and more exposed upper ledge.

ARRIVAL: immediately beyond the rib you rope up, because the Southeast Glacier starts there, between roughly 6,500 and 7,000 ft. Snow under your feet on the far side of the rib is the route.

COUNTABLE CONFIRMATION ON THE RIDGE: between Luna Pass and the heather chute the crest throws up one distinct rock step of about 25 ft with a climbable vertical crack, class 3. That step is the only rock climbing before the glacier. If you have done several such steps you are on the ridge crest too long and have missed the point where it drops away.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE: this route climbs the true right, i.e. climber's-right, side of the Southeast Glacier on moderate 20-40 degree snow and works around a bergschrund near 7,900 ft, usually passable on its left. If you are on the left-hand margin of the ice looking for a way onto rock, you are heading for the East Ridge, not this route.

AND THE ONE FEATURE THAT IS UNMISTAKABLE EVEN BLIND: the last of the route steepens from 30-40 degrees to nearly 50 degrees, firm enough to front-point but not always secure for flat-footing, then narrows to a short snow arete before the summit rocks. When the snow narrows to a crest with air on both sides, there is nothing above but the top.
hazards: A mile of genuine bushwhacking up Access Creek through devil's club, deadfall and huckleberry with biting insects
A long loose scree chute to Access Col with no shade
Notoriously steep heather between Access Col and Luna Pass; an axe is worthwhile on the short steep sections
Crevasses on the Southeast Glacier and a bergschrund near 7,900 ft
A final snowfield to nearly 50 degrees, with crampon-balling reported on wet snow
Wet, mossy rock on the lower of the two rib ledges

approach_variants.name: Luna Col, then the 6,300-6,600 ft traverse across the ribs to the 7,050 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
The line in is the standard one: SR-20 to the Ross Dam trailhead between mileposts 134 and 135, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the resort boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, then 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail through old-growth cedar past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, and another mile or so north.

Watch on the left for a small cairn or a scratched arrow on a split log marking the cut-off, and cross Big Beaver Creek on a log just north of where Access Creek enters it; some years you wade. Then the Access Creek bushwhack: valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the north side and climb directly upslope through huckleberry, then several hours of heavy forest, deadfall and slide alder. Near 3,800 ft cross back to the south bank where the brush pinches out between a tongue of forest and a tongue of talus, then follow cairns and a faint path up talus into Access Creek Basin at about 4,300 ft, a good first camp.

From the basin, up the long grungy scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft, then the notorious traverse on very steep heather, talus and slabs to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft, the standard high camp on glacially polished slabs. Some parties wear crampons for traction on the heather.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS AT A NUMBERED NOTCH AND THE WHOLE APPROACH IS A CONTOUR TO REACH IT. From Luna Col drop a few hundred feet east, then traverse RIGHT at about the 6,600 ft level across ribs, gullies and small basins to the crest of a subsidiary ridge running southeast. Cross the large basin in front of you DROPPING NO LOWER THAN 6,300 FT, and from 6,300 ft in the middle of that basin start an ascending traverse northwest to the 7,050 FT NOTCH. That notch is where the route proper begins.

SO THE TEST IS AN ALTIMETER TEST, AND IT WORKS IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT NEEDS NO VIEW: the traverse is held between 6,300 and 6,600 ft, and then and only then does it climb. If you are below 6,300 ft you have dropped too far into the basin and will pay for it; if you never got below 6,600 ft you are still on the ribs and have not crossed the basin at all.

ARRIVAL: a notch is a gap you can stand in with ground falling away on both sides. From it the ridge runs west toward Fury and there is an exposed, level stretch the route's own account calls the sidewalk in the sky. Reaching an airy horizontal crest immediately above the notch confirms it.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing the ascending traverse past the notch, or contouring on around, puts you under the Southeast Glacier, which is the standard route's ground and a different climb.

COUNTABLE FEATURE ON THE ROUTE ITSELF: there is one 20 ft step on the east ridge that parties rappel on the way down off a medium cam or chock. One step, not several.
hazards: Route-finding across the ribs and gullies between Luna Col and the notch, in terrain with no path
Very steep heather on the Access Col to Luna Col traverse; some parties use crampons on it
Class 3-4 downclimbing on the east ridge, kept just south of the crest
Parties on this side of Fury routinely take six hours from the summit back to camp and finish in the dark
No shortcut off the peak; everything is a reversal

approach_variants.name: Luna Col, then over the back and 2,400 ft down into Luna Cirque to camp at Luna Lake
approach_variants.notes:
The modern approach mirrors the Luna Col line and then drops over the back: SR-20 to the Ross Dam trailhead, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, another mile to the marked cut-off, a log crossing of Big Beaver Creek just north of Access Creek, and the Access Creek bushwhack to Access Creek Basin at 4,300 ft.

From there the scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft and the steep heather traverse to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft. The whole approach is given as about 17 miles and 7,000 ft of gain from the water-taxi dock.

What is different begins at Luna Col: this route DESCENDS from it, north-northwest into Luna Cirque to Luna Lake at about 4,800 ft, then southwest to a camp on the cirque floor beneath the buttress. That descent costs 2,400 ft which has to be regained on the way out.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 2,400 FT OF DESCENT IS THE TEST, AND IT IS THE ONLY ROUTE ON THIS PEAK THAT ASKS FOR IT. Every other line from Luna Col goes up or across. This one goes DOWN, and a long way down, into the cirque on the far side. If you have left Luna Col and are not losing height fast, you are on the wrong side of the ridge.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP: LUNA LAKE AT ABOUT 4,800 FT IS THE CONFIRMATION AND IT IS A WATER FEATURE, which is what makes it findable in bad visibility. Camp is on the cirque floor beyond it, beneath the buttress. Standing at a lake at the bottom of a cirque with walls on three sides, having descended roughly 2,400 ft from a col, is unambiguous.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: the buttress rises directly above that camp on the peak's north side. This is a 20-pitch line and the base is the toe of the buttress at the back of the cirque, not a feature part way along the wall.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing southwest along the cirque floor past the buttress toe brings you under the west side of the massif and the connecting ridge toward West Fury, which is a different objective and offers no way up here.

THE COMMITTING FACT THAT SHOULD SHAPE THE DECISION AT CAMP: the buttress is an ascent line only. The standard exit is over the top and down the Southeast Glacier on the other side of the mountain, and a party that camped in Luna Cirque still has to regain roughly 2,400 ft to Luna Col afterwards to retrieve gear and get out.
hazards: 2,400 ft of descent into Luna Cirque that must be regained on the way out
The Access Creek bushwhack and the loose scree chute to Access Col
No descent down the buttress; the exit crosses the summit and the Southeast Glacier
Steep summit snow of about 300 ft, 40 degrees at the base to nearly 50 at the top, on the exit
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no realistic bailout

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek to Access Col, then the sidehill traverse around Luna Peak to the Fury-Luna connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at milepost 134, this is a multi-day approach and not a day hike. The standard option follows the Big Beaver Trail: hike, or take the seasonal water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, roughly 6 miles up the west shore of Ross Lake to the Big Beaver Creek trailhead, then the maintained trail up-valley through old-growth cedar past the Big Beaver and Luna camps to a point about 1.5 miles north of Luna Camp, roughly 10-11 trail miles in.

Leave the trail there, ford Big Beaver Creek and climb steep pathless forest and heather along the north side of Access Creek to break out into the open, meadow-floored Access Creek basin below Luna Peak, which is relatively brush-free compared with neighbouring drainages. Continue up-basin past a camping area near the headwaters, then climb a steep gully and heather system to a notch around 6,100 ft, Access Col, which gives the first view north into Luna Cirque and the Southern Pickets skyline.

From the col a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass and Luna Cirque, then gains the Fury-Luna connecting ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS ENTERED FROM A SMALL GLACIER, NOT FROM A RIDGE, AND THAT IS THE DISCRIMINATOR. The northwest side of West Fury is reached by a small glacier tucked beneath the peak, gained from the ridge system running toward Luna. Snow travel on it is reported as straightforward and kickable in good conditions. If you are scrambling rock to reach the start of this route you are in the wrong place; the start is where you step off snow onto dirty, ledge-broken ground on the northwest flank.

THE ROUTE-FINDING WARNING IS THE BASE FINDING, BECAUSE THE MISTAKE HAPPENS HERE: leaving the glacier, you work up broken ledge bands to gain the west ridge crest. The rock is poor and vegetated with few obvious anchors, and A WRONG TIER WILL CLIFF YOU OUT. Route-finding through the ledge bands is the real difficulty, not the climbing. Pick the tier that keeps going; if you have to make a hard move to stay on a ledge, you are on the wrong one.

CONFIRM HIGHER: from the crest, an ascending traverse east across loose rock leads into a chute that tops out slightly EAST of the summit. Topping out east of the top and having to walk back west is correct on this line, not an error.

WHAT DOES NOT BELONG HERE: this line is documented mainly as a DESCENT by parties traversing the Northern Pickets rather than as a commonly repeated ascent. Expect to be route-finding from first principles and treat any confident-sounding description of the ledges, including this one, as less precise than it sounds.

A NAMED NAVIGATION HAZARD LOWER DOWN, WHICH IS WHERE THE DAY IS ACTUALLY LOST: poor visibility has caused parties to pick the WRONG DRAINAGE off the Big Beaver Trail. Some parties cairn the correct creek crossing on the way in. Access Creek's basin is the open, meadow-floored, relatively brush-free one; if you are fighting continuous brush you are in a neighbouring drainage.
hazards: Picking the wrong drainage off the Big Beaver Trail in poor visibility, a documented error here
Cliff-band route-finding on broken ledges where a wrong tier cliffs you out
Poor, vegetated rock that takes gear badly, and shockingly mobile large talus on the summit ridges of the massif
Gullies dropping into Access Creek involve cliffy downclimbing and occasionally short rappels
Water is abundant along Big Beaver and Access Creeks but scarce above Access Col
One of the most remote summits in the range, with no quick way off

approach_variants.name: Climb East Fury first; the traverse starts on its summit
approach_variants.notes:
This route has no approach of its own in the ordinary sense. It is the connecting ridge between the two summits of Mount Fury, and the only way to arrive at its start is to have climbed East Fury, which is reached from the Ross Dam Trailhead by water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, the Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col, Luna Col and the Southeast Glacier.

Budget the East Fury ascent as a full day in its own right before this one begins, and note that the traverse is about half a kilometre of ridge, which says nothing useful about how long it takes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS ROUTE IS A SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE ONE THING ON A MOUNTAIN YOU CANNOT WALK PAST. You are at the start when you are standing on the top of East Fury with the ridge running west toward the West Peak. There is no gully to find, no bench to identify and no chance of starting the wrong line: if you are not on East Fury's summit, you have not started.

WHAT THAT MEANS IN PRACTICE, AND IT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A LANDMARK: the commitment happens at the first rappel, not at the summit. Getting off each tower on the traverse means rappelling off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, and EACH RAPPEL DOWN MAKES RETREAT PROGRESSIVELY HARDER. The place to decide whether the weather and the hour justify the traverse is on East Fury's summit, before the first pull.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, ON THE OTHER END: once off the traverse, the way home is back over East Fury and down its east side to the saddle on loose class 2-3 talus, then down the Southeast Glacier to Luna Col. Descending anywhere off the north side of the connecting ridge drops you into Luna Cirque, 2,400 ft below the col you camped at.
hazards: Poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, with each rappel making retreat harder
A committing position on a ridge between two of the most remote summits in the range
Loose class 2-3 talus on the descent of East Fury's east side
The whole outing sits behind a full day's climb of East Fury and a multi-day approach

approach_variants.name: The backdoor: over the summit of East Fury and down the connecting ridge to the toe of the Southwest Buttress
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is identical to the standard East Peak route for its first 12-plus miles and then continues much farther. From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134, walk about a mile to the Ross Lake water taxi dock and cross to Big Beaver Landing, then follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail 11.5 miles up-valley, passing Luna Camp at roughly the 4.7-hour mark.

About 29 minutes past Luna Camp, leave the trail at a large log crossing of Big Beaver Creek and turn up the Access Creek drainage: roughly a mile and 1,900 ft of gain through devil's club, a mid-height creek crossing near 3,800 ft, then huckleberry and talus into Access Basin. From the basin, a long grungy scree chute gains about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft.

From Access Col most Mongo Ridge parties do not stop at Luna Pass. They continue over the connecting terrain and up the Southeast Glacier route to the summit of East Fury, then descend north along the connecting ridge to the base of the Southwest Buttress to rack up. Most parties treat this as a multi-day expedition with a camp at Luna Pass or on the connecting ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE AT THIS ROUTE FROM ABOVE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE MODERN APPROACH. The buttress toe sits at the bottom of the Goodell Creek side, and the historically brutal, brush-choked Goodell approach is what the backdoor exists to avoid. So the sequence is: summit East Fury, then GO DOWN the connecting ridge to the base of the Southwest Buttress. If you are still gaining height after East Fury's summit, you have not started descending to the base yet.

WHY THAT MAKES THE BASE UNMISTAKABLE: there is exactly one summit between you and the start, and it is one you have to climb. A party that has not stood on East Fury has not reached the base of Mongo Ridge by this approach, whatever else it has found.

THE DECISION POINT, WHICH MATTERS MORE HERE THAN THE LANDMARK: the descent to the toe is time you will have to buy back, and the ridge above it holds roughly half a dozen major gendarmes and pinnacles including the tower nicknamed the Pole of Remoteness. Getting off each of them takes a rappel, and roughly a dozen rappels total along the crest before you regain East Fury. Every one of them is irreversible once the ropes are pulled.

WHAT ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING LOOKS LIKE: rack up where the ridge stops descending and the first tower rises in front of you. Above that point the route is 25 pitches to Grade VI, 5.10.
hazards: Roughly a dozen rappels along the crest, almost entirely off improvised anchors: loose blocks, horns and old tat
Retreat gets progressively harder the farther along the ridge a party commits
A rappel rope has been reported severed by rockfall mid-descent on this ridge
The Access Creek bushwhack and the loose scree chute to Access Col before any of it
A full ascent of East Fury simply to reach the start

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek into Luna Cirque, rather than the Luna Creek bushwhack
approach_variants.season: Jun to early Aug. The hanging glacier is the crux of the route and can be impassable in late season, which is why the window is early
approach_variants.notes:
Reaching Luna Cirque is the crux of the trip. The historical line follows the Big Beaver Trail from Ross Lake, with a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort cutting about 6 miles off the hike, up to Luna Camp, then climbs steeply beside Luna Creek into the cirque. That bushwhack was described by the first-ascent party as the worst imaginable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows and alder.

Most contemporary parties instead approach via Access Creek, which branches off the same Big Beaver Trail rather than a separate trailhead. Continue on maintained trail past Luna Camp to the unmarked Access Creek and Big Beaver Creek confluence, then leave the trail and follow the Access Creek drainage, with an occasional bootpath, up into the cirque. Longer, and far less brutal.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS THE GLACIER IMMEDIATELY SOUTH OF THE PEAK, AND THE TEST IS THAT IT NARROWS. From the floor of Luna Cirque, get onto the hanging glacier that lies directly south of Phantom and follow it up to where it NARROWS AND STEEPENS as it flows down from higher on the mountain. That constriction is the route; there is nothing subtle about walking into a narrowing throat of ice with rock on both sides.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROCK, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL BASE OF THE CLIMBING: where the narrows END, turn NORTH and climb over a rock step to reach the highest snowfield on the peak. That turn is the transition from snow to rock and the point at which the party commits to the upper route. The whole climb above the cirque is only about 400 ft in four pitches, so if you have been climbing rock for more than a few rope lengths without reaching a summit block you are not on this line.

COUNTABLE CONFIRMATION: one rock step, two to three pitches of easy slab to the ridge, then a summit block of about 25 ft. Four pitches, 4th class with a move of easy 5th. Parties carry runners and a few pieces rather than a full rack, because placements on the slab are where the features allow rather than where you want them.

THE TURNAROUND TEST, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING ABOUT THIS ROUTE: the hanging glacier has to be recrossed to get home. A party that finds it in poor condition ON THE WAY UP should treat that as the turnaround decision rather than pressing on. Timing is the main decision this route asks of a party, and the answer is taken at the base, not at the top.
hazards: A hanging glacier that is the route's crux and can be impassable in late season
The Luna Creek approach, if chosen, is among the worst brush in the Cascades
Sparse protection on the slab pitches
Recrossing the glacier on the descent, on the same conditions that decided the ascent

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes:
The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine.

Expect 2-3 days of travel each way. Note that the row's stored trailhead record names a different trailhead than this prose does; see _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS A SADDLE INSIDE THE BUTTRESS, AT ABOUT 6,100 FT, AND YOU GET THERE BY LOSING HEIGHT FIRST. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 FT DESCENDING TRAVERSE EAST across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft WITHIN the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

SO THE TEST IN CLOUD IS THE SHAPE OF THE GROUND, NOT THE VIEW: you go DOWN and EAST for a thousand feet, then UP a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.
hazards: A bergschrund on the summit snow finger, crossed via a slabby rock step
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully section, with natural anchors only
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
A 1,000 ft descending traverse that has to be regained on the return
The Chilliwack cable-car crossing and the Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
approach_variants.notes:
The on-file line, and the one the stored distance reflects. From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 14 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required.

From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IN THIS DRAINAGE THE NAVIGATION RULE IS ABOUT HEIGHT, NOT DIRECTION, AND IT IS THE ONE THING THAT MAKES THE DAY WORK. The creek must be forded in places, and FORDS GET HARDER THE LOWER AND FARTHER DOWNSTREAM YOU ARE. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

ARRIVAL, WHICH IS UNAMBIGUOUS EVEN WITH NO VISIBILITY: above the brush line the drainage OPENS into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

FROM THERE THE BASE TEST IS THE SAME ONE THE NORTHERN APPROACH USES: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A REAL RISK PECULIAR TO THIS APPROACH, RECORDED BECAUSE IT HAS HAPPENED: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, at roughly half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder the lower you are
High risk of falling into a hole hidden by brush, and of separating from a partner
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
No trail, no cairns and real disorientation on the way back down

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier to a bivy under Ghost Peak
approach_variants.notes:
An involved two-day approach. Roughly 10 miles on trail up and over Hannegan Pass, wading the Chilliwack River, then the scenic 5-mile traverse of Easy Ridge, soloing exposed 4th-class terrain across the Imperfect Impasse, climbing through Perfect Pass and over the Challenger Glacier, then descending and traversing steep snow, talus and more glacier to a bivy site.

The route was first climbed in July 2021 and is documented in a single first-ascent account, so treat everything about it as sparsely reported.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BIVY IS THE VIEWPOINT AND THAT IS THE POINT OF IT: the camp sits UNDER GHOST PEAK, Phantom's neighbour immediately to the NORTH, and the first-ascent party chose it because THE FULL WEST RIDGE COMES INTO VIEW FROM THERE. So the test is not a feature at the base of the climb but a named peak overhead: if the summit above your camp is not Ghost Peak, and Phantom is not the next summit SOUTH of you, you are camped in the wrong place.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL HERE: this ridge has one published ascent. Nobody has recorded a marker at its toe, and inventing one would be inventing the only fact that matters. What is recorded is the vantage point, so use it: from camp, with the ridge in view, pick the line and note it BEFORE the cloud comes in. This is a route to reconnoitre the evening before rather than to find in the morning.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, ON THE APPROACH: past Perfect Pass, the Challenger Glacier is crossed and then LEFT again on the far side. If you are still gaining height on ice you have not started the descent toward the Ghost Peak bivy.

ON THE DESCENT, AND WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU START: the way off is the southeast face, including a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall. The first-ascent party noted that crossing would be more straightforward earlier in the season with more snow cover.
hazards: The Imperfect Impasse, soloed as exposed 4th class on the way in
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier
A rockfall-exposed snowfield crossing on the descent, worse later in the season
A single published ascent, so no accumulated route-finding knowledge to fall back on
Wading the Chilliwack River

approach_variants.name: Access Creek to Access Col and Luna Pass, then straight up the broad south ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Lake Trailhead off Hwy 20 near Ross Dam, most parties take the seasonal water taxi across the reservoir to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft, skipping roughly 7 rolling lakeshore miles. From there the maintained Big Beaver Trail runs about 8 miles to Luna Camp, the standard permit basecamp, then roughly another 1.5 miles north.

Watch on the left, the west, for a boot path near where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek, and cross Big Beaver Creek there. A log crossing is sometimes usable, otherwise wade. That is where maintained trail ends.

Follow a surprisingly well-defined boot path along the north bank of Access Creek through semi-open forest. NEAR 3,700 FT THE BRUSH TURNS THICK WITH SLIDE ALDER, SO CROSS TO THE SOUTH BANK AROUND 3,800 FT; several trip reports warn specifically that skipping this crossing leads to a miserable bushwhack. From the south bank, cairns and a fainter path link talus benches into the open upper basin at the Access Creek headwaters, the usual basecamp, with reliable water.

From camp, the Access Couloir gains roughly 1,500-2,000 ft of steep loose scree and talus, with a notably loose upper section of dirt and heather clumps, to Access Col at about 6,300 ft. From the col a faint path traverses west across heather and talus to Luna Pass, the Luna-McMillan col at about 7,200 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT LUNA PASS THE TWO ROUTES ON THIS PEAK PART COMPANY, AND THE TEST IS SIMPLE: THIS ONE GOES STRAIGHT UP. From the pass, turn directly up the broad south ridge on class 2 talus, roughly 1,000-1,100 ft of gain, straight to Luna's false, southern summit. There is no traverse and no contour. If you are sidehilling across snowfields on Luna's southeast flank you are on the Southeast Slopes route, which is the other line from this same pass.

ARRIVAL AT THE PASS ITSELF, WHICH IS THE HARDER FIND: Luna Pass is the col between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left, at about 7,200 ft, reached by a faint traverse west from Access Col. It is a gap on a crest, not a shoulder. If the ground ahead of you keeps rising instead of dropping away on the far side, you have not reached it.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, ON THE RIDGE: this route as scoped tops out at the FALSE, SOUTHERN summit. Continuing past it toward Luna's true summit means a separate exposed class 3-4 ledge traverse across the notch between the two summits, where some parties use a rope and running belays. That is beyond this route, and the notch is where you decide whether to take it on.

A NAMED APPROACH ERROR, BECAUSE MULTIPLE PARTIES HAVE MADE IT: several report initially following the WRONG DRAINAGE out of Big Beaver. Access Creek is the one with the boot path on its north bank and the 3,800 ft bank change; if there is no boot path, you are in the wrong creek.
hazards: Swift, sometimes swollen crossings of Big Beaver and Access Creek
Heavy slide-alder bushwhacking and genuine route-finding difficulty in Access Creek; multiple parties report following the wrong drainage
Loose rock in the Access Couloir and on the south ridge, with real rockfall risk onto climbers below
Lingering snow and possible avalanche exposure on the couloir and southeast snowfields in early season
No water above the Access Creek basin

approach_variants.name: Access Creek basin, then the gap south of Point 6,730 and the 6,600 ft basin traverse to Luna Col
approach_variants.notes:
The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at about 2,050 ft, with parking right off the highway. About 0.8 mile of trail leads down to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft. The lake crossing is a logistical step rather than an afterthought, since the resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can reach the trailhead at all.

From the Big Beaver Trailhead, about 8 miles of well-graded trail through old-growth cedar along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek reach Luna Camp. Continue roughly 1.5 miles past it and watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek at about 2,460 ft. Ford Big Beaver Creek there.

Around 3,700 ft the brush thickens; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint path use talus benches to dodge the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This stretch is the approach crux. The path deposits you in the open basin at the Access Creek headwaters at about 4,400 ft, the common base camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE CONTOURS WHERE THE SOUTH RIDGE CLIMBS, AND THE DIFFERENCE STARTS ABOVE CAMP RATHER THAN AT THE COL. From the Access Creek basin, ascend broad talus gullies, snow-filled early season, southwest toward an OBVIOUS GAP IN THE RIDGE above. Once on the ridge, TRAVERSE SOUTH OF POINT 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's southeast side, then cross that basin AT ABOUT THE 6,600 FT LEVEL to Luna Col at 7,200 ft.

SO THE FOG TEST IS AN ALTIMETER TEST: the basin crossing is held at roughly 6,600 ft. Losing height into the basin or gaining it toward the crest both cost you, and both are what happens when you navigate by feel. Hold the contour and it delivers you to the col.

ARRIVAL: Luna Col at 7,200 ft is the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. You are there when the ground drops away on the far side.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB, AND THE COUNT IS SHORT: above the col the route is roughly 1,100 ft of class 2-3 talus and scree to the FALSE, SOUTHERN summit, then ONE short connecting ridge to the true summit. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left at the false summit.

THE ONE TECHNICAL SPOT, AND ITS TELL: drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit onto a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest with a snow-covered cliff falling several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff dropping the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the worst of it by dropping onto a ledge on the SOUTHEAST side and scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit. If you are on a crest with snow on your left and bare rock on your right, you are in the right place and there is one short section of it.

NO WATER ABOVE THE ACCESS CREEK BASIN. The summit push is done on what you carry.
hazards: Sustained bushwhacking, blowdown and route-finding in the Access Creek drainage, the approach crux
A ford of Big Beaver Creek that can run high with snowmelt
A narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest between the false and true summits, with cliffs on both sides
Loose talus and scree on the upper ridge with rockfall risk onto parties below
No reliable water above the Access Creek camp except lingering snowmelt
Losing the boot path in poor light on the way down, which several trip reports record

approach_variants.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 11 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A SADDLE BETWEEN TWO NAMED SUMMITS AND YOU REACH IT BY HAVING CROSSED BOTH SUMMITS OF FURY. That is a hard test to fail and a hard one to pass: there is no way to arrive at the Swiss-Fury saddle by this line without having traversed West Fury, so if you have not climbed Fury, you are not there.

ARRIVAL: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the NORTHWEST ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route.

WHY THIS ENTRY IS THINNER THAN ITS NEIGHBOURS, SAID PLAINLY: Swiss Peak carries one route in the catalog and no first-ascent record, its area row has NO STORED COORDINATE AT ALL, and nothing published locates a feature at the foot of the southwest face. What is locatable is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing northwest along the crest past Swiss takes you toward the ground the Northern Pickets traverse uses, with no easier way down on that side.
hazards: A full traverse of both Fury summits simply to reach the saddle
Glaciated terrain between Luna Col and the Fury summits
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no independent descent
No stored coordinate for the peak and very little published route detail

approach_variants.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length and is described only in outline, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PICKELL PASS THE SOUTH SIDE OF SWISS IS CLIMBED DIRECTLY, AND THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE GOING UP RATHER THAN ALONG. Camp is a heather bench at the pass; the climbing starts on the class 3 south side immediately above it. Parties on this line downclimb the same class 3 south side back to the bench, so the ascent and descent are the same ground, and a party that has to traverse to find its line has left the route.

HOW TO KNOW YOU ARE AT PICKELL PASS RATHER THAN ANOTHER SADDLE ON THE SAME RIDGE SYSTEM: it is reached by descending Mount Crowder's NORTHEAST ridge. The last named summit before the pass is Crowder. If you have not been on Crowder, you have not arrived by this line.

WHY THIS SIDE MAY BE THE BETTER CHOICE, AS A PLANNING FACT RATHER THAN A LANDMARK: the northern line requires traversing Luna, East Fury and West Fury. This one does not require crossing Fury at all. The cost is a long ridge sequence with no trail and no bailout.
hazards: A long off-trail ridge sequence with no maintained tread
No independent descent; exiting the range means committing to one of the long approach drainages
Very little published detail for either approach to this peak

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 8-9 hours and 12-13 miles in for a strong party. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE THE CAMP ENDS: FROM PERFECT PASS, HEAD NORTH AND UP ONTO THE BROAD SOUTH SNOWFIELD. That snowfield is the lower margin of the Whatcom Glacier, the angle is moderate, and the line aims at a CONSPICUOUS COL IN THE SUMMIT RIDGE above. Reports describe it as long but straightforward, roughly an hour from the pass.

SO THE AIMING POINT IS A NOTCH IN A SKYLINE, AND IN CLOUD THE SUBSTITUTE FOR IT IS THIS: keep climbing snow at a moderate angle until the snow RUNS OUT AGAINST ROCK. The snowfield is left at the col. Where snow meets rock is where a moat or a lip of hard snow is most likely to be awkward, and it is worse late in the season, which is exactly why you will notice it.

CONFIRM ABOVE: the final stretch along the crest is SHORT, on the order of a hundred feet, but very exposed with drops on both sides, on poor rock with limited protection. Many parties belay it even though the moves are only third to fourth class. If you are on a long ridge rather than a hundred-foot one, you are not on this route.

THE VARIATION THAT IS NOT AN ERROR: some parties break out onto ramps and ledges to the NORTHEAST of the col and rejoin the crest higher. Both reach the same place.

THE IMPASSE, WHICH IS THE OTHER THING YOU HAVE TO FIND ON THIS APPROACH: it is a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 rock step, which many parties belay, to regain the ridge on the far side. Dropping 800 ft to get past a notch feels wrong and is correct.
hazards: A thigh-deep, swift ford of the Chilliwack River at mid-summer flow
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs, and an 800 ft descent to an exposed class 4 step as the workaround
Moats where the south snowfield meets the summit rock, worse late season
A short but very exposed summit crest on poor rock with limited protection
No reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season

approach_variants.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
approach_variants.notes: An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT IS DEFINED BY WHAT IT AVOIDS, AND THAT IS THE TEST: IF YOU HAVE CROSSED THE IMPASSE, YOU ARE NOT ON IT. The low orbit contours around the peak's east side instead of over the ridge crest, and delivers you onto the same south-side snowfields the Easy Ridge line reaches from Perfect Pass.

ARRIVAL IS THE SAME ARRIVAL: broad moderate snow below a conspicuous col in the summit ridge, and the route is where the snow runs out against rock.

WHAT YOU TRADE FOR IT, AND WHY THE CHOICE IS A CONDITIONS CALL RATHER THAN A PREFERENCE: the low orbit exposes you to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the WHATCOM GLACIER, so it should be treated as glacier travel with a rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season. The Impasse is a rock problem; this is a glacier problem. Pick the one your party is equipped for.
hazards: Moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier; treat as glacier travel in early season
Scree and snow sidehilling with no path
The same summit crest exposure as the Easy Ridge variant

approach_variants.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp, then turn up at the Brush Creek Trail junction and climb through US Cabin Camp, Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. A cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack exists near U.S. Cabin Camp as an alternative to fording. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BROAD TOE OF THE RIDGE, AND YOU FIND IT BY WALKING SOUTH OFF THE PASS UNTIL THE PATH DIES. From Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads DIRECTLY SOUTH, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge. The path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and from there the route-finding rule is STAY ON THE CREST rather than follow any marked line.

SO THE FOG TEST IS A HANDRAIL TEST, AND IT IS THE BEST KIND: once you are on the crest, keep it under your feet. Any time you find yourself sidehilling with the crest above you, you have come off it. There is nothing to identify on this ridge except the ridge.

ARRIVAL AT THE START: you are on the route as soon as the informal path stops being a path and the ground becomes broken rock rising to a crest. That transition happens within a few hundred feet of the pass; this is not a route with a long walk to its base.

WHAT THE UPPER RIDGE IS LIKE, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHETHER YOU COME BACK THIS WAY: the final several hundred feet below the summit are described bluntly by climber reports as a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class terrain, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it is shorter. Many parties instead go over the summit and down the South Spur side.

AND THE OTHER THING THIS RIDGE IS: it is the direct line from Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass that Challenger parties are told NOT to take. It is loose, extremely exposed and called a formidable obstacle. If you are on it as a shortcut rather than as your objective, you have chosen the wrong tool.
hazards: Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack, which reports rate as the riskier option
An unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge

approach_variants.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER WAY YOU ARRIVE AT WHATCOM PASS, THE BASE TEST IS IDENTICAL: leave the maintained trail, head DIRECTLY SOUTH on the faint climbers' path, and stay on the crest once the path dies. The two approaches differ only in how you get to the pass.

THE ONE THING THIS SIDE CHANGES, AND IT IS A LOGISTICS FACT RATHER THAN A NAVIGATION ONE: your car is at Ross Lake, not at Hannegan. That rules out the common descent option of crossing the summit and coming down the South Spur side to Perfect Pass, unless you are prepared to loop back around the peak's east side or across the Whatcom Glacier to regain Whatcom Pass.

HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE PASS AND NOT AT A CAMP BELOW IT: the last stretch from the Big Beaver junction is a steep switchbacking climb through big fir. The pass is where that climb stops.
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
The same loose upper ridge as the western approach
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass, then onto the Whatcom Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. THE RIVER IS CROSSED VIA A HAND-PULLED CABLE CAR NEAR US CABIN CAMP RATHER THAN A FORD, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE'S OWN GROUND IS THE GLACIER, AND YOU ARE ON IT AS SOON AS YOU LEAVE WHATCOM PASS. From the pass, leave the trail and climb and contour SOUTH AND EAST to gain the Whatcom Glacier at roughly 5,200-5,500 ft, then rope up and travel toward Perfect Pass, the notch and saddle south of the peak.

SO THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER TWO ROUTES ON THIS PEAK IS THE FIRST MOVE OUT OF WHATCOM PASS, AND IT IS THREE-WAY: SOUTH and up the crest is the North Ridge. SOUTH AND EAST onto ice at 5,200-5,500 ft is this route. Nothing from Whatcom Pass is the South Spur, which is approached from Easy Ridge on the other side.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING PROPER: from the glacier's high point near Perfect Pass, the route ascends the broad SOUTH-FACING snowfield below the summit and finishes on an exposed but moderate class 3 scramble along the south ridge crest. The snowfield is the same one the South Spur uses. The two routes share their last hour and differ entirely in everything before it.

WHAT THE GLACIER DOES THROUGH THE SEASON, WHICH IS THE REAL VARIABLE: crevasses and moats open as the year goes on and the surface can go from soft neve early to bare, polished ice with exposed water channels by mid to late summer. On the descent they are typically MORE open than on the way up as the afternoon sun softens the snowpack, so budget time for careful navigation rather than a quick glissade.

AN ALTERNATE EXIT WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU NEED IT: if the summit notch is badly melted out and choss-prone, a descent drops about 200 ft north of Peak 7347 to reach the Wiley Glacier instead of reversing through the notch.
hazards: Crevasses and moats on the Whatcom Glacier, deteriorating to bare ice with gaping moats later in the season
A steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path above Graybeal Camp
The creek near Graybeal can run dry by late summer
An exposed class 3 summit ridge on poor rock
A glacier that is more open on the descent than on the ascent

approach_variants.name: Baker River Trail to the suspension bridge, then the unmarked Blum Creek climbers' path to the Blum Lakes basin
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Baker Lake Road, Forest Road 11, 25.5 miles north from WA-20 at milepost 82 near Concrete, to its end at the Baker River Trailhead at 774 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and there is a vault toilet on site.

Hike the maintained Baker River Trail #606 roughly half a mile, about ten minutes, to the Baker River suspension bridge. Cross it, then look for a faint, unmarked climbers' path beginning ABOUT 175 YARDS DOWNSTREAM OF THE BRIDGE, and about 25 yards UPSTREAM of a stringer bridge, following Blum Creek's north bank.

The path climbs steeply and indistinctly through dense forest and understory, becoming more defined higher as it follows Blum Creek Ridge; around 5,100 ft it contours the ridge's south side through huckleberry brush and talus into the Blum Lakes basin at roughly 5,000-5,700 ft. Figure 4-4.5 miles and 4,000-4,300 ft to the basin, about 5 hours for a fit party; the full round trip is about 9 miles and 7,000 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HARD FIND ON THIS ROUTE IS THE TRAILHEAD END OF IT, NOT THE MOUNTAIN END, AND IT IS COUNTABLE. Cross the suspension bridge and then measure: the climbers' path starts roughly 175 YARDS DOWNSTREAM of the bridge and roughly 25 YARDS UPSTREAM of a stringer bridge. Two bridges bracket the start. If you have walked past a second bridge you have overshot by about 25 yards; if you have gone more than a couple of hundred yards from the suspension bridge without finding tread, turn round.

HANDRAIL ABOVE THAT: the path follows BLUM CREEK'S NORTH BANK and then the crest of Blum Creek Ridge. Water on your right going up, the ridge under your feet higher. Around 5,100 ft it contours the ridge's SOUTH side. If you are contouring the north side you have crossed the crest.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP: the Blum Lakes basin. Lakes are the confirmation, and there is more than one of them; the middle lake is the usual camp.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: from the basin, the line goes up a SNOW COULOIR BELOW THE SOUTH RIDGE SADDLE. Snow in a confined gully leading to a gap in the ridge above is the start; open heather and talus is not. The route above the saddle is class 3.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing north past the northernmost of the Blum Lakes and over the northwest shoulder takes you into the glacial basin below the NORTH Ridge, which is the peak's other route and needs glacier travel gear this one does not.
hazards: A faint, unmarked path start that is easy to walk past in either direction
Steep, indistinct climbing through dense forest and understory low down
Huckleberry brush and talus on the contour around 5,100 ft
A snow couloir below the south ridge saddle, wanting an axe when firm
7,000 ft of gain on a 9-mile round trip

approach_variants.name: The same Blum Creek path to the lakes, then past the northernmost lake and over the northwest shoulder into the glacial basin
approach_variants.notes:
Trailhead and approach are identical to the South Ridge as far as the Blum Lakes basin: Baker Lake Road to the Baker River Trailhead, the maintained trail to the suspension bridge, the unmarked climbers' path starting about 175 yards downstream of it on Blum Creek's north bank, and the steep climb up Blum Creek Ridge to the lakes.

What is different starts at the lakes. Carry glacier travel gear for this one; the South Ridge does not need it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LAKES ARE A SEQUENCE AND THIS ROUTE USES THE LAST ONE. Continue to the NORTHERNMOST of the Blum Lakes, then cross the NORTHWEST SHOULDER into the glacial basin below the North Ridge. The count is the test: if you stop at the first or middle lake you are set up for the South Ridge, which is the other route from this basin.

ARRIVAL: you are in the right basin when you have crossed a shoulder and there is GLACIER below the ridge in front of you. The South Ridge side has a snow couloir; this side has a glacial basin. Rope and crevasse gear are needed for the crossing itself, which is a fair signal that you are where you meant to be.

WHAT THE DESCENT TELLS YOU ABOUT THE GROUND, AND IT IS WORTH READING BEFORE YOU GO UP: parties come down near the summit around the south or southwest side of a FALSE SUMMIT, following cairns past known bivy spots, down a snowfield, then skier's right into the top of a broad gully, then skier's right again through scrub pine to the creek and lakes basin. So there is a false summit on this peak, there are cairns and bivy spots on its south side, and the exit is a broad gully with scrub pine. Any of those seen on the way up are confirmation you are on the right mountain even if you are not on the ridge crest.
hazards: A glacial basin crossing requiring rope and crevasse-rescue gear
A false summit that can be mistaken for the top
The same faint, easily missed climbers' path start at the Baker River
Scrub pine and a broad loose gully on the standard exit

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek path, past Terror Basin to a Crescent Creek Basin camp, then over the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft off Hwy 20 near Newhalem. Follow the old roadbed and climbers' path along Goodell Creek for about 4 miles, gaining only about 1,000 ft, to a junction around 1,700 ft marked by a stone arrow, a post and a large cairn. That junction is the standard jump-off for EVERY Southern Pickets objective and the last easy, reliable water before the climb steepens.

The unmaintained Terror Creek climbers' trail cuts uphill to the right and turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 4,000-4,700 ft in well under 3 horizontal miles through old-growth forest and brush, with head-high slide alder and devil's club depending on the season, before breaking out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft onto heather benches, slabs and snowfields.

From treeline, rather than stopping at Terror Basin, continue a rising traverse west-northwest staying near the 5,800-6,400 ft band into Crescent Creek Basin, reached via a steep initial drop into the basin on mixed snow and talus followed by roughly an hour of traversing.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS REACHED BY GOING OVER A COL AND THEN DOWN THE FAR SIDE, AND THE DOWNHILL IS THE TEST. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp, climb east or northeast onto the ridge to gain the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then DOWNCLIMB AND SCRAMBLE ROUGHLY 500 FT down broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered ground on the FRENZEL SPITZ side to reach the base of the South Route proper. If you are still on the col, or above it, you have not started.

WHICH SIDE OF THE COL IS WHICH, AND IT IS THE ONE FACT THAT KEEPS PARTIES OUT OF TROUBLE HERE: the SOUTH, Crescent Creek side of that col is the friendly side, loose but moderate 3rd and 4th class scrambling. The NORTH side is sustained loose 5th class and drops into a broken couloir and glacier and moat terrain, and parties commonly need a rappel to get down it. If the ground below you needs a rope to descend, you are on the north side and you are heading for the Mustard Glacier, not Frenzel Spitz.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP, WHICH IS THE OTHER PLACE THIS DAY GETS LOST: Crescent Creek Basin, not Terror Basin. Terror Basin is where the McMillan, Inspiration and Terror parties stop. The Frenzel Spitz, Himmelhorn, Ottohorn and Chopping Block camp is the NEXT basin west, reached by holding the 5,800-6,400 ft band and traversing about an hour further. Stopping at the first flat ground above treeline puts you a basin short.

NO DEPENDABLE WATER above the Terror Creek junction until snowmelt or tarns near camp; carry enough for 4,500-plus ft of climbing in between.
hazards: Head-high slide alder and devil's club on a relentlessly steep unmaintained path
No dependable water for roughly 4,500 ft of climbing
Broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered ground on the 500 ft descent to the route's base
The north side of the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col is a rappel proposition with glacier and moat terrain below it
Glacier edges near the col have been described as unable to hold body weight late season

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone arrow, Stump Hollow, the Barrier, and the Himmel-Otto col gully
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Campground and trailhead on SR-20 just west of Newhalem at about 600 ft, follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the south side of Goodell Creek. It is flat and easy for roughly 4-4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft.

Watch on the right for a cairn and stone marker, which climbers call the stone arrow, at the end of the roadbed. This marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. Steep, root-and-duff footing, brushy in spots, but reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher. No reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek.

Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block. From there, rising-traverse on meadow, slab and early-season snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft, then cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives.

NOTE ON THE NAME, WHICH IS SETTLED AND SHOULD NOT BE RE-ARGUED: this row is titled Southeast Route, but the published standard route on this peak is on the NORTHWEST aspect, and the row's aspect column already records NW. Its prose has been corrected; the rename is pending.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A COL YOU REACH BY A NARROW GULLY, AND THE GULLY'S CHARACTER CHANGES COMPLETELY THROUGH THE SEASON. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the HIMMEL-OTTO COL. In early season that is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top. By late season it turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and AN OVERHANGING BOULDER NEAR THE COL OFTEN FORCES A LOOSE, EXPOSED CLASS 3-4 BYPASS ON THE LEFT, climber's left.

SO THE MARKER IS THE BOULDER, AND IT IS A COUNTABLE ONE: there is one overhanging boulder near the top of the gully, and getting past it on its left is the last obstacle before the col. If you have bypassed several such blocks, you are in the wrong gully.

ARRIVAL: you are at the col when the gully tops out into a gap with ground falling away on the far side. From there the standard route continues on easier ground, scrambling to low 5th class, onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit.
