TWO CROSSINGS OF THE BARRIER EXIST AND BOTH ARE CORRECT: a LOWER crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a HIGHER crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mount Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour. Both are loose enough that a party above another is the real danger.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: descending north from the Himmel-Otto col rather than climbing from it. The north side is a different and harder proposition and leads onto the Mustard Glacier.
hazards: An icy, choss-and-moat gully to the col in late season
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass
Two Barrier crossings, both loose and exposed, with rockfall onto any party below
No reliable water between the Goodell roadbed and treeline
No bolted or fixed rappel stations anywhere on the route; all anchors are built

approach_variants.name: From a high camp below the Chopping Block, up the snow slope and 600 ft of ramps to the grassy col at the base of the wall
approach_variants.notes:
The approach to camp is the standard Southern Pickets line: Goodell Creek trailhead, the old roadbed to the stone arrow at about 1,700 ft, the steep unmaintained climbers' path to treeline, Stump Hollow, and a crossing of the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin. This route's own camp is described as being BELOW THE CHOPPING BLOCK above Crescent Creek Basin rather than in the basin floor.

The first-ascent party left camp at 4 a.m. and was at the snow slope below the wall by 5 a.m. This is an eight-pitch line with a single published ascent, so treat the detail as one party's account rather than accumulated knowledge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE RACK-UP POINT IS A GRASSY COL, AND IT SITS 600 FT ABOVE THE SNOW. From the snow slope below the wall, climb roughly 600 FT OF EASY ROCK RAMPS AND LEDGES to a GRASSY COL at the base of the wall. That col is where the first-ascent party racked up, and it is the base of the route.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS THREE THINGS AND YOU CAN COUNT THEM IN CLOUD: camp, then a snow slope, then 600 ft of easy ramps, then grass in a gap with the wall rising above it. Grass underfoot at the foot of a steep wall is the confirmation; a rock ledge is not, and neither is the top of the snow.

TIMING AS A CHECK, BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE MEASUREMENT THE FIRST ASCENT LEFT: about an hour from camp to the snow slope below the wall. If you have been walking for three, you are not below Stonehenge.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing past the wall toward the narrow gully that climbs to the Himmel-Otto col puts you on the peak's standard route, which is a different objective and a different side of the mountain.

WHY THIS ENTRY IS SHORTER THAN ITS NEIGHBOURS: the route has one recorded ascent and its published description stops at the grassy col. Nothing locates a particular crack or flake at the start, and inventing one would be inventing the fact a party in fog would rely on.
hazards: A single published ascent, so no accumulated route-finding knowledge
600 ft of easy but unprotected ramps and ledges simply to reach the rack-up point
Loose rock on the descent through the notch between the summit tower and the adjacent pinnacle
The standard Southern Pickets approach: a relentlessly steep unmaintained path, no water, and a Barrier crossing

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Barrier notch and Stump Hollow, then the Crescent Creek Basin traverse to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit with parking but no trailhead sign, follow the old logging roadbed along the east bank of Goodell Creek. The first 1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts before a faint trail emerges in the timber; the tread then levels around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile.

Around mile 3.5, at about 1,700 ft, the trail crosses a stream, the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up the Barrier. Fill bottles there.

From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees, to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Heather benches and slabs then lead to the crest of the Barrier, a roughly 6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and a common bivy. From the notch, descend about 250 ft into Stump Hollow, then contour on a long rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin holding roughly the 5,800 ft level to a camp near Mount Terror and Himmelhorn.

A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS AT THE OTTOHORN-HIMMELHORN COL AND YOU CRAMPON THE LAST OF THE WAY THERE. From camp, continue the rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin toward the col, and crampon up the final snow and scree pitch to the col itself. Once melted out late season that last pitch turns to loose, chossy class 3-4 scrambling, with AN OVERHANGING BOULDER NEAR THE TOP sometimes forcing a chossy class 3 or 4 bypass on the LEFT.

SO THE OVERHANGING BOULDER IS THE ARRIVAL MARKER: one block near the top of the gully, passed on its left, and then the col. The route text stops at the col because the col is the start.

THE NEGATIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT LINE IN THIS ENTRY: FROM THE COL, THIS ROUTE GOES UP THE EAST RIDGE AND ITS WALK-OFF RETURNS DOWN THE SOUTH SIDE, BACK INTO CRESCENT CREEK BASIN. THE NORTH SIDE OF THE COL IS A DIFFERENT AND HARDER PROPOSITION. Parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn and the Mustard Glacier descend that side by a single-rope rappel from an established station about 150 ft below the col, or a steep snow couloir when well filled in. If you are looking down at a glacier and rigging a rappel, you are on the wrong side of the col for this route.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB, AND THE MEASUREMENTS ARE SMALL: from the col the summit is reported as easy scrambling, class 3, and parties have done it from the col in roughly an hour round trip, some without taking rope or rack out of camp. It is one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class. If you are on sustained fifth class you are not on the standard line.

ONE CONDITIONS-DEPENDENT COMPLICATION, RECORDED BECAUSE IT CHANGED A PARTY'S DAY: at least one party found the easy line broke into a FRESH ROCKFALL SCAR about 30 ft below the summit ridge and backed off rather than cross it, returning with a rope for about two pitches of juggy 5.7. Do not commit to the last 100 ft until you can see it.

THE MOAT AT THE COL IS THE THING TO SCOUT ON THE WAY UP: where the snow meets the rock it is a non-event when snow-filled early season and can be an overhanging pit by August. Note where you crossed it; you will want that on the way down.
hazards: A steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees on the Barrier climb
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose exposed bypass
A moat at the col that can become an overhanging pit by August
A fresh rockfall scar reported about 30 ft below the summit ridge
The north side of the col takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors; do not descend it by mistake
Steep grassy ledges on the Barrier that are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek climbers' path to the 6,200 ft notch and Terror Basin, then the Terror Glacier to the Inspiration-McMillan col gully
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Upper Group Campground trailhead just east of Goodell Creek Campground off SR-20 near Newhalem, pick up the unsigned climbers' path that starts BEHIND A LARGE BOULDER near the campground. There is reliable running water right at the start and then none again until Terror Basin.

The path switchbacks up through second-growth and old-growth forest along a spur ridge south of Terror Creek and is notorious for blowdown; expect to climb over or duck under dozens of downed logs for the first couple of miles. Around 3,200 ft it gains the crest of the forested ridge and settles into roughly 4,000 ft of gain over about 2 miles. Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, circles left, makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band at about 4,800 ft, then kicks up a final steep gully. Heather benches and open slabs then lead north for a couple of miles to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft, the high point of the approach.

The north side of that notch is the crux of the approach, not of the climb: in late-season low-snow conditions it is steep, loose, chossy terrain for about 400 vertical feet, and you should STAY SKIER'S RIGHT rather than going straight down. Early season it holds a firmer snow finger with a short headwall reported up to about 80 degrees for the last 20-30 ft, which some parties rope up for. Below the notch, a small flat gravelly basin near 5,800 ft with running water is the standard Terror Basin camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE FOOT OF A SNOW AND ROCK GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS THE ONLY ONE THAT LEADS TO A NAMED COL. From Terror Basin camp, a long traverse over benches and granite slabs, trending slightly downhill, reaches a GLACIAL LAKE OUTLET and then slabs below the Terror Glacier remnant. The glacier crossing is short and low-angle. This leads to the base of the snow and rock gully that climbs to the 7,200 FT COL BETWEEN INSPIRATION PEAK AND WEST MCMILLAN SPIRE, and that is where the technical climbing begins.

SO THE COUNTABLE HANDRAIL IS: camp, lake outlet, slabs, ice, gully. Three of those five are unmistakable underfoot in cloud. A lake outlet is running water leaving a lake; slabs are bare rock you can walk on; ice is ice.

WHAT DISCRIMINATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE OTHER LINE ON THE SAME SPIRE, AND IT IS THE END OF THE GLACIER YOU AIM FOR: this route takes the gully to the col between Inspiration and West McMillan. THE SOUTHWEST RIDGE ROUTE INSTEAD CONTINUES TO THE EAST END OF THE TERROR GLACIER. If you are walking east along the ice past the obvious gully, you are on the Southwest Ridge approach, not this one.

AND THE COL IS THE CONFIRMATION: axe and crampons get used in the gully even by parties who crossed the glacier unroped. Late in the season the gully loses its snow and the top of it can hold a moat where the snow has pulled back from the rock. Topping out of a steep snow gully into a gap between two peaks at about 7,200 ft is the start of the climbing.

ABOVE IT, THE ROUTE RELAXES, WHICH IS ITSELF A TEST: the ridge above the gully is a long, mellow 3rd to 4th class scramble on scree, heather and more scree, with no sustained difficulty. If the ground above the col is technical, you are not on the West Ridge.
hazards: Dozens of downed logs in the first couple of miles of the climbers' path
No water between the trailhead and Terror Basin
400 ft of steep, loose choss on the north side of the 6,200 ft notch late season; stay skier's right
An early-season snow finger with a headwall reported to about 80 degrees at the notch
A moat at the top of the summit gully late season
Poor footing and rockfall onto a party strung out below on the scree ridge
Concentrated exposure in the last few moves between the false and true summits

approach_variants.name: As for the West Ridge to the Terror Glacier, then all the way to the glacier's EAST end
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the West Ridge approach for its whole length: Goodell Creek trailhead, the climbers' path behind the large boulder, the blowdown-choked forest, the 6,200 ft notch and its loose north side, Terror Basin camp, the bench-and-slab traverse to the glacial lake outlet, and the slabs onto the Terror Glacier.

This is a six-pitch 5.8- line and the row carries little detail of its own beyond where on the glacier to leave it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHOLE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS ROUTE AND THE STANDARD ONE IS WHICH END OF THE GLACIER YOU STOP AT, AND IT IS A DIRECTIONAL TEST YOU CAN MAKE IN FOG. From the Terror Glacier, CONTINUE TO ITS EAST END to reach the base of the southwest ridge, RATHER THAN taking the west-ridge gully that the standard route uses.

SO: IF YOU HAVE ROPED UP AT THE FOOT OF A SNOW GULLY LEADING UP TO A COL, YOU ARE ON THE WEST RIDGE, NOT THIS. The West Ridge gully climbs to the 7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan. This route does not go there at all; it leaves the ice further east, on the spire's own southwest flank.

WHAT CONFIRMS IT AFTERWARDS, AND IT IS AN ASYMMETRY WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: the descent from the summit is by the WEST RIDGE, not by reversing this ridge. Parties downclimb the West Ridge's 3rd-4th class scramble and its snow and ice gully back onto the Terror Glacier rather than rappelling the southwest ridge. So you will meet the other route's ground on the way down whether you looked for it or not; a party that cannot find the west-ridge gully on the way up will have to find it on the way down anyway.

WHY THIS ENTRY DOES NOT NAME A FLAKE OR A CRACK AT THE TOE: nothing published locates one. The east end of the glacier is what is recorded, and it is a real, walkable, unmistakable limit rather than an invented marker.
hazards: The same 400 ft of loose choss on the north side of the 6,200 ft notch
A short glacier crossing that can show bare ice by late summer
A descent by a different route than the one you climbed, which has to be found while tired
No published marker at the toe of the ridge itself

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek to Terror Basin, then the Terror Glacier and the 40-degree snow gully to the West-East McMillan col
approach_variants.notes:
From SR-20 near Newhalem, park at the Goodell Creek Group Campground at about 600 ft just east of Goodell Creek. The climbers' path starts BEHIND A LARGE BOULDER at the back of the campground and climbs steeply north through forest, gaining a timbered ridge crest around 3,200 ft within the first 1.5-2 miles. Two creek crossings low on the path can run high and fast on hot afternoons from snowmelt.

The tread then eases onto roughly 4 miles of rougher, brushier but less steep going along the ridge, with deadfall and a handful of washouts, before reaching an obvious cairn around mile 3.5-4 where the route angles right and south to follow above Terror Creek. Benches of heather, slabs and rock lead into Terror Basin at about 5,800 ft, roughly 5,200 ft of gain and 6-7 miles in, the standard base camp with reliable water and flat tent sites.

From camp, a long ascending traverse across snow, slabs and heather, crossing a shallow snow-fed depression near 5,500 ft, gains the Terror Glacier below West McMillan Spire.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A SADDLE BETWEEN TWO SPIRES AND THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO IT, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART: A STEEP SNOW GULLY, OR A REDDISH LEDGE. From the Terror Glacier, continue up glacier and snow toward the col between WEST AND EAST MCMILLAN SPIRES. The standard line follows a steep snow gully that STEEPENS TO ROUGHLY 40 DEGREES FOR THE FINAL 200-300 FT to the saddle. Parties who prefer rock over steep snow instead follow a REDDISH, RIGHTWARD-TRENDING LEDGE SYSTEM and a short 4th-class rib on the TRUE-LEFT side of the gully to reach the same saddle.

SO THE COLOUR IS THE MARKER FOR THE ROCK VARIANT AND THE ANGLE IS THE MARKER FOR THE SNOW ONE. A gully that stays at a walking angle to the top is not this gully; this one kicks back hard for its last 200-300 ft.

ARRIVAL: the saddle. From it, easy but exposed 3rd-class scrambling along the connecting ridge crest, which is the west ridge, leads directly to East McMillan Spire's 7,992 ft summit. That last stretch is the whole climb.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE NEIGHBOURING SPIRE, AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH GULLIES RISE OFF THE SAME GLACIER: the col between INSPIRATION AND WEST MCMILLAN is the one the West McMillan route uses, at about 7,200 ft. The col between WEST AND EAST MCMILLAN is this one. If the summit above your col on the right is the one you just walked under, check which two peaks the gap is actually between before committing to the ridge.

WHAT THE DESCENT SAYS ABOUT THE BASE, WHICH IS A USEFUL CROSS-CHECK: the crux of the way down is the short rock step just below the saddle, and most parties make ONE rappel there off a natural anchor. One rappel, not a sequence. There is no fixed or bolted hardware anywhere on this route.
hazards: Two creek crossings low on the path that run high and fast on hot afternoons
Deadfall and washouts on an unmaintained boot path
Crevasses can open on the Terror Glacier despite firm late-season travel being common
A snow gully steepening to about 40 degrees for its final 200-300 ft
Exposure on the summit ridge, the route's main hazard on both ascent and descent
Loose, eroded tread on the steep upper section of the path on the way out

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone-arrow boot path to Terror Basin, then the crevassed Terror Glacier to the bergschrund below the west end of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground just west of Newhalem off SR-20 and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail. The first roughly 4 miles follow an old streamside roadbed at easy grades from about 500 to 1,600 ft, crossing the creek and passing the LAST RELIABLE FLOWING WATER AROUND 1,600 FT. Fill up there; the trail is dry above.

A cairned stone-arrow junction, sometimes marked and sometimes not, sends climbers off the valley trail onto a steep, switchback-free boot path that claws straight up the forested hillside, gaining roughly 3,400-4,000 ft in about a mile and a half of unrelenting root-and-dirt tree climbing with no water and no easy grades. Parties widely describe this as the crux of the whole approach.

The boot path breaks out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft into meadows, slabs and often snow, and a rising traverse north-northeast leads to a broad saddle at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. Camp is typically just below it in Terror Creek Basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A BERGSCHRUND AND CLIMBS 300 FT OF GULLY TO THE TOE OF THE RIDGE, AND THAT IS AN EXACT INSTRUCTION. From camp, cross heather and snow slopes trending north-northwest, losing a little elevation to cross the outlet drainage from a small tarn just southeast of the McMillan Spires, then regain ground on slabs and snow up to the edge of the Terror Glacier. LEAVE THE GLACIER AT THE BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END OF THE PEAK and climb roughly 300 FT OF GULLY to reach the toe of the west ridge, where the roped climbing begins.

SO THE SCHRUND IS THE MARKER AND THE 300 FT IS THE MEASURE. The schrund and the moat where snow meets rock are the variable part; they open through the season and the crossing is easiest with continuous snow early. A party that has climbed a short gully and reached the toe of a ridge is at the base; a party still on ice has not started.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE SOUTH FACE, WHICH STARTS OFF THE SAME GLACIER AND IS THE COMMONEST CONFUSION HERE: the SOUTH FACE starts at the LOWER-LEFT CORNER of the south face WHERE A SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS MEETS THE GLACIER. This route starts at the WEST END of the peak, at a schrund, and goes UP A GULLY FIRST. If you are roping up at a buttress toe that touches the ice directly, with no gully above you, you are on the South Face.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: the first pitches work through corner systems and LICHEN-COVERED LEDGES on compact rock where placements are scarce. Above them the line gains the crest itself and the rock quality improves steadily, described as extremely good on the crest. Total climbing above the schrund is about 1,300 ft in 14 pitches. If the rock is good from the first pitch, you are not on the lower corners of this route.

A HOUSEKEEPING RULE FROM THE ROUTE'S OWN PRACTICE: loose blocks sit on the lower ledges and the standard practice is to clear them deliberately once the second is out of the fall line rather than leave them for a following party.
hazards: A heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing below the peak's south side; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
A bergschrund and a moat at the base that open through the season
Compact rock with scarce placements on the lower pitches
Loose blocks on the lower ledges
No water for the last 3,500 ft of the climb to camp
A rappel descent of 12-14 stations, with traversing raps that are rockfall-prone and stations that are hard to spot

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek to the Glee Peak saddle camp, then through the Terror Glacier icefall to the buttress at the lower-left corner of the face
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the first ascent was made in mid-June in a low-snow year
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the small pullout just before Goodell Creek Campground at about 600 ft and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail heading north from the Highway 20 corridor. The first 3.75-4 miles follow an old, gently graded forest roadbed along Goodell Creek, brushy with some downed logs in the first mile, and crossing TWO BOULDER-STREWN WASHOUT SECTIONS where the tread disappears into the creek's flood debris and you pick a line across large boulders. That is the trickiest route-finding of the lower approach.

ABOUT 200 YARDS PAST THE SECOND WASHOUT, AT AN OBVIOUS CAMPSITE WITH A FIRE RING, an unsigned climbers' boot path breaks right off the roadbed, historically marked by a stone arrow on the ground at roughly 1,700 ft. That is the turn for Terror Basin; missing it means continuing pointlessly up the McMillan Spire approach.

From the turnoff the boot path climbs steeply and directly through forest, hand-over-hand in places on roots and branches, and breaks out of the trees around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline a rising traverse across meadow, slab and early-season snow reaches a saddle or notch at about 6,200 ft near Glee Peak; the standard camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. A seasonal trickle down a rock outcrop a few hundred feet below camp is the early-season water source; by late summer parties melt snow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AIM FOR THE LOWER-LEFT CORNER OF THE SOUTH FACE WHERE A SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS MEETS THE GLACIER. THAT BUTTRESS IS THE START OF THE ROUTE. It is a place where rock touches ice directly, with no intervening gully, and that is what tells it apart from the peak's other lines.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE WEST RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME GLACIER: the West Ridge leaves at a BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END of the peak and then climbs ABOUT 300 FT OF GULLY before any ridge. If there is a gully above you, you have gone past this route's corner and are set up for the West Ridge.

GETTING THERE IS THE ICEFALL PROBLEM, NOT A NAVIGATION ONE: from camp, rope up and cross the Terror Glacier. THE ICEFALL IN ITS MIDDLE IS BROKEN AND OFTEN HAS OPEN CREVASSES; parties commonly work a LEFT-TRENDING SNOW RAMP OR ICE BRIDGE ABOVE A LARGE CREVASSE to get through it onto gentler slopes beyond. That crossing gets more serious as the season progresses.

SO THE HANDRAIL THROUGH THE ICEFALL IS THE LARGE CREVASSE ITSELF: the way through is above it, trending left. If you are dropping below the big crevasse looking for a bridge, you are on the wrong side of the feature parties use.

A COUNTABLE APPROACH MARKER LOWER DOWN THAT SAVES THE WHOLE DAY: TWO WASHOUTS, then 200 yards, then a fire ring. That is how you find the turn in poor light. A stone arrow may or may not still be there; the second washout and the fire ring are ground features that do not move.
hazards: Two boulder-strewn washouts where the tread vanishes, the lower approach's route-finding crux
A broken Terror Glacier icefall with open crevasses that worsens through the season
A camp water source that dries out by late summer
A sustained multi-rappel descent down the West Ridge with no fixed or bolted stations anywhere on the peak
Loose rock in the descent gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on traversing rappels

approach_variants.name: As for the West Ridge and South Face to the Terror Glacier, then around and across the glacier BELOW the South Face to the col at the east end
approach_variants.notes:
Shares the Goodell Creek trailhead and the same long approach as the West Ridge and South Face: about 4 easy miles along the creek to roughly 1,600 ft and the last reliable water, then a steep switchback-free climbers' boot path grinding up 3,400-4,000 ft of forested hillside with no water to timberline around 5,000-5,200 ft, then a rising traverse on meadow, slab and snow to the broad saddle at 6,000-6,200 ft with camp just below it in Terror Creek Basin.

From camp the ground to the base runs across glacier-scoured slabs and onto the Terror Glacier beneath Inspiration's South Face. This is consistently rated one of the longer, more strenuous approaches in the North Cascades, and reaching the base alone typically consumes most of a full day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ROUTE YOU REACH BY KEEPING GOING, AND THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE STRONGEST THING ABOUT IT. Unlike the West Ridge and South Face lines, the East Ridge start is reached by CONTINUING AROUND AND ACROSS THE GLACIER BELOW THE SOUTH FACE and gaining a col at the far end that puts you at the true start of the ridge.

SO, IN ORDER, WHAT YOU PASS AND MUST NOT STOP AT: first the BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END with a 300 ft gully above it, which is the West Ridge. Then the SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS AT THE LOWER-LEFT CORNER OF THE SOUTH FACE where rock meets ice, which is the South Face. If you have roped up at either, you have stopped one or two routes short of this one. Keep walking east until the face ends and the ground rises to a gap.

ARRIVAL: a col at the east end of the peak. From there the ridge climbing begins IMMEDIATELY with sustained exposure, which is itself the confirmation. There is no walk-in above this col and no easing-off; if the ground above you is scrambling terrain, you are not on the East Ridge.

WHY THIS ENTRY IS HONEST ABOUT ITS LIMITS: nothing published names the col or gives it a height, and this is a Grade IV 5.9 with very light traffic. What is recorded is its POSITION IN A SEQUENCE, which is why the base finding is written as a sequence rather than as a feature.

AND THE FACT THAT SHOULD BE READ BEFORE STARTING, NOT AFTER: there is NO established East Ridge descent. The way down combines the upper West Ridge and the South Face, the same descent West Ridge climbers use, because the East Ridge is reported as distinctly poorer, looser rock for descending and nobody downclimbs it. So you will have to find the other two routes' ground anyway, in the dark, tired, from above.
hazards: A low-angle but heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
Sustained exposure from the first moves off the col
Poorer, looser rock than the peak's other lines
No established descent; the way down is 12-14 rappels on other routes' ground
An approach that consumes most of a full day before the climb starts
Parties commonly finish the exit after dark

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek log crossing, Stump Hollow to the Chopping Block camp, then the upper Barrier crossing
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Goodell Creek Trailhead at the Goodell Creek Group Camp, about 500-600 ft, off SR-20 just west of Newhalem. The first stretch follows an old logging-road grade and climbers' path along Goodell Creek for a little over a mile before narrowing to a boot-beaten track.

Roughly 1.5-2 miles in, near Roost Creek at about 1,600 ft, watch for the unmarked junction where the Terror Creek climbers' path splits off, historically flagged only by a rock arrow, a post and a large cairn. Route-finding here is a genuine crux; the path is well-defined at first but dies out into creek-bottom brush and devil's club lower down.

Cross Terror Creek at about 2,000 ft. THE CUSTOMARY CROSSING IS A LARGE LOG ROUGHLY 500 FT UPSTREAM OF WHERE THE PATH HITS THE CREEK, but in high water that log is sometimes submerged and parties have had to scout alternates. From the creek the path grinds directly up the opposing hillside, gaining close to 4,000 ft in under two miles through forest and then open heather. It eventually merges into Stump Hollow and follows the narrow crest north to the basecamp area near Chopping Block Camp at about 6,000-6,400 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS THE NOTCH IMMEDIATELY SOUTH OF THE SUMMIT, AND THAT NOTCH IS ALSO THE UPPER BARRIER CROSSING. Those are the same feature, which is what makes it findable: it is a place hundreds of parties pass through for a different reason. From camp, traverse Stump Hollow to the roughly 6,400 ft saddle near the Chopping Block, descend about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin, make the Barrier crossing, then cross a snowfield and small glacier below Degenhardt's south side and CLAW UP DIRT AND BROKEN ROCK TO THE NOTCH IMMEDIATELY SOUTH OF THE PEAK.

TWO BARRIER CROSSINGS EXIST AND THIS ROUTE WANTS THE HIGHER ONE: a LOWER crossing over loose ledges at the base of the Terror Glacier, or a HIGHER crossing over moats and steep choss near the top of the glacier JUST BELOW DEGENHARDT. The higher one is the preferred option precisely when Degenhardt, Pyramid or Terror is the objective, because it puts you at the notch. If you took the low ledges you will have to climb back up.

HOW YOU KNOW THE NOTCH WHEN YOU ARE IN IT, IN CLOUD: it is the top of the worst rock on the route, and the route's own description says this ground marks THE END OF ANY GOOD CLIMBING IN THE AREA. Dirt and broken rock underfoot steepening into a gap in a rib, with the Terror Glacier behind you and the ridge running north above you, is the place.

FROM THERE THE COUNT IS SHORT AND THE ERROR IS ALWAYS THE SAME ONE: follow the ridge north over exposed but moderate ground. PARTIES REPORT TRAVERSING MUCH TOO LOW AND HAVING TO REGAIN HEIGHT. Stay near the crest. A SMALL TOWER guards the final notch and is TURNED rather than climbed direct, and the last moves onto the summit are short 4th class on poor rock.

Degenhardt is widely regarded as the chossiest peak in the Southern Pickets. Helmets and careful rope management matter more than the grade suggests.
hazards: An unmarked junction at Roost Creek that is a genuine route-finding crux
A Terror Creek log crossing that can be submerged in high water
Close to 4,000 ft of gain in under two miles on steep, loose ground; a torn calf muscle is on record here
The Barrier: loose, exposed, and consistently described as feeling far harder than its class-3 rating
The chossiest rock in the Southern Pickets, with running meltwater over slabby sections as a slip hazard
Old, weathered tat on the one summit-tower rappel anchor

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Basin boot path, then over the Chopping Block col through McMillan Cirque to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground, follow the old abandoned roadbed and boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4-4.5 miles of gentle grade to a stone-cairn and arrow junction near 1,700 ft.

DO NOT CONTINUE STRAIGHT PAST THE CAIRN. That fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate, notoriously brushier approach. Instead take the HARD RIGHT and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly through old-growth forest, roughly 3,000-plus ft of gain in about 1.5 miles, before breaking out above treeline around 5,000-5,200 ft.

Above the trees a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs and early-season snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,700 ft, fed by several small streams.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWFIELD AT THE BOTTOM OF THE FACE, AFTER THE WALL IS ACCESSED FROM ITS WEST SIDE. From Terror Basin the technical start is reached by traversing over the Chopping Block col through McMillan Cirque, a steep, brushy descent past slabs and heather beneath Inspiration Peak and the McMillan Spires, before rounding into position under Terror's wall. Cross the glacier remnant beneath the face, then start JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWPATCH at the bottom.

THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK AT THE BASE IS THE USUAL OBSTACLE, AND IT IS ALSO THE MARKER: you are at the base when you are standing at the gap between the snowpatch and the wall, on its left.

THE DECISION THAT DEFINES THIS ROUTE, AND IT IS MADE BEFORE THE HARD CLIMBING RATHER THAN DURING IT: THE FACE IS SPLIT BY TWO RIBS, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE RIGHT, OR WESTERN, ONE. The main risk on the lower face is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib. Long, mostly third-class pitches climb above the snowfield while TRAVERSING STEADILY RIGHTWARD; the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse. If your traverse is taking you left, you are on the wrong half of the wall.

TWO CONFIRMATIONS HIGHER, BOTH VISUAL AND BOTH USABLE IN THIN CLOUD: aim for the right or western crest of the buttress about TWO THIRDS OF THE WAY UP THE LOWER FACE, IDENTIFIABLE BY THE ROCK DARKENING. And A SHARP PROW marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Darkening rock and a sharp prow are features of this rib and not of its neighbour.

WHAT THE UPPER FACE GIVES YOU: a LONG SNOW FINGER forming a ramp that carries the route a good distance, then scrambling on a wildly exposed crest, a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits, an exposed easy-fifth hand traverse over the false summit, a downclimb, and the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top.

On the descent, and worth memorising before you leave camp: DO NOT RAPPEL INTO THE LOW NOTCH NORTH OF THE CHOPPING BLOCK. The correct line into Crescent Creek Basin is ABOUT 100 YARDS NORTH OF THAT NOTCH, AT A FLAT, BIVY-SITE SHELF ON THE RIDGE.
hazards: Committing to the wrong rib on a 2,000 ft face with limited options to reverse
A heavily crevassed, mostly unbridged Terror Glacier remnant at the base by mid-season
Steep, extremely loose rock near the top; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a block that had appeared solid
A narrow, rockfall-prone descent gully with an undercut melted-out moat by mid to late season
Stuck ropes in the confined descent gully, and a loose, marginal final 100 ft
Retreat from high on the route is genuinely difficult

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and Terror Basin, over the Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin, then slabs and talus on the east side to the Terror-Degenhardt saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead off SR-20 near Newhalem, follow the old roadbed and Terror Basin climbers' path, about 4 miles then a steep cairned side trail, to the 5,800 ft Terror Basin camp, then continue over the roughly 6,400 ft Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin.

Note that the stored id for this row says southeast face while its name and aspect both say EAST RIDGE; see _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE SADDLE BETWEEN TERROR AND DEGENHARDT, AND YOU REACH IT FROM THE BASIN BY ITS EAST SIDE ON SLABS AND TALUS. That saddle is a gap between two named summits, which is what makes it findable without a view: ground rising on both sides of you, falling away ahead.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER LINES, AND IT IS A SIDE-OF-THE-MOUNTAIN TEST: the NORTH FACE and Stoddard Buttress are reached by going OVER the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col or through McMillan Cirque and down onto the north side, and they start at a snowpatch at the foot of a 2,000 ft wall. The WEST RIDGE tops out at the notch between Terror's true and false summits, marked by a large chockstone. This route starts from the Terror-Degenhardt saddle on the EAST. If you are on the north side of the mountain, or at a chockstone, you are not here.

ARRIVAL AT THE SADDLE: from Crescent Creek Basin the ground to it is slabs and talus, taken on the saddle's east side. Five pitches at Grade III-IV 5.6 follow. If you are on sustained harder ground, or on more than a handful of pitches, you are not on the East Ridge.

WHAT YOU DO NOT DO ON THE WAY DOWN, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING THE ROW RECORDS: the standard descent is NOT a reversal of this ridge. It is the WEST RIDGE GULLY back into Crescent Creek Basin, with multiple rappels off a large chockstone. So the day is a traverse of the peak, up one side and down the other, and the chockstone at the top of the west gully is the feature to identify from the summit.
hazards: A descent by a different route than the one climbed, off a large chockstone in a loose gully
The Chopping Block col and Crescent Creek Basin traverse before any climbing
Loose rock throughout, in a range where that is the defining characteristic
The full Goodell Creek approach with roughly 6,000 ft of gain to camp

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Terror Creek crossing and the flagged climber's track into Crescent Creek Basin, then the west gully to the chockstone notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed about 4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track marked with pink flagging past moss-covered cliffs, gaining roughly 1,600 ft, to reach Crescent Creek Basin. Total approach gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.

This is the standard descent route for every north-side line on the peak, so it sees traffic in both directions and its features are described mostly from above.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOP OF THIS ROUTE'S GULLY IS MARKED BY A LARGE CHOCKSTONE, AND THAT CHOCKSTONE IS THE SINGLE BEST FEATURE ON THE PEAK FOR ORIENTING IN CLOUD. From Crescent Creek Basin, the west gully system climbs to the notch between Terror's TRUE and FALSE summits, and a large chockstone sits at the head of it. Everything on this side is described relative to that block.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS COUNTABLE FROM BELOW: climb a narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully out of Crescent Creek Basin and keep going until a chockstone blocks it near the crest. That is the notch. Above it the route is a short summit tower.

THE ENTRY POINT IS THE THING PARTIES GET WRONG, AND IT IS RECORDED AS AN EXPLICIT WARNING FROM THE DESCENT SIDE: DO NOT USE THE LOW NOTCH NORTH OF THE SUB-PEAK KNOWN AS THE CHOPPING BLOCK. The correct line between Crescent Creek Basin and this ridge is ABOUT 100 YARDS NORTH OF THAT NOTCH, AT A FLAT, BIVY-SITE SHELF ON THE RIDGE. A flat shelf big enough to sleep on, 100 yards north of the obvious low notch, is the marker.

WHAT THE GULLY IS LIKE, SO YOU KNOW YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT ONE: narrow, with little shelter from rockfall, frequently holding an undercut melted-out snow moat by mid to late season, and with a loose and marginal final stretch. Roughly 3-5 rappels get parties down it, on a mix of pre-existing slings and natural chockstone and horn anchors.

AT THE TOP: the summit tower is downclimbed or a short section rappelled back to the notch off existing sling anchors. One short step, not a sequence.
hazards: A narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully with little shelter
An undercut, melted-out snow moat in the gully by mid to late season
A loose and marginal final 100 ft of the gully
Stuck ropes in the confined terrain
Rappelling into the wrong notch north of the Chopping Block
Early-season snow and ice in the choss gully

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then 40 ft LEFT along the base
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the hairpin turn on WA-20 just east of Washington Pass and park at the pullout on the curve. THIS IS A DIFFERENT TRAILHEAD FROM THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD used by the southwest and northwest face routes, and confusing the two costs an hour and a mountain.

Walk back toward the pass and find the small pond on the south side of the highway. A cairned climbers' path leaves the pond's EAST END and switchbacks up through forest for roughly a mile, breaking out into a talus field directly beneath Liberty Bell's East Face. The approach is short, about an hour, but steep in its upper section with loose talus underfoot near the top. No water; carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS, TRAVERSE 40 FT LEFT ON THIRD AND FOURTH CLASS LEDGES. That is the instruction and it is a measured one: forty feet, climber's left, on ledges you scramble rather than climb, and then the crack system starts.

LIBERTY CRACK IS THE REFERENCE LINE FOR THE WHOLE FACE, WHICH MEANS EVERY OTHER ROUTE HERE IS DESCRIBED AS SO-MANY-FEET LEFT OR RIGHT OF IT. Get this one right and the rest of the wall becomes navigable. Left to right along the base the order is: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft LEFT of Liberty Crack, then LIBERTY CRACK, then FREEDOM OR DEATH just right of it, then THIN RED LINE, then LIBERTY AND INJUSTICE FOR ALL about 10 m right of that, then LIVE FREE OR DIE, then THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE at the far right or north edge.

SO THE POSITIVE TEST IS: you are on the crack system that runs continuously up the centre of the wall, reached by scrambling LEFT rather than right from where the path meets the talus.

THE NEGATIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS IN POOR LIGHT: IF YOU ARE LOOKING AT A SMALL LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP WITH BOLTS VISIBLE ABOVE IT, YOU ARE ON FREEDOM OR DEATH, ONE LINE TO THE RIGHT. And if you scrambled RIGHT from the talus instead of left, you are among the Thin Red Line and Independence starts, which are further right again.

WHERE THE ROUTE ENDS AND HOW YOU GET DOWN, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHICH CAR YOU WALK BACK TO: this line tops out at the same alcove and bolted anchor the original aid route uses. From there, ledges lead to a double-bolt rap anchor and two rappels drop into the BECKEY GULLY, the same rap line the standard Liberty Crack and Beckey Route descents use, landing near a tree anchor. That gully runs down to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch on the WEST side of the mountain, which is the opposite side from the East Face pullout you parked at.
hazards: Loose talus in the upper approach
No water on the approach
A start that is only forty feet from a different route's start
A descent that lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face trailhead
Snow lingering in the base talus into early summer

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then the leftward-trending ramp just RIGHT of Liberty Crack
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. Roughly an hour, steep near the top, no water.

Four pitches, all belays bolted. The route can be rappelled with a 60 m rope from the top of pitch 3, or continued into the shared terrain of Liberty Crack toward the summit.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS A SMALL LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP, AND BOLTS SHOULD BE VISIBLE ABOVE IT. That is the whole test, it is visual, and it works at arm's length in cloud where nothing else on this wall does: a ramp leaning LEFT, low down, with bolts on the face above it.

POSITION: JUST TO THE RIGHT OF LIBERTY CRACK. Not fifty yards right, just right. If you had to walk more than a few paces from the base of Liberty Crack, you have gone past it toward the Thin Red Line starts.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: LIBERTY CRACK IS REACHED BY TRAVERSING 40 FT LEFT ON 3RD AND 4TH CLASS LEDGES FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS. IF YOU ARE SCRAMBLING LEFT ON LEDGES, YOU HAVE OVERSHOT PAST THIS ROUTE IN THE WRONG DIRECTION.

A SECOND CONFIRMATION IF THE RAMP IS AMBIGUOUS: this is a four-pitch route with EVERY BELAY BOLTED. There is no gear anchor to hunt for at the top of pitch 1. If you finish a rope length and find no bolts, you are not on it.

AND THE ROUTE THAT SHARES THIS START, WHICH IS WHY GETTING IT RIGHT MATTERS TWICE: A Servant to Liberty climbs the first THREE pitches of this route before stepping right into Thin Red Line. Two parties standing at the same ramp may be going to two different places.
hazards: A start only a few paces from Liberty Crack's, on a wall where several routes begin within a short distance
Loose talus in the upper approach
No water on the approach
Rappelling from the top of pitch 3 needs a 60 m rope

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the Freedom or Death ramp
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as Freedom or Death and Thin Red Line: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

This route was established rope-solo in August 2016 and originally documented under an earlier name. It climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death, then steps right to join Thin Red Line for its upper pitches.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE DOES NOT HAVE A START OF ITS OWN. IT STARTS ON FREEDOM OR DEATH, AND THAT IS THE FACT TO CARRY UP THE TALUS. So the base finding is Freedom or Death's base finding: A SMALL LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP JUST TO THE RIGHT OF LIBERTY CRACK, WITH BOLTS VISIBLE ON THE FACE ABOVE IT.

WHY THAT IS ACTUALLY USEFUL RATHER THAN A DODGE: it means you are not hunting for a fifth start among the East Face cluster. There are three pitches of shared, well-bolted climbing before this route becomes its own thing, and the decision point is up on the wall where you can see it, not down in the talus where you cannot.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: LIBERTY CRACK IS 40 FT LEFT ALONG THIRD AND FOURTH CLASS LEDGES FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS. If you are scrambling left on ledges you are heading for Liberty Crack. If you have walked well right past a series of starts you are among the Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice and Independence lines.

COUNTABLE ON THE CLIMB: three pitches of 5.10, 5.11 and 5.11, then a step RIGHT. If you are still going straight up after three pitches you have missed the junction with Thin Red Line.

AND THE DESCENT FOLLOWS THIN RED LINE'S, NOT FREEDOM OR DEATH'S: rappel with two ropes off M&M Ledge from a fixed pin and wire, then move climber's-left to bolted anchors for four double-rope rappels back to the base. Five rappels, all on bolted stations after the first.
hazards: No independent start; a party that mislocates Freedom or Death mislocates this route
A fixed pin and wire as the first rappel anchor off M&M Ledge
Two ropes needed for the descent
Loose talus in the upper approach

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then RIGHT of Liberty Crack
approach_variants.notes:
From the Highway 20 hairpin curve on the east side of Washington Pass, locate the small pond on the south side of the road; the pullout is on the north side of the highway. Follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond eastward into forest and up to the East Face talus.

Note that this row's stored trailhead coordinate does not agree with the one every other East Face row on this peak carries; see _DEFECTS. Use the pond and the hairpin, not a stored point.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS CLIMBER'S RIGHT OF LIBERTY CRACK, AND THE PUBLISHED METHOD FOR FINDING IT IS TO WORK DOWNWARD FROM THE FEATURES ABOVE RATHER THAN ALONG THE BASE. Look climber's right of Liberty Crack and connect the line down from the features higher on the wall. Some mellow snow travel is usually necessary to reach the base.

SO THIS IS THE ONE EAST FACE ROUTE WHOSE START IS HONESTLY DESCRIBED AS A SIGHTING PROBLEM, AND THAT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE THE CLOUD COMES DOWN. Fix the line from the talus while you can see the wall. If you cannot see the wall, you cannot locate this start by walking the base, and no description will change that.

WHAT YOU CAN DO WITHOUT A VIEW IS BOUND IT, BECAUSE THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE IS KNOWN. Left to right: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, LIBERTY CRACK, FREEDOM OR DEATH just right of it on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, THIN RED LINE, LIBERTY AND INJUSTICE FOR ALL about 10 m right of Thin Red Line, LIVE FREE OR DIE, and THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE at the far right or north edge of the face beneath a red roof and alcove called the Baer Ceiling about 85 m up.

SO: IF YOU ARE STANDING AT A LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP WITH BOLTS ABOVE IT, YOU ARE ONE ROUTE LEFT, ON FREEDOM OR DEATH. IF YOU CAN SEE A RED ROOF ABOUT 85 M ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE WALKED ALL THE WAY RIGHT TO THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE.

THE DESCENT DECIDES WHICH CAR YOU END AT, AND THIS ROUTE HAS BOTH OPTIONS: from the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face, returning to your pack and the East Face approach. If you instead continue to the true summit and take the standard Liberty Bell notch descent, you finish on the WEST side of the mountain and need a shuttle or a road walk back.
hazards: A start that has to be sighted from a distance rather than found along the base
Snow travel at the base into early summer
Several route starts within a short distance of each other on the same wall
A summit descent that strands you on the opposite side of the mountain from your car

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then about 10 metres right of Thin Red Line
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as the other Liberty Crack-area routes: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

Five pitches, about 200 m of climbing, established rope-solo in 2014. It shares some climbing with the old aid route Liberty Loop.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS ABOUT 10 METRES RIGHT OF THIN RED LINE, AND TEN METRES IS THE ENTIRE MARGIN FOR ERROR ON THIS WALL. That is a measured offset from a known line, which is the best that exists here, and it means you must locate Thin Red Line first.

HOW TO BOUND IT WITHOUT SEEING THE WHOLE FACE, USING THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft LEFT of Liberty Crack, then LIBERTY CRACK, then FREEDOM OR DEATH on a small leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, then THIN RED LINE, then THIS ROUTE 10 m right of it, then LIVE FREE OR DIE, then THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE at the far right or north edge under a red roof.

THE STRONGEST CONFIRMATION IS THE HARDWARE, AND IT IS COUNTABLE: EVERY STATION ON THIS LINE IS A TWO-BOLT ANCHOR WITH FIXED BINERS. If you top out a pitch and find no bolts and no biners, you are not on it. From the top of pitch 3 you can skip the pitch-2 anchor and rappel directly to the pitch-1 anchor, so two rappels get you back to the ground from P3.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: keep walking right and the next thing you meet is the ground Live Free or Die and the Independence Route use, at the far right end of the face. The Independence Route's own marker is unmistakable when visible: a red-coloured roof and alcove, the Baer Ceiling, about 85 m above its start.

AND WHERE IT GOES: at five pitches the route joins the top of pitch 7 on Thin Red Line, from which you either continue climbing or rappel Thin Red Line's line back to the base.
hazards: A ten-metre offset from a neighbouring route as the only positional marker
Several closely spaced starts on the same wall
Loose talus in the upper approach
Two ropes needed if descending Thin Red Line's line from high on the route

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the ground between Thin Red Line and the Independence Route
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as Liberty Crack: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face.

Eleven pitches, climbed in 2017. The route takes the East Face for eight pitches to M&M Ledge at roughly mid-height, then shares its final three or four pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS SANDWICHED, AND THE SANDWICH IS THE TEST: IT LIES TO THE LEFT OF THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE AND TO THE RIGHT OF THIN RED LINE. Those two neighbours are the most identifiable lines at that end of the face, so bound the ground between them and the route is inside it.

THE RIGHT-HAND BOUND IS THE ONE YOU CAN SEE FROM FURTHEST AWAY: the Independence Route starts at the FAR RIGHT, or NORTH, EDGE of the East Face, and a RED-COLOURED ROOF AND ALCOVE, the Baer Ceiling, sits about 85 m above its start. If a red roof is above you, you have walked one route too far right.

THE LEFT-HAND BOUND: Thin Red Line is climber's right of Liberty Crack, and Liberty and Injustice for All sits about 10 m right of Thin Red Line on two-bolt anchors with fixed biners. If you are at a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners a rope length up, you started too far left.

AN HONEST WARNING FROM THE FIRST ASCENT, AND IT CHANGES HOW YOU READ THE WALL: the party recorded that the route's initial crack pitches WERE 700 FT UP THE WALL and seemed to have been reached by rappel from other routes, with no obvious way to reach them from below. So the visible feature that names this route is not at its base. Do not try to identify the line by the cracks; identify the ground between Thin Red Line and Independence and start there.

DESCENT, WHICH IS THIN RED LINE'S: from M&M Ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber's-left to a set of bolted anchors and make four double-rope rappels back to the talus at the base of the East Face. All stations on that exit are bolted; no natural or v-thread anchors are involved.
hazards: The route's identifying crack pitches sit roughly 700 ft up the wall, not at its base
A start defined only by the two routes on either side of it
A fixed pin and wire as the first rappel anchor off M&M Ledge
Two ropes needed for the descent
Loose talus in the upper approach

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then all the way RIGHT to the north edge of the face
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face.

TWELVE PITCHES, FIRST CLIMBED WALL-STYLE IN 1966 WITH 180 PITONS AND FIVE BOLTS OVER FOUR DAYS, and later freed. The line takes the profusely overhanging northeast corner of the East Face and joins Thin Red Line at M&M Ledge.

THE ROW'S OWN STORED APPROACH DESCRIBES THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD AND FOURTH-CLASS LEDGES ACROSS THE WEST FACE. That contradicts every published account of this route and is recorded in _DEFECTS; the approach written here is the East Face one.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
START ON THE FAR RIGHT, THE NORTH EDGE, OF THE EAST FACE, AND CONFIRM IT BY LOCATING THE RED-COLOURED ROOF AND ALCOVE OF THE BAER CEILING ABOUT 85 M ABOVE. That is the marker, it is coloured, it is high enough to be visible when the base is in cloud, and no other route on this wall has one.

SO THE TEST IS A COLOUR AND A HEIGHT: a red roof roughly 85 metres up, at the right-hand end of the face. If there is no red roof above you, keep walking right.

THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE, WHICH BOUNDS IT ON THE OTHER SIDE: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft LEFT of Liberty Crack, LIBERTY CRACK, FREEDOM OR DEATH on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, THIN RED LINE, LIBERTY AND INJUSTICE FOR ALL 10 m right of that, LIVE FREE OR DIE, and THIS ROUTE last. You cannot go further right and still be on the East Face; the ground beyond turns the corner onto the northeast aspect, where Dark Side of Liberty lives.

A SECOND CONFIRMATION FROM THE SHAPE OF THE ROCK: this is the PROFUSELY OVERHANGING northeast corner. If the wall above your start leans back rather than out, you have not reached the corner.

WHERE IT GOES, WHICH ALSO SETTLES THE DESCENT ARGUMENT: the route joins Thin Red Line at M&M Ledge, so the natural exit is Thin Red Line's bolted rappel line back down the East Face to your pack, rather than continuing to the true summit and finishing on the far side of the mountain.
hazards: A profusely overhanging corner, first climbed over four days with 180 pitons
A stored approach description that sends parties to the wrong trailhead and the wrong side of the mountain
Several closely spaced starts on the same wall
Loose talus in the upper approach

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then LEFT along the base to the loose corner system
approach_variants.notes:
Standard East Face approach: park at the pond pullout near the hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile to the East Face talus.

Fourteen pitches. Although it is technically the easiest all-free route up the East Face, the route takes about one and a half times as much effort as Liberty Crack, on often poor rock and gear, and apart from where it intersects Liberty Crack there are no bolted belay stances.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ONLY ROUTE ON THE EAST FACE THAT STARTS TO THE LEFT OF LIBERTY CRACK, AND THAT MAKES IT THE EASIEST START ON THE WALL TO CONFIRM BY ELIMINATION. It begins at a LOOSE CORNER SYSTEM ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF LIBERTY CRACK.

SO THE TEST IS DIRECTIONAL AND COUNTABLE: from Liberty Crack, walk LEFT roughly 100 ft to a corner system. Every other line here is to the RIGHT of Liberty Crack. IF YOU ARE WALKING RIGHT ALONG THE BASE, YOU ARE WALKING AWAY FROM THIS ROUTE, and everything you meet in that direction belongs to something else: Freedom or Death, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All, Live Free or Die and the Independence Route in that order.

AND LIBERTY CRACK ITSELF IS FOUND BY TRAVERSING 40 FT LEFT ON THIRD AND FOURTH CLASS LEDGES FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS, so this route is roughly 140 ft of leftward travel from where the path meets the rock.

A HARDWARE TEST THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY FROM THE REST OF THIS FACE: there are NO BOLTED BELAY STANCES on this route except where it crosses Liberty Crack. Several of its neighbours are fully bolted. IF YOU REACH A BOLTED ANCHOR EARLY, YOU ARE PROBABLY NOT ON FREEDOM RIDER.

WHAT TO EXPECT SO YOU DO NOT SECOND-GUESS THE FIND: the corner system is described as loose, and the rock and gear on the route generally as often poor. Poor rock at the start is consistent with this line, not evidence you are off it.

DESCENT: the shared East Face rappel line into Beckey Gully, or downclimbing the sheltered Beckey Route slab in good conditions. Both put you on the west side of the mountain, away from the East Face pullout.
hazards: Poor rock and poor gear over fourteen pitches
No bolted belays except where the line crosses Liberty Crack
Roughly one and a half times the effort of Liberty Crack for an easier grade
A descent that lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the trailhead

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout, then contour off the East Face path onto the NORTHEAST aspect
approach_variants.notes:
The shortest approach of the major Liberty Bell technical lines. The first-ascent party describe the wall as about 20 minutes from the road. Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, the same general area as the East Face approach, and follow the cairned path from the pond toward the East Face.

Ten pitches, 1,100 ft, bolted ground-up by rappel over two seasons and completed in August 2019. Expect scrambling and scree underfoot near the base; carry a helmet through the loose sections.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS A TIME AND A TURN: ABOUT TWENTY MINUTES FROM THE ROAD, AND YOU LEAVE THE EAST FACE PATH BEFORE IT REACHES THE MAIN EAST FACE TALUS. Contour toward the NORTHEAST aspect of the wall rather than continuing all the way in. If you have walked a full hour and are standing in the big talus field under the East Face, you have gone past this route and are under Liberty Crack's wall instead.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE STRONGEST ONE HERE, BECAUSE THE POSITIVE ONE IS SHORT: THE EAST FACE APPROACH TAKES ABOUT AN HOUR. THIS ONE TAKES ABOUT TWENTY MINUTES. A THREEFOLD DIFFERENCE IN WALKING TIME IS MEASURABLE IN ANY VISIBILITY.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: the wall is 1,100 ft on the northeast face, and it is the ground BEYOND the right-hand, north end of the East Face. The Independence Route marks that end, at the profusely overhanging northeast CORNER with a red roof, the Baer Ceiling, about 85 m up. Dark Side is round the corner from it.

CONFIRM BY THE HARDWARE, WHICH IS DISTINCTIVE ON THIS PEAK: the route was bolted with ANCHORS AT ROUGHLY 40 M INTERVALS ALONG GOOD STANCES, all fixed and bolted, so no natural gear is needed to descend it. Most parties rappel the route itself on a single 80 m rope, working out at eight or nine rappels of up to 40 m. A fully bolted rap line at even 40 m spacing is not what any other line on this mountain offers.
hazards: Scree and scrambling near the base, with rockfall potential
A 5.13-plus grade over ten pitches with no easier escape
An 80 m rope needed to rappel the route as designed
A short approach that makes it tempting to start without a full weather margin

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path toward Concord, then the ten-foot step onto the northwest plateau
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,200-5,400 ft on WA-20 roughly 1.5 miles WEST of Washington Pass, follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles through forest to a small meadow below Liberty Bell. THIS IS THE OPPOSITE TRAILHEAD FROM THE HAIRPIN POND PULLOUT USED BY THE EAST FACE ROUTES.

Leave the Blue Lake Trail on the well-beaten climbers' path that splits LEFT just past a small stream crossing, and follow it up through slabs, talus and heather benches toward Concord Tower. Roughly 2,000-plus ft of gain over 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The gully below the plateau can hold snow into early summer and sheds rockfall as it melts, so helmet up through the talus and gully.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ENTIRE FIND IS A TEN-FOOT STEP, AND THE ROUTE'S OWN DESCRIPTION MAKES IT A NEGATIVE TEST: IF YOU ARE CLIMBING MORE THAN ABOUT TEN FEET OF EASY FOURTH OR LOW-FIFTH CLASS TO GAIN THE PLATEAU, YOU HAVE MISSED THE SPOT.

HOW YOU GET TO IT: rather than dropping into the main Beckey and Liberty Bell-Concord gully, STAY ON THE CLIMBERS' TRAIL AS IT CLIMBS TOWARD CONCORD FOR AS LONG AS IT REASONABLY CAN, then break LEFT onto that short, well-trodden step. The step gains the little-visited northwest plateau of Liberty Bell, a bench of LARCH GROVES below the northwest face proper.

SO THERE ARE TWO CONFIRMATIONS AND BOTH WORK WITHOUT SEEING THE SUMMIT: the step is TEN FEET AND WELL-TRODDEN, and above it you are standing on a BENCH WITH LARCH TREES ON IT. Larches on a bench, on the northwest side, below a wall, is the plateau.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTES OFF THIS PATH, WHICH IS WHERE PARTIES ACTUALLY GO WRONG: if you have dropped into the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord and are climbing scree toward a notch, you are on the Beckey Route and Overexposure approach, not this one. THIS ROUTE NEVER ENTERS THAT GULLY.

WHERE THE DAY ENDS UP, WHICH IS NOT WHERE IT STARTED: from the west summit you downclimb and scramble to the top of the Beckey Route line and descend that way rather than reversing the northwest face. Rappel about 20 ft down the upper Beckey pitch to a ledge, traverse left, east, to a TREE HUNG WITH RAP SLINGS, one single-rope 60 m rappel to a flatter stance, then a double-rope rappel from a bolted anchor to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft, and downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers' path.
hazards: A rockfall-prone approach gully that holds snow into early summer
A ten-foot step that is easy to overshoot, leading parties onto harder ground
Queues at the popular Beckey rappels in busy weather; parties have reported stacking up several deep
One pitch of the descent can run slightly over 60 m, so a single-rope party may have to downclimb a short section
A loose gully downclimb from the notch

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Beckey gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then scramble ABOVE it
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route as far as the notch: Blue Lake Trailhead and Forest Trail #314, about 1.5 miles of maintained trail to the small meadow and stream crossing, then the climbers' boot path through slabs, talus and meadow to the fork below the notch, staying LEFT to the notch itself at about 7,300 ft. Roughly 2 miles and 2,100 ft of gain, 1.5-2.5 hours.

Expect the same early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS RIGHT AT THE TOP OF THE NOTCH BETWEEN LIBERTY BELL AND CONCORD TOWER, AND SPECIFICALLY IT BEGINS ABOVE THE NOTCH RATHER THAN AT IT. That distinction is the whole find: Beckey Route parties stop at the notch and start climbing from it. This route asks for a little extra scrambling UP from the notch into the initial belay.

WHICH NOTCH, BECAUSE THERE ARE TWO ON THIS RIDGE AND THEY ARE ONLY A FEW HUNDRED FEET APART: the LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD notch, at about 7,300 ft, is the one this route uses. The CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch is further along and serves Concord's south face and Lexington's north face. The discriminating test at the top of the gully is what the wall in front of you offers: THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH FACES A CRACK SYSTEM. The Concord-Lexington notch gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges.

SO: CRACK SYSTEM IN FRONT OF YOU AT THE TOP OF THE GULLY MEANS YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT NOTCH FOR THIS ROUTE.

CONFIRM BY THE LENGTH OF THE CLIMB, WHICH IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: four pitches at Grade II 5.8, and THE SECOND PITCH TOPS OUT AT THE SAME BOLTED ANCHOR SYSTEM THAT STARTS THE STANDARD LIBERTY BELL DESCENT. Most parties either stop there or continue a few hundred feet of fourth and low-fifth scrambling to the true summit. If you have climbed four pitches and are nowhere near a bolted descent anchor, you are not on this route.

BUDGET EXTRA TIME AND CARE FOR THE SCRAMBLE INTO THE FIRST BELAY compared with Beckey Route parties, because it is exposed and it is where this route differs.
hazards: Exposed opening moves off the notch, above the gully
Early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe
Rockfall in the approach gully as it melts out
Two notches on the same ridge that are easy to confuse
Congestion at the main descent line, which shares anchors with the Beckey Route

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path, then RIGHT at the gully fork to the Beckey Route start
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the meadow, then take the climbers' path left past the small stream up through slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.

Four pitches at 5.8. The route shares its FIRST PITCH with the Beckey Route, so the approach is the standard Beckey approach to the same base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FORK IN THE GULLY IS THE DECISION, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE RIGHT-HAND BRANCH. Follow the standard Beckey approach and STAY RIGHT AT THE GULLY FORK to reach the same base the Beckey Route uses. This route's first pitch IS the Beckey Route's first pitch, so if you are on Beckey's first pitch you are on route.

THE NEGATIVE TEST, AND IT COVERS THE TWO WAYS PARTIES LEAVE THIS APPROACH: STAY LEFT AT THE FORK and you are heading for Serpentine Crack and the Independence-style ledges across the west face. NEVER DROP INTO THE GULLY AT ALL, staying instead on the climbers' trail toward Concord and breaking left onto a ten-foot step, and you are on the Northwest Face approach to the larch-covered northwest plateau. Both are different routes on the same mountain from the same trailhead.

WHAT MAKES THIS ROUTE'S EXIT DIFFERENT, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE THING THAT SETS IT APART LATER: after the scramble and short 5.6 slab to the ridge, you downclimb the ridge and a 5.6 boulder problem, then follow AN OBVIOUS, TREE-FILLED GULLY EAST to the first set of rappel bolts, and two single-rope rappels reach the ground. THAT IS A DISTINCT EXIT FROM THE MAIN BECKEY AND NOTCH DESCENT LINE: it drops climber's RIGHT, east, into its own gully rather than back toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. A tree-filled gully heading east is the marker.
hazards: A gully fork where left and right lead to entirely different routes
Early-season snow and rockfall in the approach gully
A 5.6 boulder problem downclimbed on the descent
An exit gully separate from the peak's main descent line, so a party following the crowd will end up somewhere else

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Beckey gully, stopping a couple of hundred feet BELOW the notch at the side gully with the large cave
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Beckey line: Blue Lake Trailhead, about 1.5 miles of maintained trail to the meadow and stream crossing, then the climbers' boot path up through slabs, talus and meadow into the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.

Three pitches. The route rejoins the Beckey Route line near its top, so the descent is the standard two single-rope rappels off chain and bolted anchors down to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STOP SHORT OF THE NOTCH. A COUPLE OF HUNDRED VERTICAL FEET BELOW THE TOP OF THE LIBERTY-CONCORD NOTCH, LOCATE A SIDE GULLY ON CLIMBER'S LEFT WITH A LARGE CAVE IN IT. Walk partway up that side gully, then move RIGHT onto a TREED LEDGE to start.

SO THERE ARE THREE THINGS TO FIND AND ALL THREE ARE TACTILE RATHER THAN VISUAL: a SIDE GULLY on the left, a LARGE CAVE inside it, and a LEDGE WITH TREES on its right-hand side. Trees on a ledge are unmistakable underfoot.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE MOST USEFUL LINE HERE, BECAUSE THE ERROR IS ALWAYS THE SAME ONE: IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE NOTCH, YOU HAVE GONE ROUGHLY TWO HUNDRED FEET TOO FAR. This route leaves the main gully below its top. Everything at the notch itself belongs to the Beckey Route, Overexposure and the standard descent.

A SECOND ROUTE SHARES THE CAVE, SO THE LEDGE IS WHAT SEPARATES THEM: Sidewinder also scrambles to a major shelf or ramp BELOW the cave feature. This route goes PARTWAY UP the side gully and then steps RIGHT onto the treed ledge. Below the cave is Sidewinder's ground; up and right of it is this one.

WHERE IT GOES: three pitches rejoining the Beckey Route near its top, then the standard two single-rope rappels off chains to the notch and the gully back to the trail.
hazards: A start that is passed by every party heading for the notch
A cave feature shared with a neighbouring route
Rockfall in the main gully, which sits directly above the start
Early-season snow in the approach gully

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then up and LEFT into the Concord-Lexington gully rather than the Liberty Bell-Concord one
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft, roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop and a quarter mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook. A day-use fee or Northwest Forest or Interagency pass is required and the small lot fills early. Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the LEFT, marked by a large cairn.

The South Face routes are reached from the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which is a DIFFERENT SADDLE from the Liberty Bell-Concord col that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. Rather than trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers; higher up, a reasonable climbers' path appears along its LEFT side and is better than fighting up the gully bed. It sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT SADDLE WHEN CONCORD IS ON ONE SIDE OF YOU AND LEXINGTON IS ON THE OTHER, AND THE CONCORD WALL IN FRONT OF YOU GIVES ONTO LOW-ANGLE, GRAVELLY LEDGES RATHER THAN A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM. IF YOU ARE FACING A CRACK SYSTEM, YOU ARE AT THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH AND LOOKING AT THE NORTH FACE.

That is the notch test, and it is the one that matters, because the two saddles are a few hundred feet apart on the same ridge and both are reached from the same trailhead by the same path.

ARRIVAL AT THIS PARTICULAR ROUTE, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM ARRIVAL AT THE NOTCH: LOOKING FROM THE NOTCH, START UP THE OBVIOUS CRACK IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WALL. This route takes the centre of Concord's south face, climbs through a bulge, and continues trending LEFT. Two right-facing corners put you at a TREE right below the summit block.

SO THE COUNT IS: one crack in the middle, one bulge, two right-facing corners, one tree. If your line runs up the edge of the wall rather than its centre, you are on the tower's other south-face route.

WHY THE NOTCH TEST AND THE ROUTE TEST BOTH MENTION CRACKS WITHOUT CONTRADICTING EACH OTHER: at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch a STEEP crack system rises directly in front of you, which is the North Face. At the Concord-Lexington notch the wall reads as low-angle and gravelly overall, and this route's crack is the obvious feature UP THE MIDDLE of that easier-angled wall. Judge the wall first, then the line.

DESCENT: downclimb or make one full double-rope rappel from the summit back to the notch; with a single rope, use two shorter rappels off intermediate anchor stations.
hazards: Two notches a few hundred feet apart on one ridge, reached by the same path
A gully bed that is better avoided in favour of the path along its left side
Far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col, so less obvious tread
A small trailhead lot that fills early

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then DROP 50 feet down the north side
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft, roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop and about a quarter mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest or Interagency pass is required.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climbers' boot path breaking off just past a small stream, climbing through slabs, talus and meadow to the gully between LIBERTY BELL AND CONCORD TOWER. That gully is often snow-filled and icy into late June and carries high rockfall risk after snowmelt.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE NOTCH, DROP ABOUT 50 FEET DOWN THE GULLY ON THE NORTH SIDE OF CONCORD TOWER TO THE START OF THE TWO DIAGONAL CRACKS THAT MARK THE ROUTE. That is a measured descent and a countable feature: fifty feet down, then TWO cracks running diagonally.

SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU GO DOWN, NOT UP. Every other line off this notch starts at the notch or above it. If you have arrived at the notch and started climbing straight away, you are on the standard North Face or one of its variations, not on this route.

WHICH NOTCH, BECAUSE THE PEAK HAS TWO AND THEY ARE REACHED THE SAME WAY: this is the LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD notch, and the test at the top of the gully is that A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM RISES IN FRONT OF YOU. If instead the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges, you are at the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which serves the tower's south face, and you are on the wrong side of Concord.

COUNTABLE ON THE ROUTE: three pitches at 5.8 R. If you are more than three pitches up and still climbing, you have linked into something else.

DESCENT: the same as the standard North Face. Rappel chains at the summit allow a doubled-rope rappel toward the notch, or downclimb and scramble back to it.
hazards: An approach gully that is often snow-filled and icy into late June
High rockfall risk in the gully after snowmelt
A 5.8 R grade, so a fall on the wrong ground is consequential
Two notches on one ridge reached by the same path

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout, the steep forest path, and the treed ledge below the east face
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pond pullout on the south side of SR-20 about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass, a small dirt turnout marked by a roadside pond. The climbers' path starts just left, west, of the highway's east-side guardrail and immediately begins gaining elevation through forest.

It pops out of the trees onto an open scree-and-boulder slope that climbs directly toward the Liberty Bell group towers, with Lexington Tower's east face visible above. Figure 30-45 minutes, some parties closer to an hour, of steep hiking and scrambling from the pullout to the base, gaining several hundred feet over roughly a third of a mile. No water; carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A TREED LEDGE, AND THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO IT AND SNOW DECIDES WHICH. From the talus, either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge. Snow lingering in the talus and at the base of the wall into early-mid summer affects whether you gain the ledge from the left or the right.

SO THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A LEDGE WITH TREES ON IT, PART WAY UP THE WALL, NOT GROUND LEVEL. Trees underfoot on a bench beneath a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation, and it works without seeing the tower above.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE FROM THE SAME LEDGE, AND IT IS A LEFT-RIGHT TEST: TOOTH AND CLAW BEGINS NEAR THE LEFT SIDE OF THE TREED LEDGE AND ANGLES RIGHTWARD ACROSS SLABS TO ITS FIRST BOLT. If you are traversing right across slabs looking for a bolt, you are on Tooth and Claw, a 5.12a, not on the East Face.

HELMET UP BEFORE THE GULLIES, NOT AFTER: both gullies flanking the ledge see fairly frequent rockfall.

WHERE THE DAY ENDS, WHICH IS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE RIDGE: the standard descent is a walk-off from the NOTCH BELOW THE TRUE SUMMIT, not from the summit itself. Head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left, about twenty feet of third class; old rap slings are present but most parties downclimb. From the base of that gully, traverse RIGHT, north, until you intersect the well-worn climbers' and cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road walking.
hazards: Frequent rockfall in both gullies flanking the treed ledge
A 5.8 pitch as one of the two ways to gain the base
Snow lingering in the talus into early-mid summer
No water on the approach
A descent that finishes at the Blue Lake Trail, not at the pond pullout

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout to the treed ledge, then its LEFT side and rightward across slabs to the first bolt
