approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the East Face: from SR-20, park at the informal pullout on the north shoulder of the highway a short walk east of the small pond, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass. No permit needed.

A well-beaten climbers' trail leaves the east end of the pond and climbs steeply through timber; in roughly 30 minutes it breaks out at the edge of the large boulder and talus field that lines the eastern base of the Liberty Bell group, meaning Liberty Bell, Minuteman, Concord and Lexington Towers. From there, work up and LEFT across the talus toward Lexington Tower's east side, 30-45 minutes total from the car for most parties. No reliable water; the roadside pond is not worth using.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TOOTH AND CLAW BEGINS NEAR THE LEFT SIDE OF THE TREED LEDGE AND ANGLES RIGHTWARD ACROSS SLABS TO THE FIRST BOLT. Those are three checkable things in sequence: the LEFT end of a ledge with trees on it, a rightward line across SLABS, and a BOLT.

GETTING ONTO THE LEDGE IS THE FIRST PROBLEM AND SNOW DECIDES IT: either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge. Snow in the talus and at the base into early-mid summer determines whether you gain it from the left or the right. Helmet up well before committing to either gully; both see fairly frequent rockfall.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE ROUTE THAT SHARES THIS LEDGE: the EAST FACE, 5.9-plus and ten pitches, is the other line here. This one is 5.12a and it is the one that traverses RIGHT off the left end of the ledge to a bolt. If you are starting up cracks from the middle of the ledge without traversing, you are on the East Face.

HARDWARE AS A CHECK, AND IT IS A MIXED SIGNAL WORTH READING CAREFULLY: the descent stations lower on the route are described as obvious, good-quality anchors on trees or bolts, but SOME ORIGINAL 1989 QUARTER-INCH-CLASS BOLTS REMAIN DESPITE A POST-2016 REBOLTING PUSH, and at least one older fixed-nut and sling anchor is noted as aging. New-looking bolts are not proof of a modern line here.

DESCENT, AND THE ROPE LENGTH IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: from the top, the first anchor is a bolted station roughly 20-30 ft ABOVE the old pitch-6 slung-block anchor. WITH DOUBLE 70 M ROPES you can rappel from the very top; DOUBLED 60 M ROPES WILL NOT REACH THAT FIRST STATION. Most parties instead take the walk-off from the East Shoulder: an exposed, somewhat sketchy fourth-class traverse west, bordering on unprotected fifth-class slab in spots, to gain the same descent gully the East Face uses.
hazards: Frequent rockfall in both gullies flanking the treed ledge
Doubled 60 m ropes do not reach the first rappel station from the top of the route
Surviving original 1989 bolts and an aging fixed-nut anchor despite rebolting
The walk-off traverse borders on unprotected fifth-class slab; many parties stay roped
No water on the approach

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch, then its FAR EASTERN edge
approach_variants.notes:
Reach the Concord-Lexington notch via the standard Blue Lake Trailhead approach, trending toward the col between Concord and Lexington Towers rather than toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully. Higher in that gully a climbers' path appears along its left side and is better than the gully bed.

Three pitches. Sources disagree about the first ascent: one gives Cramer, Anderson, Schuler and Stanley in 1965, another Anderson and Scott in 1964 at 5.7. See _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE'S FIRST BELAY STARTS FROM THE FAR EASTERN EDGE OF THE NOTCH. So there are two finds and they nest: the right notch, then the right end of it.

WHICH NOTCH: THE CONCORD-LEXINGTON NOTCH IS THE ONE WHERE CONCORD IS ON ONE SIDE OF YOU AND LEXINGTON ON THE OTHER, AND THE CONCORD WALL IN FRONT OF YOU GIVES ONTO LOW-ANGLE, GRAVELLY LEDGES RATHER THAN A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM. IF YOU ARE FACING A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM, YOU ARE AT THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH, ONE SADDLE BACK, AND LOOKING AT CONCORD'S NORTH FACE.

WHICH END OF IT: the FAR EASTERN edge. The notch is a gap with two ends; walk to the eastern one before racking up. Concord's south-face routes go the other way, up the wall on the notch's Concord side.

CONFIRM BY HARDWARE, BECAUSE THIS ROUTE HAS A DISTINCTIVE ONE: THERE IS A BOLTED SUMMIT ANCHOR. Parties either make one single-rope rappel to an intermediate bolted anchor partway down the face and continue down, or run a full double-rope rappel directly back to the Concord-Lexington notch. A bolted top and a bolted mid-face station on a three-pitch route is what this line offers.

FROM THE NOTCH THE APPROACH GULLY AND CLIMBERS' TRAIL LEAD BACK TO THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, which is the same car you started from. That is not true of Lexington's east-side routes, which start at the hairpin pond pullout on the other side of the ridge.
hazards: Two notches a few hundred feet apart on one ridge
A gully bed better avoided in favour of the path along its left side
Far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col, so fainter tread
Conflicting first-ascent records, which is a sign the route documentation is thin

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail into the basin, PAST South Early Winters Spire, then left along the base
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft on WA-20 west of Washington Pass, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, PASS SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE, and traverse LEFT along the base to the shared start with the Northwest Corner. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base.

Six pitches, 5.11-, first climbed in 1965 and freed in 1985.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TWO SPIRES ARE PASSED IN ORDER AND THIS ROUTE IS ON THE SECOND ONE, WHICH IS THE WHOLE NAVIGATION PROBLEM ON THIS SIDE. Coming up the climbers' path into the basin, SOUTH Early Winters Spire comes first. YOU MUST WALK PAST IT. NORTH Early Winters Spire is beyond, and this route is on its west face, reached by traversing LEFT along the base.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS: IF YOU HAVE STOPPED AT THE FIRST WALL YOU REACHED, YOU ARE UNDER SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE, WHICH CARRIES ITS OWN CLUSTER OF WEST-SIDE ROUTES AND IS A DIFFERENT PEAK.

THE FEATURE THAT SEPARATES THE TWO SPIRES, AND IT IS THE BEST LANDMARK IN THIS BASIN: A MASSIVE CHASM, A CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY, SPLITS NORTH AND SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRES. It is the Chockstone Route's line. You must have that chasm behind you or beside you before you are under North Early Winters Spire's west face.

ARRIVAL: this route shares its start with the Northwest Corner, reached by traversing LEFT along the base after passing the chasm. It also sits immediately RIGHT of Labor Pains, which climbs the clean face between the Chockstone Route and this one. So the order across this wall, from the chasm outward, is: CHOCKSTONE ROUTE in the chasm, LABOR PAINS on the clean face beyond it, then THE WEST FACE.

DESCENT, WHICH GIVES YOU A THIRD CONFIRMATION IF YOU TOP OUT UNSURE: two options exist. The original drops down the left side through a notch with THREE single-rope rappels, including ONE FREE-HANGING RAPPEL OVER A CHOCKSTONE, and finishes with scrambling back to the base. The bolted alternative is FOUR RAP STATIONS STARTING ABOUT 15 FEET RIGHT OF WHERE PITCH 6 TOPS OUT, and is generally faster and less committing.
hazards: Two spires in a row on the same approach, with the near one carrying its own routes
A free-hanging rappel over a chockstone on the original descent line
Sustained 5.11- climbing over six pitches
No water in the basin

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Chockstone Route start, then up and LEFT to the ledge below the clean slab
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, the Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path lead into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group and past South Early Winters Spire to the west side of the two Early Winters Spires.

This route shares its start with the CHOCKSTONE ROUTE. From there, head up and LEFT toward a ledge below a clean slab to begin Labor Pains, which climbs the clean face between the Chockstone Route and The West Face. Five pitches, 5.11a, first climbed in September 1988.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CHOCKSTONE ROUTE'S START IS THE ANCHOR POINT AND IT IS THE MOST UNMISTAKABLE FEATURE ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN: IT IS OBVIOUS, AT THE BASE OF THE MASSIVE CHASM SEPARATING NORTH AND SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRES. A chasm splitting two spires is not something you can be uncertain about, in any weather where you can see the rock at all.

FROM THERE THE INSTRUCTION IS TWO WORDS AND A FEATURE: UP AND LEFT, TO A LEDGE BELOW A CLEAN SLAB. Clean rock is the marker. This route takes the clean face; the ground either side of it does not read as clean.

SO THE ROUTE IS SANDWICHED, AND YOU CAN BOUND IT BOTH WAYS: THE CHOCKSTONE ROUTE IS TO ITS RIGHT, IN THE CHASM. THE WEST FACE IS TO ITS LEFT. If you are in the chasm you have not left the shared start; if you have traversed all the way left to the shared start with the Northwest Corner, you have gone past.

CONFIRM BY WHAT YOU ARE STANDING ON: A LEDGE, below a SLAB. Not a chimney, not a corner.

DESCENT, AND IT IS NOT A REVERSAL: rappel down the CHOCKSTONE ROUTE line, using the same bolted stations that route uses, rather than reversing the Labor Pains pitches. That means you finish where you started, back at the chasm.
hazards: A start defined by its neighbours on both sides on a wall of closely spaced lines
5.11a over five pitches with a rappel descent down a different route
The approach passes South Early Winters Spire first; stopping there puts you on the wrong peak
No water in the basin

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pullout on the EAST side, staying RIGHT of the gully that divides the two spires
approach_variants.notes:
This route is approached from the hairpin turn pullout on SR-20 east of Washington Pass, not from the Blue Lake Trailhead that serves North Early Winters Spire's west-side routes. Approach as if heading for the Direct East Buttress on South Early Winters Spire.

Ten pitches, 5.10b, first climbed in 1965 and freed onsight solo in 1990.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAY RIGHT OF THE GULLY THAT DIVIDES THE TWO SPIRES, AND SCRAMBLE TO A FLAT LEDGE. Those are the two things to find: the DIVIDING GULLY, kept on your left, and a FLAT LEDGE where the route starts.

WHY THE GULLY IS THE RIGHT HANDRAIL TO USE HERE: North and South Early Winters Spires are separated by a single continuous cleft, a chockstone-filled chasm on the west side and a gully on the east. It runs the full height between the two peaks, so it is the one feature on this side you cannot lose. Keep it on your LEFT and you are on North Early Winters Spire's ground; cross it and you are on South Early Winters Spire, where the Direct East Buttress and Southern Man start.

ARRIVAL: a FLAT LEDGE, gained by scrambling. Flat ground on a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation.

THE TRAILHEAD TEST, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT COSTS AN HOUR IF YOU GET IT WRONG: this route is on the EAST side and is reached from the HAIRPIN PULLOUT. The other two North Early Winters Spire routes here, The West Face and Labor Pains, are on the WEST side and are reached from the BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, which is about 2.5 miles away by road on the far side of Washington Pass. Those are different cars.

AND THE DESCENT CROSSES BACK OVER THE MOUNTAIN, WHICH YOU SHOULD PLAN FOR BEFORE STARTING: from the summit, traverse to the WEST side of the peak and rappel either the Chockstone Route with a 60 m rope or the bolted West Face anchors with a 70 m rope. Both require crossing over from the east-side climbing line to the west-side descent infrastructure.
hazards: A descent that requires crossing to the opposite side of the peak from the climb
Two trailheads on opposite sides of Washington Pass serving the same summit
A 70 m rope is needed for the bolted West Face rappel option
No water on the approach

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the northwest clearing, then the basin below the west face and the steep corner system
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1-1.25 miles, roughly an hour, to the clearing and meadow on the spire's northwest side. Leave the trail on the well-worn climber's path and ascend talus and heather into the basin directly below the northwest face.

THIS IS THE SAME BASIN USED TO ACCESS THE SOUTHWEST RIB, MOJO RISING AND FREE MOJO, so route-finding to the base is shared and only the last few dozen feet along the wall separate the lines.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS IDENTIFIABLE BY A STEEP CORNER SYSTEM, AND THE FIRST PITCH TRAVERSES INTO IT. That is the positive test: a steep CORNER, not a face and not a chimney, entered by traversing rather than climbing straight up. The first pitch makes committing moves at about 5.10 up to a prominent ledge, where some parties belay while others continue to a tree-anchored stance.

THE LANDMARK EVERY LINE ON THIS WALL IS MEASURED FROM, AND THE ONE TO FIND FIRST: A LARGE CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY AND NOTCH between the two spire formations. Get to that and the wall becomes readable.

RELATIVE TO IT, THE ORDER IS COUNTABLE AND IN FEET: MOJO RISING starts on an obvious bolted face ABOUT 20 FT DOWNHILL of the chockstone chimney, just LEFT of this route's first pitch. FREE MOJO starts ROUGHLY 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT of the same chimney, on a nondescript crack leading to a two-piece fixed anchor on a pedestal.

SO THE THREE-WAY DISCRIMINATOR IS: BOLTED FACE 20 FT DOWNHILL OF THE CHIMNEY MEANS MOJO RISING. NONDESCRIPT CRACK 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT MEANS FREE MOJO. STEEP CORNER ENTERED BY A TRAVERSE MEANS THIS ROUTE. If you are clipping bolts off the ground you are not on the Boving-Pollock.

SIX PITCHES, WHICH MAKES IT THE SHORTEST OF THE WEST-SIDE LINES ON THIS SPIRE, and parties typically continue to the true summit rather than rappel it, then take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete, third and fourth class with a short fifth-class step, to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.
hazards: Several closely spaced starts on one wall, separated by tens of feet
Committing 5.10 moves on the first pitch before any belay
No documented rappel-the-face option; bailing mid-route means natural gear anchors
No water in the basin

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the basin below the west face, then 20 ft DOWNHILL of the chockstone chimney
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the Northwest Face: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail about 1-1.25 miles to the northwest-side clearing, then the climber's path up talus into the basin below the west face.

Nine pitches, 5.11b, first climbed in 2006. Pitches 7-9 are typically simul-climbed or pitched out onto the well-travelled Southwest Rib finish to the true summit.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS AN OBVIOUS BOLTED FACE ABOUT 20 FT DOWNHILL FROM A LARGE CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY AND NOTCH, JUST LEFT OF PITCH 1 OF THE NORTHWEST FACE. THE CHOCKSTONE CHIMNEY IS THE KEY LANDMARK FOR LOCATING THE START AMONG SEVERAL CLOSELY SPACED LINES ON THIS WALL.

SO THE TEST IS: FIND THE CHIMNEY WITH CHOCKSTONES JAMMED IN IT, THEN GO 20 FT DOWNHILL, AND LOOK FOR BOLTS ON A FACE. Bolts off the deck are the distinguishing feature. The Northwest Face beside it starts by traversing into a steep CORNER with no bolts at the base.

THE OTHER NEIGHBOUR, AND THE DIRECTION SEPARATES THEM CLEANLY: FREE MOJO starts ROUGHLY 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT OF THE SAME CHIMNEY, ON A NONDESCRIPT CRACK. This route is 20 ft down and LEFT-ish of the chimney, on bolts. Down and right on a crack is the other route; down and left on bolts is this one.

CONFIRM BY WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU BAIL, WHICH IS A HARDWARE COUNT: to descend the route itself, rappel the FIRST THREE PITCHES with a single 60 m rope from BOLTED AND CHAIN ANCHORS back to the ground. A three-pitch fully bolted rappel line off the deck is what this route offers and its corner-system neighbour does not.

AND THE FULL-ROUTE FINISH ENDS SOMEWHERE ELSE: the top three pitches join the Southwest Rib to the true summit, from which the standard South Arete descent runs down to the RABBIT EARS and then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully.
hazards: Several lines starting within tens of feet of each other on the same wall
A finish that merges onto a different route's terrain
No water in the basin
Talus and heather with no maintained tread above the trail

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the basin below the west face, then 40 ft DOWN AND RIGHT of the chockstone chimney
approach_variants.notes:
Same basin approach as Mojo Rising and the Northwest Face: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail to the northwest-side clearing, then the climber's path up talus into the basin below the west face.

Six pitches, 5.11-.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS ROUGHLY 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT OF THE LARGE CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY BETWEEN THE TWO SPIRE FORMATIONS, ON A NONDESCRIPT CRACK THAT LEADS TO A TWO-PIECE FIXED ANCHOR ON A PEDESTAL.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS AT THE TOP OF PITCH ONE, NOT AT THE BOTTOM, AND THAT IS THE HONEST WAY TO USE THIS ROUTE: the crack itself is described as NONDESCRIPT, which means you will not identify it by looking at it. What you can identify is where it ends. A ROPE LENGTH UP, THERE IS A TWO-PIECE FIXED ANCHOR ON A PEDESTAL. If you arrive at a stance with no fixed gear, come down and move along the wall.

PITCH TWO GIVES A SECOND CONFIRMATION: OBVIOUS DOUBLE INCIPIENT CRACKS leading up to a series of ledges. Two thin parallel cracks, not one.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE TWO NEIGHBOURS, AND THE MEASUREMENTS ARE THE POINT: MOJO RISING is ABOUT 20 FT DOWNHILL of the chimney on an OBVIOUS BOLTED FACE. The NORTHWEST FACE, Boving-Pollock, is entered by TRAVERSING INTO A STEEP CORNER. THIS ROUTE IS 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT ON A PLAIN CRACK. Bolts mean Mojo Rising; a corner means Boving-Pollock; a plain crack forty feet right of the chimney means Free Mojo.

RETREAT FROM LOW ON THE ROUTE IS STRAIGHTFORWARD, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING WHEN YOU ARE UNSURE OF THE START: a party retreating after pitch 2 rappels P2 then P1 back to the ground from the fixed anchors on a 60 m rope. There is no penalty for starting, finding the ground wrong, and coming back down.
hazards: A start explicitly described as nondescript, confirmed only at the first belay
Three routes starting within about 60 ft of each other on one wall
No water in the basin

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch at the base of the Southwest Rib, then three pitches up before this route starts
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the Southwest Rib: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail about 1.25 miles to the northwest clearing, then the climber's path up into the basin.

Three pitches at 5.10b as counted here, but understand what the route is: it is pitch 5 of a combined line, about 100 ft of sustained climbing under and through a pair of roofs.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE HAS NO GROUND START, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT ABOUT FINDING IT. You reach it by climbing THE FIRST THREE PITCHES OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and THEN GOING LEFT AT A LEDGE WHERE THE TWO ROOFS COME INTO VIEW.

SO THE BASE OF THE DAY IS THE BASE OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, AND THAT HAS A LANDMARK YOU CAN STAND UNDER: THE Y-SHAPED LARCH TREE AT THE BASE OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, LEFT OF THE SOUTHWEST COULOIR. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

THE IN-ROUTE TEST IS VISUAL AND BINARY: GO LEFT AT THE LEDGE WHERE THE TWO ROOFS COME INTO VIEW. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A HAZARD RIGHT AT THE START OF THE PITCH, RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS EXACTLY WHERE A PARTY IS COMMITTING: THERE IS A LOOSE BLOCK RIGHT AT THE START OF THE ROOF PITCH.

WHAT NOBODY DOES HERE, WHICH ANSWERS THE OBVIOUS QUESTION: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the RABBIT EARS then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors down the gully.
hazards: No ground start; three pitches of another route must be climbed first
A loose block right at the start of the roof pitch
Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and undocumented, so bailing here means natural gear anchors
No water in the basin

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch, up two or three pitches, then LEFT to the dark chasm
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Blue Lake Trailhead on Highway 20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail roughly 1.25 miles, about an hour of easy hiking at modest gain, to the open meadow and clearing on the northwest side of the Liberty Bell massif, marked by a WOODEN TRAIL SIGN. Leave the maintained trail there and follow the well-worn climber's path up through talus and heather benches into the basin below South Early Winters Spire's west side.

A single spectacular pitch of about 75 ft at 5.9+ R, first climbed in 1967.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
DOLPHIN CHIMNEY IS NOT STARTED FROM THE GROUND. It is gained by climbing the FIRST TWO OR THREE PITCHES of the Southwest Rib or the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, then TRAVERSING LEFT OVER EASY TERRAIN TO THE OBVIOUS DARK, UNMISTAKABLE CHASM ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF THE BOVING ROOF.

SO THE FEATURE ITSELF IS THE TEST AND IT IS AS GOOD AS THEY GET ON THIS WALL: A DARK CHASM. Not a crack, not a corner, and not something you could talk yourself into. If you are unsure whether you are looking at it, you are not looking at it.

THE MEASURED OFFSET GIVES A SECOND CHECK: ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF THE BOVING ROOF. The Boving Roofs pitch is the double-roof feature reached by going left at a ledge from the same rib. Two roofs stacked above you, then a hundred feet further left, is the chimney.

THE GROUND-LEVEL AIMING POINT FOR THE WHOLE DAY: THE Y-SHAPED LARCH TREE LEFT OF THE SOUTHWEST COULOIR, at the base of the Southwest Rib. That is the landmark most parties use to start up this wall, and it is the one thing here you can find at ground level.

HOW THIS ROUTE IS ACTUALLY DONE, WHICH SHOULD SHAPE THE PLAN: it is a one-pitch add-on within a Southwest Rib or Boving-Pollock day, not a climb with its own descent. Most parties continue past it on easier cracks to rejoin the Southwest Rib and finish to the summit, then take the standard South Arete descent to the RABBIT EARS, two boulder towers with fixed rappel slings, then a short traverse and downclimb into the descent gully and three single-rope 60 m rappels to the base. A party doing the Dolphin as an out-and-back lowers or makes a single rappel back to the ledge below.
hazards: No ground start; two or three pitches of another route come first
5.9+ R with sparse gear in an offwidth and chimney
Rope management on any rappel of the chimney itself deserves extra care
No water in the basin

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the South Arete base, then down and right about ten minutes to the fir tree and double cracks
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, the climber's trail reaches the South Arete base in about an hour. Seven pitches at 5.11d, first climbed in October 1991.

The traverse to the start eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain, so expect to lose height rather than contour.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE SOUTH ARETE BASE, HEAD DOWN AND RIGHT ALONG THE BASE OF THE WALL FOR ABOUT TEN MINUTES TO A START AT DOUBLE CRACKS BESIDE A FIR TREE. A tree at the foot of a pair of cracks is the marker, and a tree is something you can walk into in cloud.

SO THE TWO CHECKS ARE A DURATION AND A TREE: TEN MINUTES OF SCRAMBLING AND TRAVERSING FROM THE SOUTH ARETE, AND A FIR. Not thirty seconds and not half an hour.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST ITS NEIGHBOUR, AND IT IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: THE HITCHHIKER BEGINS ROUGHLY 100 FT FURTHER ALONG THE SAME TRAVERSE, AT A SMALL LEFT-FACING DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS. IF YOU ARE STANDING AT A DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS IN IT, YOU HAVE GONE 100 FT TOO FAR.

AND IF YOU HAVE NOT LOST HEIGHT, YOU HAVE NOT ARRIVED: the traverse eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain. Contouring level along the wall keeps you on South Arete ground.

WHERE IT ENDS: the route is not commonly rappelled top to bottom. Parties top out and use the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete, third and fourth class with one short more exposed step, to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base, and out via the climber's trail to the Blue Lake Trail.
hazards: Two routes starting about 100 ft apart on the same traverse
Loss of height along the base to skirt steeper terrain, which has to be regained
5.11d over seven pitches with no route-specific rappel line
No water on the approach

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the South Arete base, then PAST the Passenger's fir tree another hundred feet to the four-bolt dihedral
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the Passenger: Blue Lake Trailhead climber's trail, about an hour, to the South Arete base, then traverse down and right along the base of the wall.

Nine pitches on the steep southeast face, first climbed in 2007. A long day, up to eight hours, of sustained face climbing with about twenty bolts but still requiring a full trad rack.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS A SMALL LEFT-FACING DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS IN IT, ROUGHLY 100 FT PAST THE PASSENGER'S START ALONG THE SAME TRAVERSE. FOUR BOLTS IS A COUNT, AND COUNTING IS WHAT YOU CAN STILL DO WHEN YOU CANNOT SEE THE TOP OF THE WALL.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS: South Arete base, then down and right about ten minutes to a FIR TREE WITH DOUBLE CRACKS, which is the Passenger. THAT IS NOT THIS ROUTE. Keep going roughly 100 FT FURTHER to a SMALL LEFT-FACING DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS.

THE NEGATIVE TEST BOTH WAYS: A FIR TREE AND TWO CRACKS MEANS YOU STOPPED SHORT, ON THE PASSENGER. Nothing beyond the four-bolt dihedral is documented along this traverse, so if the wall is running out and you have found no bolts, you have passed it.

A HARDWARE CHECK THAT KEEPS WORKING ABOVE THE GROUND: this route carries about twenty bolts over nine pitches, which is enough that you should keep meeting them, but not enough to climb without a full trad rack. Meeting no bolts at all after a rope length is a sign you are off the line.

DESCENT: the route tops out at the summit rather than being rappelled. Take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete with a short more exposed step to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope, which matches the rope length in the route's own protection notes, from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.
hazards: A start 100 ft beyond a similar start on the same traverse
Up to eight hours of sustained face climbing at 5.11-
About twenty bolts over nine pitches, so a full trad rack is still mandatory
No water on the approach

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pullout and Spire Gully to the last large tree, then right across the talus toward the inter-spire notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same as the Direct East Buttress: park at the hairpin pullout on Highway 20 east of Washington Pass. THIS IS THE EAST-SIDE TRAILHEAD, NOT THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD used by the spire's west-side routes.

Nine pitches. The route shares the East Buttress's first pitches, then splits off around halfway up to climb the south-facing headwall on the upper south side of the peak for its final five pitches.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
HIKE SPIRE GULLY, WHICH IS CAIRNED, TO THE LAST LARGE TREE. THAT TREE IS THE TURN. From it, traverse RIGHT across talus and snow to the gully leading to THE NOTCH BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE, then traverse LEFT to the base of the east buttress.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS THREE MOVES AND A TREE: UP the cairned gully to the LAST LARGE TREE, RIGHT across talus, then LEFT to the buttress base. The tree is the only thing in that sequence you can put a hand on, which is why it is the marker rather than the gully.

WHY THE NOTCH MATTERS EVEN THOUGH YOU DO NOT GO TO IT: the gully you aim at is the one running to the gap between the two spires, the same continuous cleft that on the west side is the chockstone-filled chimney. It is the biggest feature on this side of the group. Aim at it, then step left before reaching it.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS: IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE NOTCH ITSELF YOU HAVE GONE UP TOO FAR, and if you are on the far side of the cleft you are on NORTH Early Winters Spire, where Flycatcher Buttress starts from a flat ledge.

WHAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE EAST BUTTRESS IT SHARES A START WITH, AND IT IS A DECISION MADE HALFWAY UP RATHER THAN AT THE BASE: Southern Man splits off around mid-height onto the SOUTH-FACING HEADWALL. Its own belays are described as vague and not yet fixed, which is itself a tell: DO NOT EXPECT A FULLY BOLTED RAP LINE if you need to bail from the upper headwall. Natural anchors would be required there.

DESCENT: from the summit, the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete with a short more exposed fifth-class section to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.
hazards: Vague, unfixed belays on the upper headwall, so bailing means building natural anchors
A shared start with a much more travelled route, with the split made mid-height
Talus and snow on the traverse below the inter-spire notch
Two trailheads on opposite sides of the pass serving this peak

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then 5-10 minutes around the north face to the splitter flake
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout at about 4,310 ft near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 miles east of Washington Pass and opposite Silver Star, a boot path drops through talus into forest, passes a register box, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft.

The trail climbs east, roughly 2,200 ft, to a flat bench and campsite at about 6,460 ft, the halfway point and a common high camp, then works up through loose scree gullies and a final cairned stretch of unstable scree-over-slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770-7,800 ft. Roughly 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way.

Note that this row's stored trailhead record names a different trailhead than this prose does; see _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ACTION POTENTIAL DOES NOT START AT THE COL. FROM BURGUNDY COL, SCRAMBLE DOWN AND AROUND THE BASE OF BURGUNDY'S NORTH FACE FOR ABOUT 5 TO 10 MINUTES UNTIL YOU ARE BELOW A CLEAN SPLITTER FLAKE. THAT FLAKE IS THE ROUTE START.

SO THE THREE THINGS TO CHECK ARE A DIRECTION, A DURATION AND A FEATURE: DOWN and AROUND the north face, FIVE TO TEN MINUTES, and a CLEAN SPLITTER FLAKE. Clean is the operative word on a peak where most of the rock is not.

THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS ONE PLACEABLE: THIS ROUTE SITS BETWEEN THE NORTH FACE'S START AND ULTRAMEGA OK'S. Ultramega OK is FURTHER AROUND, well climber's-left of both, at a TWIN-CRACK SYSTEM MARKED BY OBVIOUS LOOSE BLOCKS ABOUT 60 FT UP. So: IF YOU ARE LOOKING AT TWO CRACKS WITH LOOSE BLOCKS SIXTY FEET ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THIS ROUTE.

AND IF YOU HAVE NOT WALKED AT ALL, YOU ARE ON THE NORTH FACE: that line starts at a first-pitch chimney at the col end of the base, which is also where the last rappel of the standard descent lands. A chimney at the near end, a splitter flake five to ten minutes along, twin cracks with loose blocks further still.

EARLY IN THE SEASON THE WALK ALONG THE BASE MAY BE SNOW RATHER THAN SCREE, sometimes steep enough to want an axe into midsummer. That does not change the count; it changes the footing.

DESCENT IS THE NORTH FACE'S, WHICH RETURNS YOU TO THIS ROUTE'S OWN START: five double-rope rappels from the summit area, ending with a final 60 m to the base of the first-pitch chimney, near where Action Potential and the North Face begin.
hazards: Unstable cairned scree-over-slab on the final stretch to Burgundy Col, the approach's main hazard in both directions
Loose rock and sometimes steep snow on the walk around the base of the north face
Anchors on the descent are a mix of slung boulders and horns with fixed bolts; watch for old webbing
Ledges on the face that catch a pulled rope
Water only at Early Winters Creek and a trickle near the col

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then further around the north face to the twin cracks with loose blocks
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the long highway pullout on SR-20 at about 4,310 ft near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 miles east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain. A boot path drops east through loose talus into forest; look for a WILDERNESS-REGISTRATION BOX a few minutes in.

The path fords Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft, a swift wade in early season. From the creek it climbs steadily east through forest and open slopes for roughly 2,200 ft to a broad flat bench and campsite around 6,460 ft, the approach's natural midpoint and a good high camp or bail point. Above the bench the boot path traverses loose scree gullies below Burgundy's northwest side and finishes up a final stretch of unstable, cairn-marked ball-bearing scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770-7,800 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. About 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE STARTS FURTHEST AROUND THE BASE OF ANY LINE HERE, AND THE MARKER IS COUNTABLE: A TWIN-CRACK SYSTEM WITH OBVIOUS LOOSE BLOCKS ABOUT 60 FT UP. Two cracks, and blocks visible sixty feet above you.

SO THE INSTRUCTION IS: FROM THE COL, SCRAMBLE LOOSE ROCK, OR KICK STEPS IN LINGERING SNOW WITH AN AXE INTO JULY, DOWN AND AROUND THE BASE OF BURGUNDY'S NORTH FACE, AND KEEP GOING. THIS START IS WELL CLIMBER'S-LEFT OF BOTH THE NORTH FACE AND ACTION POTENTIAL.

THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE, GOING AWAY FROM THE COL: FIRST THE NORTH FACE'S first-pitch CHIMNEY, then ACTION POTENTIAL'S CLEAN SPLITTER FLAKE about 5-10 minutes along, then THIS ROUTE'S TWIN CRACKS. IF YOU HAVE STOPPED AT A SINGLE CLEAN SPLITTER, YOU ARE ONE ROUTE SHORT.

AND THE NEGATIVE TEST FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION: there is nothing documented further around than this, so a wall with no twin cracks and no loose blocks means you have gone past the last recorded start on this side.

ARRIVAL AT THE COL, WHICH IS THE OTHER FIND ON THIS DAY: Burgundy Col is the NOTCH BETWEEN BURGUNDY SPIRE AND PAISANO PINNACLE, at about 7,770-7,800 ft, and it is reached by the last stretch of cairned ball-bearing scree over slab. Rock towers on both sides, the ground dropping away ahead, at the top of the worst scree of the day.

DESCENT, AND THE ROPE MATH IS TIGHTER HERE THAN ON THE NORTH FACE: this route has no independent rappel line and most parties merge into upper North Face terrain near Burgundy Ledge, then take the North Face's five-rappel descent. DOUBLE 60 M ROPES MAKE THAT CLEAN. Parties with a single 70 m have got down with some downclimbing between stances, but it is tighter on this line than on the standard North Face.
hazards: Unstable ball-bearing scree over slab below the col, with rockfall onto party members below
Lingering snow on the traverse around the north face, wanting an axe into July
No independent rappel line; the descent merges into another route's terrain
A single 70 m rope leaves the descent tight, with downclimbing between stances
A swift wade of Early Winters Creek in early season

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then the snow traverse south beneath Burgundy's east face onto the Silver Star Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, a steep faint climber's trail descends to Early Winters Creek. Cross the creek and follow the climber's path and talus benches switchbacking up the far side, gaining about 3,500 ft over just under 5 miles to Burgundy Col, roughly 3-4 hours car-to-col with an overnight pack. STAY CLIMBER'S-LEFT TOWARD THE OBVIOUS COL NOTCH where the boot-path braids through timber and boulders lower down.

A snow patch at or near the col is the last dependable water and is unreliable by late summer, so carry water up from the creek if climbing after midsummer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM BURGUNDY COL, DROP A SHORT SNOW AND ROCK STEP AND TRAVERSE SOUTH BENEATH BURGUNDY SPIRE'S EAST FACE, ACROSS A SMALL SNOWY RIB, ONTO THE UPPER SILVER STAR GLACIER, AND AROUND TO CHIANTI SPIRE'S OBVIOUS EAST SIDE AT ABOUT 7,900 FT. Under an hour from a col or bench camp.

SO THE SEQUENCE OF SURFACES IS THE HANDRAIL, AND YOU CAN FEEL EACH ONE UNDERFOOT: rock step down, snow traverse, a rib, then glacier. If you have not crossed onto glacier you have not gone far enough.

THE ROUTE ON THE FACE, AND THIS IS WHERE THE TWO EAST-FACE LINES ARE TOLD APART: REBEL YELL'S DIHEDRAL IS THE OBVIOUS FEATURE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE FACE. LICHEN BOUQUET'S RAMP STARTS DIRECTLY BELOW THE SUMMIT AND LEANS LEFT. SO: A BIG CORNER ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE WALL IS THIS ROUTE. A RAMP UNDER THE SUMMIT THAT LEANS LEFT IS NOT.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: seven pitches at III 5.10b, with chimney and offwidth pitches that readily snag ropes on the way down. Four double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes get you back down the route itself, trending generally climber's-right, starting from the summit block and then anchors near the top of pitch 5.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE ON THE APPROACH: continuing south past Chianti along the glacier brings you under Pernod and toward the Pernod-Chablis notch, which serves different routes and involves loose fourth-class ground.

AN ICE AXE IS WANTED FOR THIS TRAVERSE THROUGH MIDSUMMER; the snow rib and glacier margin can be firm or icy in the morning, and that is exactly when you will be crossing them.
hazards: A snow and glacier traverse that can be firm or icy in the morning; carry an axe through midsummer
The last dependable water is a snow patch at the col which is unreliable by late summer
Rope-snag hazard in the chimney and offwidth pitches on the rappel descent
Fixed anchors that should be visually checked at each station; this is not a bolted sport descent
A re-ascent of 200-300 ft back to Burgundy Col at the end of the day

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout, the bench camp and the main gully to Burgundy Col, then south on year-round snow to the ramp below the summit
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-20 to Washington Pass, then about 4 miles east to a wide pullout on the south side of the highway near milepost 166 at roughly 4,250 ft, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake road and about 2 miles east of the hairpin turn. No Northwest Forest Pass is required on the highway shoulder.

Descend a steep, faint scree path about 300 ft to Early Winters Creek, cross on logs, then follow the climbers' trail steeply uphill to a wooded bench at 6,400-6,600 ft, the standard low camp. THERE IS A YEAR-ROUND SPRING ABOUT 200 YARDS NORTH OF THE TRAIL AT THE BENCH, and a seasonal spring in the sandy gully above.

Above the bench the trail fades; follow cairns up loose gullies, trending right and up, into the main gully below Burgundy Col at 7,800-7,950 ft. The gully holds a roughly 40-degree snow finger into midsummer. Roughly 3.5 miles and about 3,700 ft of gain to the col in 3-4 hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LICHEN BOUQUET'S RAMP STARTS DIRECTLY BELOW THE SUMMIT AND LEANS LEFT. THAT IS THE TEST, AND IT IS BOTH POSITIONAL AND DIRECTIONAL: stand where the summit is straight above you, and look for a ramp that leans LEFT.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE OTHER LINE ON THE SAME FACE, AND THEY ARE GENUINELY EASY TO CONFUSE FROM BELOW: REBEL YELL'S DIHEDRAL IS THE OBVIOUS FEATURE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE FACE. IF YOU ARE UNDER A BIG CORNER ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE WALL RATHER THAN A LEFT-LEANING RAMP UNDER THE TOP, YOU ARE ON REBEL YELL.

GETTING THERE: from Burgundy Col, DESCEND 200-300 FT ON THE SOUTH SIDE AND TRAVERSE RIGHT BENEATH BURGUNDY SPIRE'S EAST FACE ON YEAR-ROUND SNOW, with seasonal rock bands, UNTIL CHIANTI'S EAST FACE IS IN VIEW. Under an hour from the col.

SO THE SNOW IS THE HANDRAIL AND IT IS THERE ALL YEAR, which is unusual and useful: if you are not walking on snow beneath a big east-facing wall, you have not started the traverse.

DESCENT, AND THE ROUTE'S OWN FINISH SUGGESTS THE ALTERNATIVE: most east-face parties descend as Rebel Yell parties do, scrambling from the summit pedestal to a TWO-BOLT ANCHOR AT THE SOUTHEAST BASE OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK and making four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes back to the snow, trending generally to the rappeller's right and pulling ropes carefully, since the flake and offwidth features snag readily. The alternative this route's finish naturally suggests is to reverse to the NOTCH BETWEEN BURGUNDY SPIRE AND CHIANTI and descend from there.

THE STING IN THE TAIL, WHICH IS A TIMING DECISION MADE AT THE BASE: whichever way you come down, you must regain the 200-300 ft to Burgundy Col, and that is MUCH EASIER ON FIRM MORNING SNOW THAN ON LATE-DAY SLUSH OR BARE SAND.
hazards: A roughly 40-degree snow finger in the main gully below the col into midsummer
Year-round snow on the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face, with seasonal rock bands
Rope-snagging flake and offwidth features on the rappel descent
A 200-300 ft re-ascent to the col at the end of the day
Sand-over-slab above the bench, described by trip reports as the worst part of the outing
Rockfall from parties above in the gullies; keep helmets on

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then traverse in to the Burgundy-Chianti notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the boot path drops to Early Winters Creek, crosses on logs, and climbs the timbered rib to the bench camp at 6,400-6,600 ft and on up the loose main gully to Burgundy Col.

This is the 1952 first ascent of Chianti Spire itself. The original party approached from a camp at the head of Silver Star Creek, climbed 500 ft of difficult rock to the notch between Chianti and Pernod, made a 250 ft rappel on the west face, and followed a loose gully to the Chianti-Burgundy notch, where the north face was found to hold the only route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE NOTCH BETWEEN CHIANTI AND BURGUNDY SPIRES, AND THE MODERN WAY IN IS TO TRAVERSE TO IT FROM BURGUNDY COL RATHER THAN TO RAPPEL INTO IT FROM THE WEST AS THE FIRST ASCENT DID. From the notch, the north face is climbed directly to the summit.

SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE IN A GAP BETWEEN TWO NAMED SPIRES WITH A WALL RISING NORTH OF YOU. Burgundy on one side, Chianti on the other, and the face you are about to climb between them.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER LINES, AND IT IS A SIDE-OF-THE-SPIRE TEST: the two EAST FACE routes are reached by descending 200-300 ft SOUTH from Burgundy Col and traversing on snow beneath Burgundy's east face until Chianti's east face comes into view. This route stops short of that, at the notch. IF YOU ARE STANDING ON SNOW LOOKING AT A BIG EAST-FACING WALL WITH A DIHEDRAL ON ITS RIGHT SIDE, YOU HAVE GONE PAST THE NOTCH AND ARE UNDER REBEL YELL.

AND THE OTHER NOTCH ON THIS SPIRE IS THE ONE AT THE FAR END: the first ascent reached the CHIANTI-PERNOD notch first, on the other side of the peak, and had to rappel 250 ft off the west face and follow a loose gully to get to this one. Two notches, one at each end of Chianti. This route uses the BURGUNDY end.

WHAT COMING BACK LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS THE SAME STING THE EAST FACE ROUTES CARRY: downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block onto the north face, reverse the line to the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy's east face and CLIMB THE 200-300 FT BACK UP TO BURGUNDY COL. Firm morning snow makes that far easier than afternoon slush or bare sandy rock.
hazards: A 200-300 ft re-ascent to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
Loose main gully below the col, with rockfall from parties above
Sand-over-slab descent above the bench, unanimously described as the worst part of the day
A short loose scramble on scree and boulders for the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway
A route with a single detailed historical account and little modern traffic

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and the bench camp, then up and right past two minor buttresses into the talus gully under the tallest wall
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff heading west from Winthrop and roughly 3.75 miles east of the Washington Pass hairpin. A climbers' boot path drops steeply off the highway shoulder through loose talus and duff and reaches Early Winters Creek at about 4,080 ft, where log crossings get you across; use caution in early-season high water.

From the creek the trail firms up for roughly a quarter mile through forest before angling steeply uphill BETWEEN TWO FEEDER GULLIES, gaining close to 2,400 ft to a flat bench at about 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard bivy and staging camp for the Wine Spires. Water there is unreliable late season; some parties find a small seasonal trickle in a dry sandy side-gully near the bench, but do not count on it.

Roughly 3,000-3,500 ft of gain over about 2-2.5 miles one-way from the car to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PERNOD'S WEST FACE IS THE TALLEST WALL IN THE WINE SPIRES, AND THAT IS THE TEST. From the bench camp, continue up and RIGHT, east, passing A COUPLE OF MINOR BUTTRESSES, to gain a BROAD TALUS AND SCREE GULLY THAT RUNS DIRECTLY TO THE BASE OF THAT WALL.

SO THE COUNT IS: TWO MINOR BUTTRESSES PASSED, THEN ONE BROAD GULLY, THEN THE BIGGEST WALL IN THE GROUP. If the wall above you is not obviously the largest thing here, you have stopped at one of the buttresses you were supposed to pass.

THE CRITICAL DIFFERENCE FROM EVERY OTHER ROUTE IN THIS BASIN, AND IT IS THE THING THAT MAKES THIS APPROACH DISTINCT: THIS ROUTE DOES NOT GO TO BURGUNDY COL. It leaves the main Burgundy Col trail at the bench. IF YOU ARE GRINDING UP LOOSE SCREE TOWARD A NOTCH BETWEEN TWO SPIRES, YOU ARE ON THE BURGUNDY COL TRAIL AND HAVE MISSED THE TURN AT THE BENCH.

THE LAST FEW HUNDRED FEET OF THE GULLY ARE LOOSE BALL-BEARING SCREE OVER SLAB, WITH CAIRNS MARKING THE BETTER LINE. Helmets should go on well before entering the gully because of rockfall from any party above.

EIGHT PITCHES AT 5.10-PLUS R. Descent is NOT back down this face: rappel EAST down the gully to the PERNOD-CHABLIS NOTCH, then a couple more rappels down steep slabs to the neve below, three rappels total, on two 60 m ropes. From the neve, trend north around the base of Chianti Spire and climb back up to Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' path to the bench and the boot path to the highway.

SO YOU COME DOWN THE OTHER SIDE AND WALK OUT PAST A COL YOU NEVER VISITED ON THE WAY IN. Budget real time: the three rappels only reach the neve, after which there is a substantial re-ascent to the col before the walk-off begins.
hazards: The only fixed rappel anchor on the route is on the summit ridge, where nuts have been left in place
Old aid bolts on the route, one reported missing a hanger and another loose in its hole
Ball-bearing scree over slab in the last few hundred feet of the approach gully
A descent onto the opposite side of the spire followed by a substantial re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Unreliable water at the bench camp late season

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and the bench camp, then contour right off the Burgundy Col trail into the gully under the west face
approach_variants.notes:
From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, directly across the highway from the Wine Spires, a boot and climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop, and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The creek can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt.

The trail gains steeply and steadily, on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles, to a broad flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps. THIS BENCH IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER: small tarns and a creek trickle that can run dry by late summer.

Roughly 3,500-4,000 ft of gain over about 3 miles one-way, 3-5 hours for a fit party. Note that this row's aspect column says north while its own approach and descent describe the west face and an east-side rappel; see _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEAVE THE MAIN BURGUNDY COL TRAIL AT THE BENCH. THAT IS THE TURN, AND MISSING IT IS THE ONLY WAY TO GET THIS APPROACH WRONG. From the bench, contour RIGHT past a couple of subsidiary buttresses, DROPPING SLIGHTLY before regaining a large talus and scree gully that runs directly to the base of Pernod's west face.

SO THERE IS A SMALL DESCENT IN THE MIDDLE OF AN OTHERWISE RELENTLESS CLIMB, AND THAT DIP IS THE CONFIRMATION. If everything you have done since the bench has been uphill, you are still on the Burgundy Col trail.

THE GULLY IS THE ROUTE-FINDING AND FOOTING CRUX OF THE APPROACH: loose scree over slab, class 2-3, described as kitty litter, especially under a pack. Trekking poles help. Lingering snow in it into early July may require an axe or light traction for the last few hundred feet in a big-snow year.

ARRIVAL: the base of Pernod's west face, THE TALLEST WALL IN THE WINE SPIRES. Six pitches at Grade III. If the wall above you is one of the smaller buttresses you passed on the contour, you stopped too early.

AND FOR PARTIES WHO CAMP HIGH INSTEAD: Burgundy Col itself holds three or four bivy sites, one large enough for a two-person tent, with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing. Those shelters are a positive identification of the col.

DESCENT IS BY RAPPEL DOWN THE BACK, NOT BY REVERSING THE APPROACH GULLY: the first rappel drops into the notch just below and east of the top, then a string of rappels continues down the peak's EAST side into the Silver Star Glacier basin, on the order of four to five in total. Anchors are natural, slung horns and blocks with occasional aging fixed webbing, not bolts. Once on the glacier, climb back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the standard climbers' trail.
hazards: Loose scree-over-slab in the final approach gully, the footing crux of the day
Lingering snow in the gully into early July in a big-snow year
A rappel descent down the opposite side of the peak onto a glacier, followed by a re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Natural anchors only, with aging fixed webbing; carry cord to back up or replace
A single 60 m rope is tight in places on the descent; many parties run a 70 m or doubles
The bench is the last reliable water and can run dry by late summer

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col, then the loose fourth-class traverse round the east side below Chianti to the Pernod-Chablis notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the climbers' trail drops off the highway, crosses Early Winters Creek almost immediately at around 4,080 ft via logs, and climbs steeply, gaining nearly 2,400 ft, to the bench camp at roughly 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard staging area for all the Wine Spires. From there the trail works up scree gullies to Burgundy Col at 7,770 ft.

Two pitches at 5.9 A0, Grade II. Carry a rope for the final approach moves and expect loose rock underfoot the whole way in.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE NOTCH BETWEEN PERNOD AND CHABLIS, AND THERE ARE TWO WAYS TO IT THAT ARRIVE FROM OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. Both are worth knowing before you leave camp, because the choice is made at the col and not at the base.

OPTION ONE, FROM BURGUNDY COL: rather than dropping straight to Pernod's south side, most parties continue traversing and scrambling around the EAST, Silver Star Creek, side of the ridge BELOW CHIANTI, aiming for the Pernod-Chablis notch. Expect LOOSE FOURTH-CLASS TERRAIN on this stretch, which is itself the confirmation: if the ground you are on is walkable, you have not started the traverse.

OPTION TWO, AND IT IS THE COMMON ONE BECAUSE THE ROUTE IS SHORT: climb CHABLIS SPIRE'S EAST FACE first, then downclimb or make a short rappel across loose rock to reach the base of Pernod's south face. That approach arrives from above rather than along.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS ABOUT WHICH SPIRE IS ABOVE YOU: this route sits TUCKED BETWEEN PERNOD'S BIGGER WEST FACE AND CHABLIS. If the wall above you is the tallest in the group, you are under Pernod's west face and on the Direct West Face or Standard Route ground, not here. Those are reached from the BENCH, not from the col.

AND THE NOTCH IS A NAMED GAP BETWEEN TWO NAMED SPIRES, which is the most reliable kind of feature in this basin: Pernod on one side, Chablis on the other.

DESCENT IS BY RAPPEL AND IT LINKS BACK ONTO CHABLIS: two double-rope rappels on 60 m ropes bring you back down the south face. A single 70 m can just barely work in spots, but a single 60 m can leave you several metres short of the notch. Most parties reverse this sequence to rejoin the East Face rappel line on Chablis, linked by a short fourth-class scramble, and ride those raps to the base rather than re-climbing back over to Burgundy Col.
hazards: Loose fourth-class traverse around the east side of the ridge below Chianti
A two-piton summit anchor equalized with cord, and a mix of one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger lower down
A single 60 m rope can leave a party several metres short of the notch on the descent
Rope-eating cracks a few feet below a slung-horn rap station; build that anchor as high as practical
Loose rock underfoot for the whole approach

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to the Bench, then NORTH along the ridge crest to Ares Tower
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the unsigned Wine Spires pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass, roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff near milepost 166, at about 4,300 ft. A boot path drops down loose scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft.

The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700-plus ft to Burgundy Col at about 7,800 ft. A flat bench campsite, the Bench, at about 6,460 ft sits about halfway up AND IS THE MORE COMMON CAMP FOR THIS OBJECTIVE than the col itself.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
VASILIKI RIDGE AND ARES TOWER RISE DIRECTLY NORTH OF BURGUNDY COL AND THE WINE SPIRES CAMP AREA. SO THE TEST IS DIRECTIONAL AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF EVERY OTHER ROUTE FROM THIS TRAILHEAD: FROM THE BENCH OR THE COL, GO NORTH.

Every Wine Spires objective, Burgundy, Chianti, Pernod, Chablis, is reached by going to Burgundy Col and then SOUTH or EAST from it. Ares Tower is the one you reach by contouring and scrambling NORTH along the ridge crest. IF YOU HAVE DROPPED ONTO SNOW BENEATH AN EAST-FACING WALL, YOU HAVE GONE SOUTH AND YOU ARE UNDER THE WINE SPIRES.

ARRIVAL: Ares Tower is the HIGH POINT of Vasiliki Ridge at about 8,190 ft. Following the crest north, you are at the base when the ridge stops being scrambleable and rises into a tower. Two pitches, Grade II-III, fifth class.

CONFIRM BY THE HARDWARE, AND ON THIS ridge IT IS THE ONE PIECE OF FIXED GEAR WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: THERE IS A FIXED ANCHOR AT THE ARES TOWER SUMMIT, and the standard descent is a single rappel from it down to the notch to retrieve stashed gear, then a reversal of the fourth-class ridge scramble.

SO THE PATTERN OF THE DAY IS: stash gear at a notch below the tower, climb two pitches, rappel back to your gear. If there is nowhere sensible to leave a pack, you are not at the tower yet.

CAMP CHOICE AS A PLANNING FACT: the Bench at about 6,460 ft is the more common camp for this objective than Burgundy Col, which is 1,300 ft higher and in the wrong direction.
hazards: A class 4 ridge traverse with real exposure to reach the tower
Loose scree-covered talus on the initial drop from the highway
A log crossing of Early Winters Creek
The whole approach shares a trail with the Wine Spires objectives and then deliberately departs from it

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek Trailhead near Mazama, gaining the ridge at the Cedar and Early Winters Creek confluence
approach_variants.notes:
THIS IS THE ROUTE'S DEFINING LOGISTICAL FACT: IT USES A DIFFERENT TRAILHEAD FROM EVERY OTHER ROUTE ON THE PEAK. Start from the Cedar Creek trailhead near Mazama, at the end of Sandy Butte-Cedar Creek Road #200 about 4.25 miles west of Mazama off SR-20, NOT the Silver Star Creek or Wine Spires pullouts on SR-20 that serve the Glacier and Northeast Ridge routes.

Gain the ridge near the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters Creeks, then follow the crest north and west for roughly 3.5 miles to the summit.

The row's stored waypoint names the Silver Star Creek pullout while its approach text names Cedar Creek; see _DEFECTS. And note this is SILVER STAR MOUNTAIN IN OKANOGAN COUNTY at 8,876 ft above Washington Pass, not the Silver Star Mountain in Clark County near Vancouver, Washington, which is a different peak entirely.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAILHEAD IS THE TEST, AND IT IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL ONE IN THIS BATCH BECAUSE THE TWO OPTIONS ARE SEVERAL HIGHWAY MILES APART. IF YOU PARKED AT A PULLOUT ON SR-20 OPPOSITE THE WINE SPIRES, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG TRAILHEAD FOR THIS ROUTE. The East Ridge is entered from CEDAR CREEK, on the Mazama side.

ARRIVAL AT THE RIDGE: gain the crest NEAR THE CONFLUENCE OF CEDAR AND EARLY WINTERS CREEKS. Two named creeks meeting is a feature you can identify by sound in fog, and the ridge rises directly above it.

FROM THERE THE HANDRAIL IS THE CREST ITSELF, FOR ROUGHLY 3.5 MILES NORTH AND WEST TO THE SUMMIT. That is a long ridge, and the navigation rule is the same as on any long ridge: keep it under your feet. Sidehilling off either side of a 3.5-mile crest at 5.9-plus is how a day here goes wrong.

AND THE DESCENT LANDS YOU AT THE OTHER TRAILHEAD, WHICH IS THE PLANNING PROBLEM THIS ROUTE SETS: from the summit, downclimb or rope down a short distance onto the SILVER STAR GLACIER, descend it west and northwest toward BURGUNDY COL, then over the col onto the Burgundy Col climbers' trail, which drops to Highway 20 near milepost 166 about 4 miles from Washington Pass. THAT IS SEVERAL MILES OF HIGHWAY FROM THE CEDAR CREEK TRAILHEAD YOU STARTED AT. Arrange a shuttle before you leave, not afterwards.

CARRY GLACIER TRAVEL GEAR, and an axe and crampons in early season: the descent crosses real crevassed glacier terrain, not just snow slopes.
hazards: A descent that finishes at a different trailhead several highway miles from the start
Real crevassed glacier terrain on the descent
A 3.5-mile ridge traverse with sustained route-finding
Two peaks in Washington named Silver Star Mountain; this is the Okanogan County one

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, the boulder-field path to Kangaroo Pass, then the traverse below Wallaby's slabs to the high notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Hairpin turnout on SR-20 at about 5,150 ft, roughly a mile east of Washington Pass. From the large pullout, pick up the climber's trail that switchbacks up into the valley to the southeast; it is faint and boulder-hopping at first through talus and sandy gullies, with cairns, and the tread firms up after the first quarter mile, passing a small dried-up tarn. STAY ALONG THE RIGHT-HAND, WEST, EDGE OF THE TIMBER as you gain the valley headwall.

This path gains roughly 2,000 ft over about 3 miles to Kangaroo Pass, a broad view-filled saddle that is the key approach landmark; budget 1-1.5 hours from the car. No reliable water on this stretch. Car-to-base is typically 1.5-2.5 hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT KANGAROO PASS, DO NOT DROP STRAIGHT DOWN THE FAR SIDE. THAT IS THE INSTRUCTION AND IT IS THE ONE PARTIES GET WRONG. Instead CONTOUR AND TRAVERSE SOUTH ALONG THE BASE OF THE SLABS DESCENDING FROM WALLABY PEAK, LOSING ABOUT 20 FT BELOW THE LEVEL OF THE PASS, to pick up a good, well-cairned climber's trail.

SO THE TEST IS TWENTY FEET, AND IT IS AN ALTIMETER-SCALE MEASUREMENT YOU CAN MAKE BY EYE: barely below the pass, not down into the valley beyond it. Follow that trail CLOSE BENEATH THE SLABS, STAYING BELOW ALL THE MAJOR SLAB BANDS, traversing toward Kangaroo Temple.

ARRIVAL: a GULLY SYSTEM LEADING UP TO THE HIGH NOTCH AT THE BASE OF THE NORTH FACE. Ascend that gully to the notch. THE NOTCH IS THE START OF THE ROUTE.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE NORTHWEST FACE, AND IT IS COUNTABLE IN FEET: ABOUT 200 FT BELOW THE NOTCH, AN OBVIOUS BENCH AND TRAIL SPLITS OFF RIGHT TOWARD THE NORTHWEST FACE. If you have taken a bench off to the right, you are on the Northwest Face approach. This route keeps going up the boulder-choked gully to the notch itself.

AND THE SOUTH FACE USES A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT LINE FROM THE SAME CAR, WHICH IS THE OTHER WAY TO END UP IN THE WRONG PLACE: it hikes southeast on the RIGHT side of the creek and NEVER CROSSES KANGAROO PASS AT ALL. If you have not been over Kangaroo Pass, you are not on the North Face approach.

CONFIRM ON THE DESCENT, WHICH IS COUNTABLE HARDWARE: three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from FIXED BOLTED CHAINS, landing on downclimbable low-fifth and fourth-class terrain just above the high notch where the route began. A 50 M ROPE ONLY JUST BARELY REACHES THE SECOND STATION, so a 60 m is strongly preferred. All anchors are fixed chains; no natural anchor building is needed.
hazards: Route-finding where the boulder-field tread disappears and reappears repeatedly before the pass
Loose talus and scree underfoot throughout
Early-season snow or ice in the approach gully, warranting an ice axe
A 50 m rope barely reaches the second rappel station; the descent line goes over a sharp lip onto vertical face
Queues at the rap stations; this is a popular club route and weekend backups are common
No reliable water on the approach

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout and Kangaroo Pass, then break off the gully about 200 ft BELOW the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The Temple is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass, the same parking used for the neighbouring Hairpin Crags and Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus, faint and intermittently cairned, up to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour.

From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Total trailhead-to-summit time runs about 7-8 hours round trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NORTHWEST FACE BREAKS OFF ONTO A CLIMBER'S TRAIL ABOUT 200 FT BELOW THE NOTCH, INSTEAD OF CONTINUING INTO THE BOULDER-CHOKED GULLY. That is the whole find and it is a measured one: two hundred feet short of the top of the gully, an obvious bench and trail splits off RIGHT.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS: IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE NOTCH, YOU HAVE GONE ROUGHLY 200 FT TOO FAR AND YOU ARE AT THE START OF THE NORTH FACE. And if you are fighting up a boulder-choked gully bed rather than walking a bench, you have missed the split.

GETTING TO THE GULLY IN THE FIRST PLACE: from Kangaroo Pass, traverse left to the GULLY BETWEEN KANGAROO TEMPLE AND LITTLE FINGER, then ascend toward the notch. Do not drop straight down the far side of the pass; contour south below the slabs descending from Wallaby Peak, losing about 20 ft below the pass, on a good well-cairned trail beneath the slab bands.

WHAT THE OTHER TWO ROUTES DO FROM THE SAME PLACE, SO THE THREE ARE SEPARABLE: the NORTH FACE goes all the way up the gully to the high notch. THIS ROUTE takes the bench 200 ft below it. THE SOUTH FACE never crosses Kangaroo Pass at all; it hikes southeast on the right side of the creek, and its face is not even visible from the highway.

DESCENT: from the summit, downclimb or scramble to the fixed rappel anchors on the NORTH side of the formation. Accounts differ slightly, with some parties making two rappels of 30 m and 50 m and others three shorter single-rope rappels, roughly 150-160-plus ft in total, to avoid rope-stuck issues, landing at or near the North Ridge notch. From the notch, the standard descent gully leads back down to Kangaroo Pass.
hazards: A 200 ft window in which to leave the gully, above and below which you are on a different route
Loose talus and a boulder-choked gully
Rope-stuck issues on the descent, which is why some parties break it into three shorter rappels
Early-season snow or ice in the approach gully
No reliable water on the approach

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, then southeast on the RIGHT side of the creek, never crossing Kangaroo Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the same hairpin pullout on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass that the Temple's other routes use, but understand from the outset that THIS ROUTE USES A GENUINELY DIFFERENT APPROACH FROM THE NORTH AND NORTHWEST FACE ROUTES.

Hike southeast on the RIGHT side of the creek on a trail that improves past several slide and boulder areas. Longer and steeper than the Kangaroo Pass line.

Seven pitches at 5.8, first climbed in summer 1965.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
NEVER CROSS KANGAROO PASS. THAT IS THE NEGATIVE TEST AND IT IS ABSOLUTE: THE NORTH AND NORTHWEST FACE ROUTES BOTH GO OVER THE PASS AND THEN TRAVERSE BENEATH WALLABY'S SLABS. THIS ONE DOES NOT GO THERE AT ALL. IF YOU ARE STANDING IN A BROAD, VIEW-FILLED SADDLE, YOU HAVE TAKEN THE WRONG APPROACH.

THE POSITIVE INSTRUCTION IS A SIDE-OF-THE-CREEK TEST, WHICH IS EXACTLY THE KIND THAT SURVIVES FOG: HIKE SOUTHEAST ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE CREEK. Water on your left the whole way up. The trail IMPROVES past several slide and boulder areas, which is the opposite of what the Kangaroo Pass path does, so the tread itself tells you which line you are on.

AND THE FACT THAT SHOULD SHAPE THE WHOLE PLAN, BECAUSE IT REMOVES THE OBVIOUS METHOD OF CONFIRMING YOUR OBJECTIVE: THE SOUTH FACE IS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE HIGHWAY. You cannot look at it from the car and pick your line, which is how most parties orient themselves at Washington Pass. Commit to the creek-side approach and read the wall when you arrive under it.

EXPECT IT TO BE LONGER AND STEEPER than the north-side approach. If your walk is taking about an hour to a pass, you are on the wrong one.
hazards: A route with no view of its own face from the road, so the objective cannot be assessed before committing
Longer and steeper than the peak's other approaches
Slide and boulder areas low on the trail
Shared parking with two routes that take a completely different line from the same car

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, cross Early Winters Creek at the talus edge, then the west gully with the chockstone
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 about a mile east of Washington Pass near milepost 163, pick up the cairned climbers' trail on the WEST side of Early Winters Creek, the same start used for Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak. Follow it roughly 0.5-0.7 mile through open timber to where it meets the edge of a talus and boulder field.

RATHER THAN CONTINUING SOUTH TOWARD KANGAROO PASS, WHICH IS THE KANGAROO TEMPLE LINE, LEAVE THE TRAIL HERE AND CROSS EARLY WINTERS CREEK. Normally an easy rock-hop, but treat it with respect during peak snowmelt or after rain; there is no bridge. Once across, the route becomes an open boot-track and light bushwhack through slide alder and slabs, trending east into the basin below Big Kangaroo.

One-way gain to the base of the roped climbing is roughly 2,700 ft over about 3 miles; budget 2.5-4 hours, longer early season. Car-to-car is commonly 6-plus hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AROUND 6,000 FT, AIM FOR THE BROAD, SHALLOW WEST-FACING GULLY THAT LEADS UP TOWARD THE NOTCH JUST NORTH OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK, IDENTIFIABLE BY A DISTINCT CHOCKSTONE PARTWAY UP. THE CHOCKSTONE IS THE MARKER. One block jammed in the gully, and you climb past or around it.

SO THE COUNT IS ONE: one chockstone, in one broad shallow gully on the west side. If you are passing several jammed blocks, or if your gully is narrow and steep rather than broad and shallow, you are in the wrong one.

FOOTING AS A CONFIRMATION, BECAUSE IT IS UNUSUALLY SPECIFIC HERE: the gully is loose underfoot and the advice is to STAY NEAR ITS EDGES OR ON THE THIN VEGETATION rather than the centre choss. It NARROWS WITH DOWNSLOPING SLABS ABOUT HALFWAY, and some parties bypass that by favouring the adjacent north-side gully. A gully that narrows onto downsloping slabs at mid-height is this one.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROPED CLIMBING: push past the chockstone and continue up class 3 slabs to A BROAD PLATFORM BELOW THE SUMMIT TOWER. That platform is where the route's three roped pitches begin. Flat ground below a tower, above a chockstone gully.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE SOUTH-FACE ROUTES, AND IT IS A CREEK-CROSSING TEST: the south-face lines, Beckey-Tate, Kearney-Thomas and the rest, follow the climbers' trail MUCH FURTHER SOUTH along the west side of the creek before crossing, then take a prominent gully with a HIGH Y-JUNCTION. If you crossed the creek at the talus edge after half a mile, you are set up for the West Face. If you are still walking south after a mile and a half, you are heading for the south side.

THE LAST MOVE IS THE CRUX OF THE WHOLE OUTING AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING NOW: an exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old rusty quarter-inch bolt to a tiny summit, downclimbed or top-roped back rather than rappelled, because there is no real anchor up top and no room to stand.
hazards: An unbridged crossing of Early Winters Creek that runs high in snowmelt
A loose gully that narrows onto downsloping slabs at mid-height
An exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old rusty quarter-inch bolt at the summit
The gully sheds loose rock readily; keep helmets on for the whole descent
Snow in the gully into July in some years

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, staying WEST of the creek longer than the West Face line, then over the Half Moon col into the south basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20, follow the cairned climbers' trail south along the WEST side of Early Winters Creek toward Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, BUT STAY ON THE TRAIL, ON THE RIGHT OR WEST SIDE OF THE CREEK, LONGER THAN THE WEST FACE LINE DOES. Do not cross the creek where that route splits off.

Continue up-valley as the trail fades into open talus and boulder fields, then work toward the head of the basin. Roughly 2 miles and 2,440 ft one-way to the base, with 3-5 hours a reasonable estimate given the route-finding through boulder fields. Noticeably longer and more sustained than the standard West Face gully route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CUT LEFT, EAST, TOWARD THE LOW POINT ON THE RIDGE BETWEEN BIG KANGAROO AND HALF MOON. That col drops and traverses you into the SOUTH-FACING BASIN DIRECTLY BELOW BIG KANGAROO'S SOUTH WALL.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROUTE ITSELF IS VISUAL AND UNAMBIGUOUS WHEN YOU CAN SEE THE WALL: THE BECKEY-TATE'S OBVIOUS CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITS THE FACE. A single ramp system running up the middle of a south wall, splitting it, is the line.

SO THE ORDER OF FINDS IS: stay west of the creek, reach the head of the basin, cut east to the Half Moon col, drop into the south basin, then look for the ramp splitting the middle of the wall.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE WEST FACE, WHICH IS THE COMMONEST ERROR FROM THIS CAR: THE WEST FACE ROUTE CROSSES EARLY WINTERS CREEK AFTER ONLY HALF A MILE, AT THE EDGE OF THE TALUS FIELD, AND TAKES A BROAD SHALLOW WEST-FACING GULLY WITH A CHOCKSTONE IN IT. If you crossed the creek early and are looking at a chockstone, you are on the west side of the mountain.

AND AGAINST THE OTHER SOUTH-FACE LINES, WHICH SHARE THIS BASIN: KEARNEY-THOMAS crosses the creek and ascends the prominent gully system TAKING THE LEFT FORK AT THE HIGH Y-JUNCTION. GOING DOWN UNDER starts at the Beckey-Tate base and then TRAVERSES RIGHT ACROSS OVERLAPS to its own start ledge. SKINNY START is ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT of the Kearney-Thomas start. So on this wall: the central ramp is Beckey-Tate, and everything else is measured from either it or Kearney-Thomas.

DESCENT IS NOT DOWN THIS ROUTE, AND THE REASON MATTERS: rappelling the Beckey-Tate is technically possible with two ropes, roughly five to six rappels off slings and trees, but the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, so rope-stuck and rockfall risk is high and most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead scramble about 20 ft up and LEFT to the notch just north of the summit block, the same notch the West Face route uses, and reverse the shared gully descent.
hazards: Talus hopping and route-finding through boulder fields for 2 miles
A lot of large loose rock on the route, making rappelling it inadvisable
An exposed unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old bolt if tagging the true summit
A steep, loose upper gully on the shared descent
Snow lingering in the approach basin and the gullies near the top of the route in early season

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout, south along Early Winters Creek about 2 miles, then cross and take the LEFT fork at the high Y-junction
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, roughly milepost 163, about a mile east of Washington Pass. Follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak climbers' path south along Early Winters Creek for roughly 2 miles, then leave the trail to cross the creek and ascend the prominent gully system to the base of the south face.

Expect 2.5 to 5 hours of approach time; water is unreliable late season. Seven pitches.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGH Y-JUNCTION IN THE APPROACH GULLY IS THE DECISION POINT, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE LEFT FORK. That is a countable, binary choice on the ground, and every south-face route on this peak depends on it.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS: roughly TWO MILES south along the creek, then CROSS, then up a prominent gully to a Y, then LEFT. Crossing after half a mile instead of two puts you on the West Face approach, on the other side of the mountain, in a broad shallow gully with a chockstone in it.

ARRIVAL AT THE WALL: the base of the SOUTH FACE. The Beckey-Tate's obvious CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITTING THE FACE is the reference feature here, because two other routes are measured from this one and from that ramp.

HOW THE SOUTH FACE STARTS SORT OUT, IN ORDER, AND THE ONE MEASUREMENT THAT SEPARATES THEM: SKINNY START IS ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT OF THE STANDARD KEARNEY-THOMAS START. GOING DOWN UNDER starts from the Beckey-Tate base and traverses RIGHT ACROSS OVERLAPS to its own ledge. THE CENTRAL RAMP IS BECKEY-TATE. SO: IF YOU HAVE WALKED THIRTY METRES RIGHT OF WHERE YOU MEANT TO BE, YOU ARE ON SKINNY START.

WATER IS UNRELIABLE LATE SEASON. Carry it from the creek before crossing, since the crossing is the last of it.

DESCENT: as with the neighbouring Beckey-Tate line, scramble to the notch just north of the true summit and follow the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.
hazards: A Y-junction where the wrong fork puts you on different ground
2.5 to 5 hours of approach with unreliable water late season
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Three routes starting within about 30 metres on the same wall

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully, LEFT fork at the Y, then 30 metres right of Kearney-Thomas
approach_variants.notes:
Same south-face approach as Kearney-Thomas and Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully taking the LEFT fork at the high Y-junction to the base of the south face.

Three pitches, established in 2012.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT OF THE STANDARD KEARNEY-THOMAS START. THIRTY METRES IS THE WHOLE MARGIN, WHICH MEANS YOU MUST FIND KEARNEY-THOMAS FIRST AND THEN PACE IT OUT.

HOW TO ANCHOR YOURSELF ON THIS WALL: the BECKEY-TATE'S OBVIOUS CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITS THE FACE and is the feature everything else is described against. Kearney-Thomas is the standard south-face start; this route is thirty metres right of it; Going Down Under starts at the Beckey-Tate base and traverses right across overlaps to its own ledge.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS DIRECTIONAL AND SHORT: IF YOU ARE LEFT OF KEARNEY-THOMAS YOU ARE HEADING TOWARD THE CENTRAL RAMP AND BECKEY-TATE. THIRTY METRES IS ROUGHLY FORTY PACES ALONG THE BASE; IF YOU HAVE WALKED A HUNDRED, YOU HAVE OVERSHOT.

A WARNING ABOUT THE DESCENT THAT SHOULD CHANGE WHAT YOU CARRY, AND IT COMES FROM A PARTY WHO ACTUALLY HIT IT: the intended descent follows the Beckey-Tate line, scrambling to the notch north of the summit and then the loose gully back to the Hairpin. AT LEAST ONE PARTY WAS UNABLE TO FIND A RAPPEL ANCHOR ALONG THE TOP OF THAT SUGGESTED DESCENT and instead had to change into rock shoes and make a high traverse to a saddle before descending. BUDGET EXTRA TIME AND BE PREPARED TO BUILD YOUR OWN ANCHORS.
hazards: A 30-metre offset from a neighbouring start as the only positional marker
A reported failure to find the expected rappel anchor on the standard descent
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Unreliable water late season

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully to the Beckey-Tate base, then traverse RIGHT across the overlaps
approach_variants.notes:
Same south-face approach as Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully taking the LEFT fork at the high Y-junction to the base of the Beckey-Tate start.

Five pitches, established in 2012.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
START AT THE BECKEY-TATE BASE AND THEN TRAVERSE RIGHT ACROSS OVERLAPS TO THIS ROUTE'S OWN START LEDGE. So the find is two-step and the first step is the easiest thing on the wall to identify: THE BECKEY-TATE'S OBVIOUS CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITS THE SOUTH FACE.

THE SECOND STEP IS A TEXTURE TEST: OVERLAPS. You traverse RIGHT across overlapping rock features to reach a ledge. If you are walking along flat ground at the foot of the wall rather than moving across overlaps, you are not on the traverse.
