WHY STARTING AT BECKEY-TATE IS AN ADVANTAGE RATHER THAN A HANDICAP HERE: the central ramp is the one feature on this face that is described as obvious, and every other line is measured from it. Find the ramp, then move right.

THE OTHER TWO STARTS ON THIS WALL, SO YOU KNOW WHEN YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR: KEARNEY-THOMAS is the standard south-face start, and SKINNY START IS ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT OF IT. If your rightward traverse has run out of overlaps and you have arrived at a plainly separate ground start, you have gone past this route into that cluster.

DESCENT: from the top, join the standard descent, scrambling to the notch just north of the true summit and following the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.
hazards: No independent ground start; the base is another route's base plus a traverse
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Several routes starting within a short distance on the same wall
Unreliable water late season

approach_variants.name: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear RIGHT into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
approach_variants.notes:
The standard approach uses the same SR-20 pullout as the South Buttress, on the north side of the highway about 1.5 miles WEST of Washington Pass. Follow the South Buttress approach: creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field.

Eight pitches at 5.7. This is the peak's classic line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT THE BOULDER FIELD, BEAR RIGHT AND NORTH INTO THE BASIN BENEATH THE NORTH RIDGE NOTCH, RATHER THAN LEFT TOWARD THE SOUTH BUTTRESS GULLY. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

THE ROUTE'S REAL BASE IS THE NOTCH, AND GETTING TO IT IS ITSELF A PITCH: from the basin, A LOOSE, RUNOUT 5.7 PG13 PITCH GAINS THE NORTH RIDGE NOTCH. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, AND THIS PITCH SHOULD BE TREATED AS THE TECHNICAL AND PSYCHOLOGICAL CRUX OF THE APPROACH, NOT OF THE RIDGE ABOVE IT.

SO THE TEST IS BLUNT: IF THE HARDEST, SCARIEST THING YOU HAVE DONE IS THE PITCH THAT GOT YOU TO THE NOTCH, YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT ROUTE. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

ARRIVAL: a NOTCH, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

THE NORTHERN ALTERNATIVE, WHICH ARRIVES AT THE SAME NOTCH FROM THE OTHER SIDE: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the PORCUPINE CREEK drainage, then climb TWO OR THREE SHORT PITCHES OF LOW FIFTH CLASS to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

DESCENT DOES NOT REVERSE THE APPROACH PITCH ALL THE WAY: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of BOLTED CHAIN RAPPEL ANCHORS and continuing down the same FOUR-RAPPEL West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.
hazards: A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch with marginal protection simply to reach the base of the ridge
A descent that leaves the ridge at the notch and continues down a different route's rappel line
Loose rock and brush on the lower approach
A more direct West Ridge descent from higher on the North Ridge exists but is considered worse for rockfall

approach_variants.name: The SR-20 pullout, over the rib south of the South Buttress into the basin EAST of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
From the long pullout on the NORTH side of SR-20 about a mile and a half WEST of Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' track from its EAST end down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak.

Six pitches, Grade III, first climbed in 1976. Note that the stored id for this row says northeast face while its name and aspect both say EAST; see _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TRAVERSE OVER THE RIB THAT EXTENDS SOUTH FROM THE SOUTH BUTTRESS INTO THE BASIN EAST OF CUTTHROAT PEAK. THAT SECOND BASIN IS WHERE THE EAST FACE ROUTES BEGIN.

SO THE COUNT IS TWO BASINS, AND THE RIB BETWEEN THEM IS THE THING YOU CROSS: first the basin below the peak's south side, which is where the South Buttress and North Ridge parties go, then over a rib, then the east basin. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A RIB, YOU ARE STILL IN THE SOUTH BASIN AND YOU ARE UNDER THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE NORTH RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME BOULDER FIELD: that route bears RIGHT AND NORTH into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch, and gains it by a loose runout 5.7 pitch. If you are roping up for a single hard pitch to reach a notch, you are on the North Ridge, not on the East Face.

A HAZARD THAT IS ALSO A ROUTE-FINDING INSTRUCTION, AND IT IS STATED IN BOTH ROWS ON THIS SIDE: AVOID THE STEEP, LOOSE SCREE CHIMNEYS DIRECTLY BELOW THE WALL ON THE WAY IN. If your line into the base is up a confined chimney full of scree, you have picked the wrong way through and should back out and go round.

WHY THIS ENTRY DOES NOT NAME A CRACK OR A FLAKE AT THE START: no per-route detail beyond this shared approach is on file for this line, and the peak's other east-side route carries no marker either. What is recorded is the basin, the rib and the chimneys to avoid, and those are all real ground features.

DESCENT: no route-specific beta exists beyond the general east-face pattern. Parties commonly descend the South Buttress with multiple rappels, or the West Ridge on fixed-anchor rappels plus downclimbing, rather than reversing the technical face.
hazards: Steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall that must be avoided rather than climbed
A descent by a different route than the one climbed, with no route-specific beta
A creek crossing and brushy climbers' path low down
No published marker at the base of the route itself

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. LEAVE THE PCT ALMOST IMMEDIATELY and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is WHISTLER MOUNTAIN ABOVE RAINY PASS in Okanogan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CLIMB UNTIL THE FOREST OPENS. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A MEADOW BASIN BELOW THE WEST RIDGE AND GULLY COMPLEX, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

FROM THE BASIN, TREND SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ON A RISING TRAVERSE TO GAIN THE COL AND BASIN BETWEEN WHISTLER AND THE SOUTHWEST PEAK OF CUTTHROAT. THAT COL IS THE AIMING POINT, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the BROAD WEST RIDGE, or the SHALLOW GULLY JUST NORTH OF IT, to the summit shoulder.

THE LAST SECTION IS THE ONE THAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE ON THE SUMMIT LINE RATHER THAN A NEIGHBOURING GULLY: A ROCK GULLY WITH A VISIBLE RAMP ALONG THE HEADWALL, OVER DOWNSLOPING SLABS AND LOOSE GRAVEL. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile BEFORE the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the WEST EDGE OF A STAND OF TREES.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAILHEAD IS UNMARKED AND THE PATH START IS A TREE-LINE EDGE, SO THE FIND IS AT THE ROAD RATHER THAN ON THE MOUNTAIN. The pullout is 0.7 MILE BEFORE THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD coming from Rainy Pass. IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, YOU HAVE DRIVEN 0.7 MILE TOO FAR. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a STAND OF TREES begins, and the boot path leaves from its WEST EDGE.

FOLLOW THE BOOT PATH UP THROUGH A MEADOW, THEN RISING-TRAVERSE EAST TO INTERSECT THE LEVEL PORTION OF WHISTLER'S SOUTH RIDGE AT ABOUT 6,180 FT. A LEVEL SECTION OF RIDGE IS THE ARRIVAL, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

FROM THERE, SCRAMBLE UP THE RIDGE AND CONNECTING GULLIES TO THE SUMMIT. THE ALTERNATIVE, WHICH IS ALSO CORRECT: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies LEFT, north, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

SO THE DECISION AT 6,800 FT IS A REAL FORK AND BOTH BRANCHES WORK: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies north for easier ground.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH, WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH START WITHIN THREE MILES OF EACH OTHER ON THE SAME HIGHWAY: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a MEADOW BASIN at 6,100 ft below the WEST ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the SOUTH ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT over Cutthroat, Granite and Methow Passes to Snowy Lakes, then the reddish boulder and the cave
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead at about 4,875 ft on SR-20, 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass at about 6,600 ft, roughly 4.9 miles. THIS STRETCH HAS ONLY INTERMITTENT SMALL STREAMS, SO TOP OFF AT THE PASS; there is little reliable water again until Snowy Lakes.

From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass at about 6,600 ft, roughly 6.5-7 miles in. Granite Pass holds snow into July or August and when snow-covered is steep and exposed enough to warrant an ice axe. Beyond it the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut blasted-out section, loses a little elevation and climbs again to Methow Pass at about 9 miles.

Roughly 10 miles in, just past Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers' use path branches RIGHT, east, off the PCT and climbs about half a mile and 400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin, the standard base camp with reliable water and good tent sites.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH FROM CAMP HAS THREE MARKERS AND ALL THREE ARE OBJECTS YOU CAN PUT A HAND ON, WHICH IS RARE AND IS WHY THIS ROUTE IS UNUSUALLY FINDABLE IN CLOUD.

FIRST: from camp near Lower Snowy Lake, head cross-country SOUTH toward Tower Mountain on a climbers' path, then make a short but strenuous traverse across a TALUS FIELD, AIMING FOR A DISTINCTIVE LARGE REDDISH BOULDER PARTWAY ACROSS. A single big red block in a talus field.

SECOND: BEYOND THE BOULDER, A RAMP ON THE LEFT SIDE OF A LARGE CAVE. THE CAVE CUTS ABOUT 25 YARDS INTO THE MOUNTAINSIDE and makes a good wind-sheltered rest stop. A cave you can walk twenty-five yards into is not something you can mistake for anything else.

THIRD: that ramp leads UP TO THE BASE OF THE MAIN SUMMIT GULLY. That gully is the route.

SO THE ORDER IS: TALUS, RED BOULDER, CAVE, RAMP ON ITS LEFT, GULLY. If you have crossed the talus and found no red boulder, you are off the traverse line. If you have found the boulder but no cave, keep going.

FROM THE BASE OF THE GULLY the route follows LEDGES ON THE GULLY'S RIGHT SIDE, zigzagging back toward the gully-notch in the ridge and up broken rock to the summit. Right-hand ledges, not the gully bed.

THE GULLY IS THE MAIN HAZARD OF THE WHOLE OUTING AND THE RULE IS ABOUT SPACING RATHER THAN TECHNIQUE: the rock is notoriously loose and rockfall-prone, so helmets on and CLIMB ONE AT A TIME THROUGH THE NARROWEST SECTIONS, staying right and moving efficiently.
hazards: A notoriously loose and rockfall-prone summit gully; climb one at a time through constrictions
Granite Pass holds snow into July or August and is steep and exposed when covered; carry an axe
Little reliable water between Cutthroat Pass and Snowy Lakes
A cliff-cut, blasted-out section of trail between Granite and Methow Passes
Roughly 10-11 miles one-way to camp before any climbing

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT over Cutthroat and Granite Passes to the Snowy Lakes spur
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct, with late September and early October favoured for larch colour and stable weather
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-20 to Rainy Pass at 4,880 ft near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount, and park at the Rainy Pass North PCT trailhead.

Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail through forest and switchbacks to Cutthroat Pass at about 6,800 ft, continue past Granite Pass at roughly 6.25 miles, where snowfields can linger into August, and along a cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. ABOUT A MILE BEFORE METHOW PASS, A SIGNED SPUR TRAIL SWITCHBACKS UP TO LOWER AND THEN UPPER SNOWY LAKE at about 6,700-7,000 ft. Roughly 10-11 miles and 2,700 ft of gain one-way. Good campsites sit in the meadow near the lakes.

Two pitches. This is also the peak's overall first ascent line, made in September 1946.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SPUR TO THE LAKES IS SIGNED, AND THAT IS THE ONE PIECE OF SIGNAGE ON THE WHOLE DAY, SO USE IT: it leaves the PCT ABOUT A MILE BEFORE METHOW PASS. IF YOU HAVE REACHED METHOW PASS, YOU HAVE WALKED ABOUT A MILE TOO FAR.

CAMP IS AT THE LAKES, AND THE LAKES ARE THE BASE OF THE DAY. From there the route is a scramble on the southwest side of the peak with only two pitches of climbing at the top.

THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS WHAT MAKES THIS ROUTE FINDABLE, AND THE DESCENT DESCRIBES IT PRECISELY: parties make A SINGLE SHORT RAPPEL OF ROUGHLY 40 FT OFF THE SUMMIT BLOCK to regain the ridge, then downclimb and scramble class 2-3 scree and talus back toward Snowy Lakes. SO THE TECHNICAL PART OF THIS MOUNTAIN IS ABOUT FORTY FEET TALL AND IT IS AT THE VERY TOP. If you are roping up low on the peak you have found something harder than the Southwest Route.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER ASPECTS, AND IT IS A DIRECTION FROM CAMP: the NORTH side is reached by travelling NORTHWEST from Snowy Lakes into Golden Horn's basin. The EAST FACE is reached by scrambling the ridge, traversing a scree field on the SOUTHWEST side, and then DESCENDING to the base of the east face. THIS ROUTE NEVER DESCENDS. It stays on the southwest flank and goes up. If you are losing height to reach a wall, you are on the east face approach.

PLUNGE-STEPPING THE LOOSE SCREE SPEEDS THE DESCENT CONSIDERABLY, which is worth knowing because the scree is otherwise the slowest part of the day.
hazards: Snowfields lingering at Granite Pass into August
A cliff-cut section of trail beyond Granite Pass
Loose class 2-3 scree and talus on the upper mountain
A 10-11 mile approach before any climbing
Little reliable water between Cutthroat Pass and Snowy Lakes

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then the unmarked path past Lewis Lake to Wing Lake
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area and Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 157.5 at about 4,850 ft, a 40-car lot with a privy. THIS IS THE RAINY PASS LAKE ANN, NOT THE LAKE ANN BELOW MOUNT SHUKSAN ON THE MOUNT BAKER HIGHWAY; the two are about 80 km apart and share a name.

Follow the Lake Ann and Maple Pass Trail #740 about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and TAKE THE RIGHT FORK TOWARD HEATHER PASS; the left continues on the Lake Ann and Maple Pass loop. Climb through meadows to Heather Pass at about 2.6 miles and 6,100 ft, WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL ENDS.

From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading NORTH, crossing two talus and boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake at about 3 miles and 6,600 ft, with timbered campsites on the north side and water. THIS OFF-TRAIL STRETCH IS THE MAIN ROUTE-FINDING CHALLENGE OF THE APPROACH, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,000 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake at about 3.5-4 miles and 6,900 ft, the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO LAKES IN SEQUENCE ARE THE APPROACH'S SPINE, AND THEY ARE WATER FEATURES, WHICH IS WHY THIS APPROACH IS SURVIVABLE WHEN THE CAIRNS ARE BURIED. LEWIS LAKE FIRST, THEN A THOUSAND FEET OF CLIMBING, THEN WING LAKE. If you have reached only one lake you are not at camp.

FROM WING LAKE, GO AROUND THE RIGHT, NORTH, SIDE OF THE LAKE AND AIM FOR THE OBVIOUS TALUS AND SNOW GULLY LEADING INTO THE COULOIR JUST SOUTH OF THE SUMMIT. Climb that gully, then ANGLE CLIMBER'S-RIGHT OUT OF IT TO AVOID CLIFF BANDS DIRECTLY BELOW THE COL, topping out at THE SOUTH COL ON THE CREST OF THE SOUTH RIDGE. THE SOUTH COL IS THE TRUE START OF THE CLIMBING.

SO THE ONE INSTRUCTION THAT KEEPS YOU OUT OF TROUBLE IS THE EXIT FROM THE GULLY: ANGLE RIGHT NEAR THE TOP. Going straight up puts you under cliff bands below the col.

ARRIVAL AT THE COL: a gap on a ridge crest with the summit pyramid to the north of you. Above it the route is cairned class 3 along the ridge to the summit pyramid, then a CAIRNED CLASS 2 LEDGE SYSTEM traversing below the summit block, exposed near its end, and finally A SHORT CLASS 4 STEP OF ABOUT 15 FT to the true summit.

SO THE COUNT ABOVE THE COL IS: cairned ridge, one ledge system, one 15 ft step. There is no other technical ground on this route. A BOULDER IS SLUNG AT THAT STEP for an optional short rappel or hand line; a 30 m rope is more than enough, and many parties skip the rope and downclimb it facing in.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S NORTHEAST RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME CAMP: that route ascends snow toward the LOW POINT IN THE NORTHEAST RIDGE, following the HOGSBACK MORAINE WIDE RIGHT and then traversing back left to the notch. A moraine underfoot and a notch on the northeast side means you are on the other route.
hazards: An unmarked off-trail stretch between Heather Pass and Lewis Lake, the approach's main route-finding challenge, worse with cairns buried by snow
Cliff bands directly below the south col if you climb the gully straight up rather than angling right
An exposed cairned ledge traverse below the summit block
A short class 4 step at the summit
Two lakes in Washington named Lake Ann; this route uses the Rainy Pass one

approach_variants.name: As for the South Ridge to Wing Lake, then the hogsback moraine wide right to the low point in the Northeast Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the South Ridge: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, the right fork at the signed junction toward Heather Pass, then the unmarked climbers' path north across two talus fields to Lewis Lake and up roughly 1,000 ft more to a camp at Wing Lake at about 6,900 ft.

Five pitches, first climbed in September 1973.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CAMP, ASCEND SNOW TOWARD THE LOW POINT IN THE NORTHEAST RIDGE. THE ROUTE-FINDING RULE IS THE USEFUL PART AND IT IS COUNTERINTUITIVE: FOLLOWING THE HOGSBACK MORAINE WIDE RIGHT AND THEN TRAVERSING BACK LEFT TO THE NOTCH IS REPORTED TO STAY ON MORE STABLE GROUND THAN A DIRECT LINE.

SO YOU DELIBERATELY GO WIDE AND THEN COME BACK, AND THE HANDRAIL IS A MORAINE, which is a ridge of rubble you can keep under your feet without seeing anything. If you are on snow with no moraine beside you, you have taken the direct line and you are on the looser ground.

A SMALL PERMANENT SNOWFIELD OR MINI-GLACIER CAN PERSIST BELOW THE COL INTO SEPTEMBER, so expect snow under the notch even late in the year. That persistence is itself a confirmation: this is the shaded side.

ARRIVAL: the LOW POINT of the ridge, a notch. Five pitches follow.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE SOUTH RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME CAMP AT WING LAKE: that route goes around the RIGHT, NORTH, SIDE OF THE LAKE and up an obvious talus and snow gully into THE COULOIR JUST SOUTH OF THE SUMMIT, exiting climber's-right to the SOUTH COL. South col and a couloir means the other route; northeast notch and a moraine means this one.

AND THE DESCENT IS THE SOUTH RIDGE'S, WHICH YOU WILL HAVE TO FIND FROM ABOVE: from the summit, work down and south toward the South Ridge route, using one rappel or a downclimb to get below the initial band of rock, then continue south to the south col. From there the descent follows the South Ridge's loose, cairned gully, described by multiple parties as tedious and choss-prone, back down to snow slopes and Wing Lake.
hazards: A permanent snowfield or mini-glacier below the col persisting into September
Unstable ground on a direct line to the notch; the wide-right moraine line is the stable one
A descent by the South Ridge's loose cairned gully, found from above
The same unmarked off-trail approach stretch between Heather Pass and Lewis Lake

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then the 6,400 ft traverse and the scree ramp between two cliff bands
approach_variants.notes:
From the paved pullout at Rainy Pass at 4,855 ft on SR-20, signed Rainy Pass Trailhead, 52 miles east of Marblemount and right where the PCT crosses the highway, start on the Lake Ann and Maple Pass Trail, well-graded and heavily used. AGAIN, THIS IS THE RAINY PASS LAKE ANN, NOT THE ONE BELOW MOUNT SHUKSAN.

At roughly 1.5 miles, STAY RIGHT at the Lake Ann junction; the lake itself, just below the junction, IS THE LAST RELIABLE ON-TRAIL WATER SOURCE. Continue climbing switchbacks through heather meadows to Heather Pass at about 6,080 ft, roughly 2 miles in, WHERE CORTEO'S EAST AND SOUTHEAST FACE COMES INTO FULL VIEW ACROSS THE BASIN.

Leave the maintained trail there. About 4-5 miles and 2,500 ft of gain from the trailhead to reach the 7,000 ft ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAVERSE IS HELD AT A HEIGHT AND THE ENTRY TO THE RIDGE IS A RAMP BETWEEN TWO CLIFF BANDS, WHICH IS THE ONE DETAIL THAT MAKES THIS FINDABLE. From Heather Pass, traverse climber's-LEFT, south, BELOW HORSEFLY PASS, HOLDING AROUND 6,400 FT across a broad talus and scree basin beneath the face. Then pick a rising traverse across scree benches and A SCREE RAMP THAT THREADS BETWEEN TWO LOW CLIFF BANDS to gain Corteo's southeast ridge AT ABOUT 7,000 FT.

SO THERE ARE TWO NUMBERS AND ONE SHAPE: HOLD 6,400 FT ACROSS THE BASIN, FIND A RAMP BETWEEN TWO CLIFF BANDS, AND GAIN THE RIDGE AT 7,000 FT. In cloud the altimeter does most of the work and the ramp is the only thing you have to see.

IF YOU CANNOT FIND A WAY THROUGH THE CLIFF BANDS, YOU ARE NOT AT THE RAMP. There is one threading line; forcing a cliff band elsewhere is how this approach goes wrong.

FROM THE RIDGE, work climber's-LEFT up ledges and short rock steps toward A NOTCH AT ROUGHLY 7,900-7,920 FT JUST EAST OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK, then finish through blocky class 3 terrain, with some parties roping up for a few class 4 moves near the top, to the 8,107 ft summit.

SO THE SEQUENCE OF HEIGHTS IS 6,400, 7,000, 7,900, 8,107, AND EACH ONE IS A CHANGE OF GROUND: basin traverse, ridge gained, notch, summit block.

A HAZARD THAT IS ALSO A TIMING INSTRUCTION: underfoot is loose, downsloping talus and scree for most of the off-trail traverse, AND THE EAST FACE SHEDS ROCK ESPECIALLY AS THE DAY WARMS. Cross the basin early.

THE DESCENT USES DIFFERENT GROUND FROM THE ASCENT AND THAT IS WORTH PLANNING FOR: it drops southwest along the ridge crest to a large notch roughly a third of the way down at about 7,600-7,700 ft, reached through an easy connecting gully with ONE DISTINCTLY STEEPER STEP, commonly protected with a single-strand rappel on one 30 m rope off natural gear since no fixed anchor has been reported. Below the step, the gully and talus lead into the west-face cirque near the Lewis Glacier's east moraine at about 6,400 ft, then talus and intermittent boot path south past Lewis Lake rejoin the trail near Heather Pass.
hazards: Loose, downsloping talus and scree for most of the off-trail traverse
The east face sheds rock as the day warms; cross the basin early and carry a helmet
Snow can linger in the Horsefly Pass basin and across the traverse well into July
One distinctly steeper class 4 step on the descent, with no fixed anchor reported
Glacier and snowfield travel past the Lewis Glacier remnant on the descent
Lake Ann is the last reliable on-trail water
